Merit Order · design notes

A gateway that spends less on every token

Merit Order is a self-hosted LLM gateway. Its job is to lower LLM spend for day-to-day use (coding agents such as pi and Claude Code, internal apps, SDKs) without users changing how they work.

Pre-production: version 0.0.1. Most of Merit Order is tested only against mocks of each provider's API, written from the provider's docs. What has been checked live, and what hasn't, is in What's verified below: OpenRouter, Anthropic and OpenAI, Claude Code sessions, the Docker Compose stack, GPUs on a local kind cluster and one SkyPilot replica on a Lambda GPU have been; the other providers, the rest of the GPU cycle on real clouds, Entra and Google sign-in, batch APIs and bills have not. Version 0.1.0 comes once the checks in the right-hand column pass (ROADMAP.md).

The name comes from power grids. Operators dispatch generators in merit order: the cheapest marginal cost first, with expensive "peaker" plants switched on only when demand needs them. Merit Order does the same with tokens. When steady load justifies it, your own GPUs become the cheap baseload. API endpoints are always available as the peakers that cover spikes and everything else. The router sends every session to the cheapest capacity that meets its quality bar.

It does three things:

  1. Routes each session to the cheapest model and backend that meets the task's quality bar.
  2. Runs open-weight models on your own GPUs (SkyPilot, Kubernetes, or servers you run) when sustained load makes that cheaper than paying per token, and turns them off when it doesn't. API endpoints (Bedrock, Vertex AI, Foundry, ...) are always on, as the fallback and the overflow.
  3. Saves tokens with provider prompt caching, cache-aware routing, careful compression and batch prices.

Around that: sign-in (Entra, Google Workspace, generic OIDC, SCIM), budgets and hard safeguards, a savings ledger that shows what every request would have cost without the gateway, and a web console to watch and control all of it: spend, savings, where every GPU runs and what it costs, and the switches to stop it.

Also one page per doc: start with the overview or how it all works.

Six ideas behind the design

  1. Marginal cost, not list price. A GPU that is already running is a sunk cost for that hour, so its spare capacity is close to free. Use it, even for a better model than the task needs.
  2. Moving a session costs money. Prompt caches live on the backend. Switching backends means paying again for the whole context, so the router counts that before moving anything.
  3. The harness owns the conversation. By default the gateway stores routing metadata (hashes, timestamps, which backend), never conversation content. The exceptions are opt-in or explicit: the response cache, the Responses API's stored mode, and batch files held (sealed) until a provider or GPU takes them.
  4. APIs are the floor, GPUs are an optimization. Every model that runs on your GPUs should also have an API route, so GPUs never become a single point of failure. The console warns about any model that doesn't before anyone stops its GPUs.
  5. Clone and run. docker compose up gives you a working gateway: on mock backends with no keys, on real ones with a single key. GPUs, sign-in and Kubernetes are opt-in layers.
  6. Every cost is visible next to the switch that controls it. Anything that spends money (a team, a GPU, the whole organization) shows what it costs and can be capped or stopped from the console.

Glossary

Term Meaning
Harness The client driving the model: pi, Claude Code, Cursor, an SDK app
Session One conversation or agent run; the unit of stickiness and caching
Backend A configured place models run: anthropic, bedrock, openrouter, or your own GPUs (gpu-qwen-coder)
Route One model on one backend, with its price; a model can have several
Level What a request sent with model: "auto" needs, per kind of work, 1 to 5 (coding:3); set from its wording and tools, never its length. Also called the quality floor (X-Route-Floor)
Score A model's quality for a kind of work, 1 to 5, from published benchmarks (Epoch AI by default) or measured with meritorder eval
Headroom Spare capacity on a running GPU replica before it misses its latency target
Shadow price The internal price for self-hosted tokens: about 0 when idle, rising toward the API price as the replica fills
Rebuild cost The cost to process a session's context again on a backend whose cache is cold
Counterfactual cost What a request would have cost on the baseline model (baseline_model, set for the organization or a team) at its API price
Ledger One row per request: who, which model and backend, tokens, cost, counterfactual cost and savings by cause; never content

How it all works (start here)

Merit Order sits between your tools and the model providers. Your tools keep speaking the API they already speak; Merit Order translates when the chosen model speaks another. For every request sent with the model name auto, it asks two questions:

  1. How hard is this? The request gets a level for its kind of work: coding or general, 1 to 5, from what it asks for, never from how long it is.
  2. What's the cheapest model that's good enough? Every model has a score for each kind of work, 1 to 5. Models scoring at least the level, with room for the conversation, qualify, and the cheapest of those wins, counting the whole rest of the conversation, not just this request. By default a dearer model wins only where its better chance saves more than it costs in what a failure would put at stake: on easy work (levels 1 and 2, questions, short chats) that's almost nothing, so the cheapest qualifying model goes; on hard work a person's time counts (section 5).

Everything else in this document is detail on those two questions: how tools connect, where the levels, scores and prices come from, what "cheapest" really means, how long conversations are handled, what happens when something fails, and when your own GPUs are worth switching on. The numbers come from the shipped configuration and its price list (config/prices.json) on 11 and 12 November 2026. Prices and scores refresh on their own, so yours will drift.

A request that names a model (claude-opus, gpt-sol, …) skips both questions: it always gets that model, and Merit Order only chooses where to run it (section 10).

1. Your tools connect as they are

Point a tool's base URL at Merit Order and give it a Merit Order key. Nothing else about the tool changes, because Merit Order speaks both common APIs:

Your tool speaks For example Merit Order endpoint
Anthropic Messages Claude Code, Anthropic SDKs /v1/messages (and /v1/messages/count_tokens)
OpenAI Chat Completions pi, Cursor, OpenAI SDKs, most other tools /v1/chat/completions
OpenAI Responses Codex CLI (over WebSocket, chaining on its connection); with a team's stored mode, clients that chain turns (Microsoft Agent Framework, the Agents SDK's previous_response_id) /v1/responses (HTTP and WebSocket), /v1/responses/compact, /v1/responses/input_tokens, and /v1/conversations in stored mode
Embeddings RAG pipelines /v1/embeddings
Batches: work that can wait a day, about half price (near free on GPUs that are running with room) OpenAI and Anthropic SDKs, meritorder batch /v1/files + /v1/batches, /v1/messages/batches

The model's own format is Merit Order's problem, not the tool's. Each provider speaks one of the two formats. When the tool and the chosen provider speak the same one, the request passes through untouched, so provider features such as Claude's cache markers and thinking signatures survive. When they differ, Merit Order converts the request, the reply and the stream both ways: messages, tool calls, images, streaming, usage and stop reasons. Two things don't cross: a model's reasoning from earlier turns (each turn still works; the model just thinks again), and temperature/top_p, which current Claude models reject. The Responses API is converted to Chat Completions inside the gateway; GPT models that need the Responses API for tools with reasoning are converted on the way out, and so are Gemini backends that use Gemini's native API (api: gemini, for thought summaries, cached-token counts and why a reply was blocked).

The model name says what you want:

  • auto: Merit Order chooses (the rest of this document). A one-line question goes to the cheapest model that meets level 1, and "write unit tests" from an agent to the cheapest at coding level 2 (section 13).
  • A model's name or one of its aliases: that model. Aliases cover the names tools already send, so claude-sonnet-5-5, anthropic/claude-sonnet-5.5 and sonnet all mean Claude Sonnet.
  • Anything else: an error saying the model isn't configured.

The gateway doesn't keep conversations, with one opt-in exception. Tools send the whole conversation every turn, and Merit Order keeps only routing metadata. A team can turn on stored mode for the Responses API (Config → Teams, with a retention it must choose): then clients may send only their new input with previous_response_id or a conversation, and the gateway holds the conversation, sealed, and rebuilds the whole of it every turn, so auto still picks the cheapest model for each turn (Caching and sessions: stateful APIs).

GET /v1/models lists auto and every model your team may use, with each one's context window.

Every reply says what happened, in headers: X-MeritOrder-Model (the model that answered), X-MeritOrder-Backend (the provider), X-MeritOrder-Session and X-MeritOrder-Request-Id, X-MeritOrder-Floor (the level, for auto), X-MeritOrder-Max-Tokens and X-MeritOrder-Max-Tokens-Source, X-MeritOrder-Failed-Over when a provider failed first, X-MeritOrder-Refused-By when a model refused first, X-MeritOrder-Substituted-For when a named model was replaced, and X-MeritOrder-Queued when it waited for a full GPU. Replies that aren't streamed also carry X-MeritOrder-Cost-Usd, X-MeritOrder-Baseline-Usd and X-MeritOrder-Savings-Usd. The console's Reports → Requests tab shows the model, provider, level and cost of every request, and why it got that level and model. Setting up Claude Code and pi is in section 11.

2. Every request gets a level

The level is how demanding the work is. It's worked out from the request itself, with simple rules and no model call, so it's instant and free:

The request Level
Plain text general 2
Plain text, and the whole request is under ~400 tokens: a question on its own general 1
Plain text with words like analyze, compare, plan, strategy, trade-offs, evaluate or reason general 3
Any tools, or text that looks like code (code fences, def, import, stack traces, file names, "refactor", "bug", SQL, …) coding 3
Coding with simple wording and nothing harder (write tests, rename, typo, lint, docstring, explain, bump a version, …; not "quick fix") coding 2
Coding with "hard" wording (race condition, security, performance, migration, concurrency, multi-file, "under load", flaky, …) one level higher for each sign, two at most; at most 5
Coding with the hardest wording (architecture, "design a…", system design, prove, codebase-wide refactor, …) coding 5
A new prompt that says the last answer was wrong ("that's wrong", "still not working", "revert", …) one level higher, at most 5

Tools say the work is coding; the task's wording says how hard. A coding agent such as Claude Code or Codex sends dozens of tools with every request, whether it was asked to fix a typo or to redesign a service, so the number of tools doesn't set the level (it did until decision 61, which made every agent task level 4 or 5; agent_by_tools: true brings that back). Words are looked for in the text of the last two messages a person wrote (anything pasted into them included), not in tool results, and not in what the harness adds to them (Claude Code's system reminders with your CLAUDE.md, Codex's AGENTS.md): a user message made only of tool results or of that text is passed over. Where the lists overlap, the hardest wins.

Length never raises the level. A long conversation isn't harder work; it needs a model with room for it. So its length only rules out the models whose context window can't hold it plus the reply (section 7), and the cheapest of the rest wins. The one place length counts is the short question, and there it can only lower a level.

Clients can take over: X-Route-Floor: coding:4 sets the level exactly, and X-Route-Hint: cheap or smart moves it one level down or up. Every auto response says what it got (X-MeritOrder-Floor).

What that means in practice:

Request Level
"What's the capital of Portugal?" general 1
"Draft a reply to this customer email" (pasted) general 2
"Compare these three vendor proposals" general 3
"Why does this function return None?" with a code block coding 3
A coding agent (40 tools) asked to "write unit tests for the date parser" coding 2
The same agent asked to "add a --dry-run flag to the deploy command" coding 3
The same agent, 300,000 tokens into that task coding 3, on a model whose window holds 300,000 tokens
The same agent asked to "fix the race condition in the scheduler" coding 4
The same agent asked to "design a plugin system for the importers" coding 5

A task keeps its level. The level is set when a task starts (a new session, or a new prompt from the person) and holds for every request of the task, so the model and its cache stay put while the agent works. A task that proves harder than its wording goes up at the next prompt, never mid-task: a prompt that says the answer was wrong is one level up, and the learned router and the outcome report (opt-in) learn from fix loops and failing tests which work needs more.

Claude Code's side jobs get lower levels. Claude Code labels each request (when its hint headers are on; section 11): a turn of the conversation, a subagent's turn, the summary it writes when it compacts a long conversation, or a side request such as a session title or summary. Those last two don't need the level of the work itself, so auto caps them:

Claude Code request Highest level
Side request (titles, summaries) 1
Compaction summary 3
Conversation or subagent turn not capped

An explicit X-Route-Floor is never capped. Auto mode's permission checks name Claude Sonnet, so they never go through auto at all. The caps are under Config → Routing → Claude Code request types.

A learned router can correct the rules (opt-in; off by default). It learns from your own traffic which requests are harder or easier than the rules say: each request's words (hashed, never stored as text) and facts such as its tool count, and what followed the answer: the same request sent again, a raised X-Route-Floor, a stopped answer. In shadow mode it only records what it would have chosen, and Reports → Learned router shows where it disagrees with the rules, what that would cost, and the outcomes; in route mode its level is used when it's sure (at least 80%, routing.learned.min_confidence), and the rules decide whenever it isn't, has no model, or its model is stale (older than 30 days, max_age_days). It never second-guesses an X-Route-Floor. Train it with meritorder router train. Details: Routing: the learned router.

A team can also give it judged labels (off by default, per team, with a monthly cap that has no default): a small sample of its requests (1%, and only while the learned router is on) is replayed on a stronger model in the background, and a judge model from another family says whether the answer each one got was good enough. That sends those prompts and answers to two more models, and the console says so, and shows the expected monthly cost, before it can be turned on. Only the verdict is kept. Details: Routing: judged labels.

The rules are settings, and everyone can see them. Reports → Levels shows each rule, its word lists, and the models good enough for each level that your team may use. Reports → Requests shows why each request got its level: the rule, and which listed word it found (never the text around it), for example classified coding:4 (coding: 40 tools; hard wording (race condition): +1). Admins change the levels, the short-question size, the word lists, and whether a tool count makes an agent (Python regular expressions, matched ignoring case) under Config → Routing → How requests get a level (routing.levels). A rule that can't work is refused when the configuration is saved: a level outside 1–5, a pattern that isn't a valid regular expression, one that matches empty text and so every request, or patterns that don't combine into one (inline flags such as (?i); case is already ignored).

3. Every model gets a score for each kind of work

A score says how good a model is at a kind of work, against a fixed bar. It isn't typed in: the worker works it out once a day from published benchmarks.

What a score means. By default (source epoch), each model's score is based on its chance of solving a task as hard as FrontierSWE, a set of real, hard software-engineering tasks. A 5 is a fixed chance, the anchor: what the best model, Claude Fable 5.2, solved when the scale was fixed (69.9% for coding and 76.9% for general work, on 12 November 2026). Every model scores in proportion to it: 5 × its chance ÷ the anchor, at most 5, at least 1. One that solves 60% as many such tasks scores 3.

Model Chance on a FrontierSWE-hard task (coding) Coding score General score
Claude Fable 5.2 69.9% 5.0 5.0
Gemini 4 Carbon 61.2% 4.4 4.3
GPT-6.1 Terra 58.2% 4.2 * 3.8
GPT-6 Astra 57.7% 4.1 4.1
Claude Opus 5.5 57.2% 4.1 4.0
Claude Sonnet 5.5 54.8% 3.9 3.5
Gemini 4 Argon 47.3% 3.4 3.5
GPT-6.1 Sol 44.3% 3.2 4.0
Claude Haiku 5.5 40.7% 3.0 † 2.1
GPT-6 Luna 31.5% 2.3 1.3
Gemini 3.8 Flash 24.3% 1.7 1.7
Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite 4.8% 1.0 * 1.0

Why a fixed bar. Until 15 November 2026 the best model you had was the 5 (scale: best). So a new, stronger model lowered every other model's score though none of them got worse, and the same work moved to dearer models with each release. A new model with a 95% chance would have taken GPT-6.1 Terra from 4.2 to 3.1 and Claude Fable from 5.0 to 3.7, leaving only itself at level 4: every agent turn would have gone to it. With the fixed bar, a new model scores 5 if it beats the anchor, and nobody else's score moves (decision 58).

* Estimated from the model's general ability: no coding results published yet. † Set by hand (quality_override). Epoch's refit of 12 November 2026 put it at 2.9, just under level 3, which would send ordinary coding to GPT-6.1 Terra at about ten times the price; our own coding evals had it pass 14 of 15 hard tasks.

Where the numbers come from. Epoch AI (CC BY 4.0) places every model on one ability scale, fitted across about 40 benchmarks, and every benchmark on the same scale by difficulty. That's what makes models comparable even when they were tested on different benchmarks, and lets a model's ability be turned into a chance of solving tasks of a given difficulty. For coding, a model's own results on FrontierSWE and FrontierCode refine its general ability, so coding strength counts; results at the effort auto uses for hard work are preferred where published. A model with neither those results nor a place on the scale (some open models) gets its coding score from older coding benchmarks (Terminal Bench, GSO, MirrorCode); they come last because they predict FrontierSWE results less well than the scale does.

The alternative source is the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index (needs ARTIFICIAL_ANALYSIS_API_KEY). It's a single number per model, so coding and general get the same score. The third option is scores written on each model by hand (config), for example from your own eval runs (Evals).

Two choices shape the scores (Config → Routing → Quality scores):

  • Scale. absolute (default): a 5 is the anchor (quality.anchor, 0.6994 for coding and 0.7685 for general work), and the rest in proportion; a new model, weak or strong, changes nobody else's score. best: the best model is 5 and the rest in proportion, so each stronger release lowers everyone else. range: the weakest model with data is 1 and the best 5, which depends on which weak models you happen to have configured. A change of scale or anchor takes effect at once: the scores are worked out again from the stored chances.
  • Reference task. A harder reference spreads models further apart and sends more work up the ladder. Against Remote Labor Index (real paid remote work, which Fable solves 37% of the time), Opus would score 2.8 for general work, and ordinary level-3 work would go only to Fable. FrontierSWE keeps level 3 within reach of models like Sonnet.

Models the source doesn't cover aren't picked by auto: a score nobody measured would compete with measured ones, and because the cheapest qualifying model wins, an optimistic guess would win. They still answer requests that name them. To put one back, give it a quality_override (Config → Models), which always wins over the source; that's also how to record that your own evals disagree with the benchmarks (Models → Evals → Apply scores… → Write as override). Measured scores use the same 1–5 scale, so the Evals page shows them beside the ones in use. On 12 November 2026, 10 open models weren't covered, among them Qwen3 Coder Next, Devstral 2 and both MiMo models (Qwen3 Coder has a 1.0 for coding, from older coding benchmarks). The Models page lists them.

Hover a score on the Models page to see how it was worked out, and the model's chance of solving work at each level (used when routing by cost per success, section 5).

4. Which models qualify

A model qualifies for a request when:

  • its score for that kind of work is at least the request's level. A level-3 coding request can go to any model with a coding score of 3.0 or more; level 5 means FrontierSWE-hard work, which today only Fable meets;
  • the conversation, plus room for the reply, fits in its context window (section 7). This is what a long conversation changes: it narrows the models, never raises the level; and
  • the team is allowed to use it (Config → Teams → allowed models and backends).

With expected total cost (the default) or cost per success (opt-in), both at the end of section 5, a model below the level can qualify too, when its chance of solving work at that level is at least 60%.

5. The cheapest qualifying route wins

Each qualifying model has one or more routes: the providers that serve it (Anthropic, Bedrock, Vertex, OpenRouter, your own GPUs, …). Merit Order prices every route and picks the cheapest.

Prices are live. The worker refreshes them every 15 minutes: OpenRouter routes from OpenRouter's catalog, direct provider APIs from the price list LiteLLM maintains, cross-checked against each other. Long-prompt prices apply (Claude Haiku 5.5 costs five times as much above 100,000 prompt tokens), and a price change, a list that can't be fetched, or two lists that disagree raises an alert.

"Cheapest" means the rest of the session, because in a conversation each turn resends everything before it, and providers charge far less for the part they still have cached:

cost of a route = rebuild + expected turns × cost per turn

rebuild       = what it costs to get this conversation into the provider's cache:
                zero if this provider already holds it, else the context at the write price,
                less the cache-read price the first turn already counts
cost per turn = the cached part at the cache-read price
                + the new tokens at the write price: what the conversation grew by since its
                  last turn, or about 2,000 for a new session
                + about 600 output tokens at the output price
write price   = the input price, where the provider caches on its own (OpenAI, Gemini, most others);
                for Claude, where caching is explicit, the cache-write price; on a backend set to
                keep its cache an hour (cache_ttl_seconds: 3600), the 1-hour write price from a
                session's second turn (its first turn, rebuild included, is written for 5 minutes)
expected turns = the turns so far, kept between 3 and 30 (a long session will probably keep going)

The four Claude backends in the shipped config (Anthropic, Bedrock, Vertex AI, Foundry) are set to an hour. A session's first turn there is written for 5 minutes, as the gateway sends it, so the rebuild and the first turn cost the same as on Claude through OpenRouter, which keeps the 5-minute default. From the second turn the router prices their writes at Claude's 1-hour write price (twice the input price, against 1.25 times for 5 minutes). What the hour buys is counted too: a later turn that comes after a pause of 5 to 60 minutes finds a 5-minute cache gone and writes the conversation again, and an hour's still there. The router expects such a pause on the share of later turns your sessions have shown (by team, leaning on the organization's share and, with little data, on one turn in ten), and adds that share of a rebuild to each later turn on routes whose cache lasts under an hour (decision 60). At one turn in ten, a new Claude Haiku session is cheaper on the direct backends than on OpenRouter, so it goes there at the default cost priority. Where sessions rarely pause, the hour's premium wins again and OpenRouter is the cheaper start. Here's what that gives for a new coding session at level 3, 30,000 tokens in, with pauses on one later turn in ten:

Model (route) Score Rebuild Per turn 3 turns
Claude Haiku 5.5 (Anthropic, Bedrock, Vertex, Foundry) 3.0 $0.0032 $0.0008, then $0.0010 $0.0060
Claude Haiku 5.5 (OpenRouter) 3.0 $0.0032 $0.0008, then $0.0011 $0.0064
GPT-6.1 Terra (Azure, OpenAI) 4.2 $0.027 $0.006, then $0.009 $0.051
Gemini 4 Argon (Vertex, OpenRouter) 3.4 $0.053 $0.013, then $0.018 $0.102

And for a level-4 agent task (hard wording, such as "fix the race condition"), 80,000 tokens in:

Model (route) Score Rebuild Per turn 3 turns
GPT-6.1 Terra (Azure, OpenAI) 4.2 $0.074 $0.009, then $0.016 $0.116
Gemini 4 Carbon (Vertex, OpenRouter) 4.4 $0.148 $0.018, then $0.033 $0.231
Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic, Bedrock, Vertex, Foundry) 4.1 $0.374 $0.038, then $0.044 $0.499
Claude Opus 5.5 (OpenRouter) 4.1 $0.374 $0.038, then $0.075 $0.562

The "then" columns are the later turns: on the direct Claude backends at the 1-hour write price; elsewhere with a tenth of a rebuild for the pauses.

Sessions stay put. Once a session is on a route, the rebuild is already paid there, so moving it must save at least 10% plus $0.01 over the rest of the session. Within a task (while the tool is sending tool results back, before the next prompt from a person) the session keeps its model outright. In practice a session moves only when a new task starts and something is clearly cheaper, its cache has expired, the conversation was compacted, it no longer fits (section 7), or its model is busy or down on every route (section 8). That's what keeps a session from bouncing between Bedrock and Anthropic and paying to rebuild each time.

How long a cache lasts depends on the route. On Claude it's as long as the request's last cache marker asked: when the gateway adds the markers (the client set none), 5 minutes after a session's first turn and an hour from its second on a backend set to an hour. A client's own markers keep their own lifetime. Other backends use their cache_ttl_seconds (5 minutes by default, 10 for the shipped GPU deployments).

A session can hold several conversations. Claude Code sends its subagents' turns and its side requests under the main session's id. Each keeps its own routing state (model, level, cache), so a subagent never resets the main conversation's; budgets, the per-session spend limit and reports still count the session as one.

Near-ties go to speed. The same model often costs the same everywhere (Claude on Anthropic, Bedrock and Vertex), so price alone can't choose. Routes within a small margin of the cheapest compete on measured speed: 2% under the default cost priority (where a better model among them goes first), 20% under balanced, 100% under speed. A team or a single request (X-MeritOrder-Priority) can choose differently. Every 10th new session may try a route within that margin whose speed is unknown or out of date, so speeds stay known.

Unpriced routes are never used: an unknown price must never look free. auto passes them by, and a request that names a model with only unpriced routes gets a 503 saying so (GPU routes excepted: they're charged by GPU time).

Or: the cheapest per solved task. The threshold treats a model just below the level as useless, though it solves nearly as much. With model_choice: cost_per_success (Config → Routing, or per team; off by default), auto picks on expected cost per solved task instead:

  • Each model gets a chance of solving work at the level from its score. One exactly at the level solves it as often as a 5 solves FrontierSWE-hard tasks (the anchor: 69.9% for coding); better models more, weaker ones less.
  • A failed try is still paid for, and the work is then redone on the model the threshold would pick: expected = cost + (1 − chance) × (that model's cost ÷ its chance).
  • In the first example above, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash (coding 2.4: a 62% chance at level 3) costs $0.0018 a try and $0.0018 + 38% × $0.0086 = $0.0051 per success, against Claude Haiku's $0.0060 a try (on the direct backends) and $0.0060 ÷ 70% = $0.0086 per success. It wins.
  • A model whose chance at the level is under 60% is never picked (min_success_chance), so a nearly free model that usually fails can't win. A client's X-Route-Floor keeps the threshold, and so does a model without a chance estimate.
  • Warm caches, stickiness and the speed tie-breaks work as above, on the expected cost per success.

Every rule: How it decides.

Or: the lowest expected total cost to finish the task. A redo costs more than tokens: someone notices the answer was wrong, says so and waits. With model_choice: expected_cost (the default since decision 62; per team too), auto counts that:

  • Each model's expected cost is its try, plus its chance of failing times the person's cost a failure puts at stake, and with the cascade on, the next attempt: the same model again or a stronger one from a cold cache, whose chance is lower after a failure.
  • The person's cost (human_cost_usd, $1 by default: a minute at $60 an hour, set per team on Controls) is for a failed level-5 agent task. Each level below 5 puts a third as much at stake (level 3: a ninth, level 1: 1/81), and a request under 8,000 tokens proportionally less, because a re-asked question costs seconds and a failed agent task minutes. After a correction ("that's wrong") the request counts as level 5 (decision 67). So level 1 and 2 work, questions and short chats go to the cheapest model that meets the level, as with the threshold.
  • The chance comes from the benchmark at the task's difficulty and, once it has learned from your outcomes and beaten the benchmark on tasks it wasn't trained on, from a fitted layer: calibrated to what your traffic counts as success, with each model's own record, and offsets for your team, repository and project.
  • In the first example, a 30,000-token coding:3 task at a $1 person's cost puts $0.11 at stake: Claude Haiku tries for $0.0060 with a 70% chance (~$0.055 expected with a redo); GPT-6.1 Terra for $0.051 with 82% (~$0.07). Haiku goes first. A level-5 task at 90,000 tokens puts the whole dollar at stake, and goes to Gemini 4 Carbon ($0.26 a try, 62%) rather than Claude Fable ($1.07, 70%).
  • With the cascade on (routing.cascade.max_escalations: 1; off by default), inside the task, if tests keep failing after edits (three failed runs in a row), or the person says "that's wrong", the task's model's chance drops, and the task moves to a stronger model when continuing would cost more: on Haiku, a failing run and "that's wrong" take it from 70% to 24%, and continuing (~$1.00, the request now counted at level 5) loses to escalating to Terra (~$0.28, its cache rebuilt there); three failed runs alone (41%) aren't enough at level 3. A new prompt that's harder than the task is a new task at its own level. At most once or twice per task, never down inside a task, never past the team's models or a budget that's 90% spent. The failed attempt's cost is charged against routing savings, once.

On the routing simulator it spends 60% less per finished task than the threshold, no more than the threshold on any kind of work, and finishes 0.2 points more (03). Every rule: How it decides; why: decisions 62 and 67.

6. Then: effort and output length

Reasoning effort follows the level, so every model works the same way for the same work (their own defaults differ): low for levels 1–2, medium for 3, high for 4–5. A model that doesn't take that effort keeps its default. The effort is set once per session on a model, because changing it would invalidate the prompt cache. A client's own effort setting always wins; one sent in Anthropic's format (Claude Code sends one) to a GPT or other OpenAI-format model goes over at the nearest level that model takes.

Output length isn't capped by a guess. A request without max_tokens may write as much as the model can (128,000 tokens for current Claude and GPT models), less what wouldn't fit in the context window, under the per-request cost limit (Controls), or within what a provider's prepaid balance covers. Only when the model's maximum isn't known does it get default_max_tokens (16,000). A client's own max_tokens is kept (lowered only to the model's maximum). The response says how much it got and why (X-MeritOrder-Max-Tokens, X-MeritOrder-Max-Tokens-Source).

7. Context windows: long conversations

Every model has a context window: the most a conversation plus its reply can hold. The windows come from the live price data, refreshed with the prices:

Window Models
about 1 million tokens Claude (all), Gemini, DeepSeek, GLM, Kimi, MiniMax, MiMo, Muse Spark, Mistral Large 4, Qwen3.8 Flash, Nemotron 3.5 Super
922,000 GPT-6 and GPT-6.1 (Astra, Sol, Terra, Luna)
524,288 Llama 4 Maverick
500,000 Grok 4.7
262,144 Qwen3 Coder (all three), Devstral 2, Mistral Small 4, Ministral 14B, Gemma 4 31B, Nemotron 3 Ultra
131,072 gpt-oss-120b, gpt-oss-20b

Two parties decide what happens as a conversation grows: the tool, which decides when to compact (summarize the history and start over from the summary), and Merit Order, which decides where the conversation can still go.

What Merit Order does:

  • Models without room drop out, and that's all length does. For auto, a model isn't a candidate when the conversation plus the reply the client asked for (its max_tokens; Claude Code asks for 32,000) fills its window past 95%. The conversation is counted in that model's tokens (below), and the 5% is a margin for what the count still gets wrong and for the reply when the client leaves its length to the gateway. The level stays what the work gives it (section 2), and the cheapest model at that level with room wins. A 300,000-token conversation never goes to gpt-oss or Qwen3 Coder; most qualifying models have about a million tokens, so something nearly always fits. The routing reason names the models ruled out, their windows and how the count was made, for example ruled out gpt-oss-120b (131,072): window too small for about 300,000 tokens plus a 32,000-token reply (estimate ×1.08, calibrated from 210 replies) (Reports → Requests). Over 85% of a window that still fits, it says "context window check close" with the same detail.
  • Too long for every model at its level: it goes to the model with the largest window anyway (the count is an estimate), and the provider decides. A higher level wouldn't help: its models are a subset. If the provider refuses, the client gets "prompt is too long", which makes Claude Code compact.
  • A session that outgrows its model moves, even mid-task. The next turn goes to a model with room at the same level, paying once to rebuild the cache there.
  • A provider that says "too long" isn't the end. If a provider refuses a prompt as too long anyway (the estimate can be off), an auto request goes to a qualifying model with a bigger window. A request that names a model can't move; its error is worded the way Anthropic's API words it ("prompt is too long: …"), whichever provider refused, because that's what makes Claude Code compact.
  • The reply shrinks to fit. When a request doesn't set max_tokens, the reply may use what's left of the window and no more, so the provider doesn't refuse prompt plus reply (section 6).

How a conversation is measured. Merit Order can't run every provider's tokenizer, and the same text comes to different token counts on Claude, GPT and Gemini. So it estimates once, from what the text is made of: prose comes to about 4 characters a token, code and JSON about 3, hashes and base64 about 2, and Chinese, Japanese or Korean about one character a token. Images count the way the model's provider counts them, from the image's size (a 1000 × 1000 screenshot is about 1,330 tokens on Claude and 765 on GPT), not as the text of their bytes; PDFs count by their pages. Then the replies correct it: each reply reports the real prompt size, and Merit Order keeps a running ratio for each model, so after a few long prompts its counts for that model follow that model's tokenizer. A model that hasn't answered yet starts from the ratio of its family (other Claude models, other GPT models). The window check, the cost estimates and the reply's allowance all use the model's corrected count, and the Models page shows each model's ratio under its context window. The details are in Routing: counting tokens.

What the tool does. A tool compacts when the conversation nears the window it believes it has. /v1/models reports each model's window, and for auto the largest window among the models auto can pick for your team (1,048,576 tokens today). That's safe because models without room drop out: a long conversation narrows the choice to the million-token models instead of failing.

  • pi: meritorder setup pi writes each model's window into pi's model list.
  • Claude Code: it knows the windows of Claude models by name. For a name it doesn't know, such as auto, it assumes 200,000 tokens unless told otherwise; meritorder setup claude-code tells it the gateway's window (section 11).
  • Other tools: give them the window from /v1/models, or leave their default; a smaller window than the real one only means compacting earlier.

8. When something fails

Nothing reaches the client until the chosen route has started answering, so a failure moves the request on:

  • Over capacity, rate-limited, missing, or down: the next route in the cost ranking. For a named model, or a session in the middle of a task, that's another provider for the same model; for a new auto task, it's the next cheapest qualifying route, whatever its model. A request gets 3 tries at most (routing.max_attempts). An auto session whose model is busy or down on every route moves to another qualifying model at its next turn, even mid-task. The failing route is skipped for a while (the provider's Retry-After, or a growing back-off) and an alert says where its traffic went.
  • Too long for the model: for auto, a qualifying model with a bigger window (section 7).
  • The model refuses: for auto, the next qualifying model (the refusal is billed and logged; a team can turn this off with refusal_fallback: false); a named model's refusal is returned as it is.
  • A provider can't cover the whole reply on its prepaid balance: the same route again, asking for what it says it can pay for.
  • Budgets and limits: organization, team, person and session budgets, rate limits, and the per-request cost limit stop requests before they're sent, with a message saying which.

Every rule and timing is in How it decides.

Work that can wait can go through the providers' batch APIs at about half price, or run on your own GPUs for almost nothing while they're running with room. Each request of a batch is routed as above, among the routes whose provider has a batch API (at batch prices) and running GPU deployments (at their shadow price); the gateway splits the batch across providers and GPUs, reserves its estimated cost against budgets, and joins the results back. GPU work runs at low priority in the headroom only, and goes to a provider's batch API if it hasn't run in 12 hours; it never starts a GPU (Request flow).

9. Your own GPUs: when they start and stop

Power grids run the cheapest generators all the time (baseload) and switch on expensive ones (peakers) only for peaks. Merit Order does the same: your own GPUs, running an open model, are the baseload when there's enough steady work to keep them busy, and the APIs are the peakers that are always there.

A GPU deployment starts only when sustained demand pays for it. Every minute the controller asks: what does the traffic this model could serve cost me at API prices?

  • Traffic it could serve means requests whose level its score covers. A model with a coding score of 3.0 counts every coding request at levels 1–3, wherever it was actually sent.
  • At API prices means what you're paying for that traffic today.
  • One replica is worth starting when that spend, per hour, exceeds the replica's hourly price plus a 20% margin, continuously for 10 minutes. The number of replicas follows the throughput (enough to run at 70% load), as long as each one pays for itself by the same rule.

A replica's hourly price is SkyPilot's cheapest offer in the allowed clouds, or on your own Kubernetes cluster the price you set for its node type (kubernetes.node_types), or else the deployment's gpu_cost_per_hour. For example, the shipped gpu-qwen-coder deployment runs Qwen3 Coder Next on four H100s with a fallback price of $16 an hour. It starts once the work it could do would cost you more than $19.20 an hour at API prices for 10 minutes straight. The controller starts GPUs through SkyPilot on cloud GPUs, or through KServe or llm-d on your cluster.

While it runs, it's the first choice. A GPU you're already paying for costs almost nothing per token while it has room, so the router prices it at 2% of the API price up to 60% load (routing.shadow_floor, routing.shadow_knee), rising with the square of the load to the full API price at 100%. Up to the knee it wins every request it qualifies for; past it, the APIs win more and more of the work, and at 100% new work spills to them. Requests that only went to the GPU because it had room (a better model than the level needed) don't count as demand, so idle capacity can't keep itself alive.

A session goes back to the replica that holds its cache. Each GPU replica has its own prompt cache, so a conversation's next turn goes to the replica that served its last one, unless that replica is full, gone, or busy enough that rebuilding the cache on an idle one costs less. Whether the cache is still there comes from vLLM's cache events where they're turned on, otherwise from an estimate of how much the replica has written into its cache since.

It stops when demand no longer pays for it. When the work it could do drops below break-even for 10 minutes, and it has been serving at least 30 minutes (hold_minutes), it drains: no new sessions, existing ones finish, and after 15 minutes (drain_minutes) the GPUs are released. If demand comes back while draining, it simply stays. Starting takes 10–20 minutes for a big model, and traffic stays on the APIs meanwhile, so the delays and margins are there to avoid paying for start-ups that don't last. A start that fails, or isn't ready within 45 minutes, is shut down and waits 30 minutes before the next try.

The GPUs page shows these states by the names above (in the API and logs: api_only, provisioning, warm, draining). An admin's pin starts a deployment at once, and a stop either drains it or stops it at once.

A self-hosted model needs a score. Demand is counted by level, so a model the quality source doesn't cover has none, and its GPUs never start for auto traffic. On 11 November 2026 that's the case for Qwen3 Coder Next: give it a quality_override (Config → Models) to have the controller consider it. Its window (262,144 tokens) also means a conversation goes to the APIs once it and the reply the client asks for are over 95% of it, about 249,000 tokens: with Claude Code's 32,000-token replies, conversations over about 217,000.

Whether a GPU can ever pay shows on Models → GPU break-even. Each open-weight model gets a machine whose GPUs hold its weights (sizes from Hugging Face), priced from SkyPilot's catalog, spot or on-demand, across the clouds SkyPilot covers: of those, the one that pays from the least traffic. The weights can be served as published, in FP8, or in 4 bits; quantizing changes what fits, not the quality scores, so measure a quantized model with an eval before trusting its level. For each quality level and each model it shows the traffic one replica needs (tokens per minute and about how many requests an hour), your busiest hour of that traffic, and what the replica can serve. The price a GPU has to beat at a level is the cheapest API model good enough for it, because that's where auto would send the work otherwise.

On 11 November 2026, with spot prices, only level-1 work could pay: gpt-oss-20b on one L4 ($0.12 an hour) from about 72,000 tokens a minute. The best level an open model could host was 2: Kimi K3.1 (coding 2.7), published in 4 bits, fits on eight B300s. Level 3 starts at Claude Haiku's 3.0, and quantizing doesn't change that, because the strongest open models already ship in 4 bits. Get latest prices has SkyPilot download its catalogs again.

A running GPU is spend whether it's busy or not. The 2% shadow price is for choosing where a request goes; it isn't what the GPU costs. Reports count the GPU at its hourly price for every hour it runs, starting and idle included, and the self-hosting savings are the API cost the GPU's requests avoided less that. A GPU up all day for a handful of requests shows as a loss: $1.62 of GPU time against $0.002 of API calls is "saved −$1.62", not "−95%". Teams are charged their requests' shares of the GPU; the rest is the organization's, shown as "GPU idle, unallocated" (08).

Admins can also stop a deployment (draining first or at once), pin a number of replicas, stop all GPUs, or cap GPU spend per month, per hour, or in replicas (GPUs page and Controls). Details: GPU autoscaling.

10. Requests that name a model

A request for claude-opus gets Claude Opus, never another model. Merit Order still picks the route: the cheapest of Anthropic, Bedrock, Vertex, Foundry and OpenRouter for the rest of the session, with the same stickiness, speed tie-breaks and failover between them. If none of its routes can run, the request fails with the reason for each, unless the team allows substituting a model at least as good. A named model is never skipped for its window: a conversation it can't hold gets the provider's error, worded so Claude Code compacts.

Claude Code sends Claude model names unless it's set to auto, so by default it gets exactly what it asks for; meritorder setup claude-code sets it to auto (section 11).

11. Setting up Claude Code and pi

Log in once (meritorder login, or meritorder use-key with a key from an admin), then:

meritorder setup claude-code     # Claude Code
meritorder setup pi              # pi

Claude Code isn't tied to Anthropic or Foundry: any gateway that speaks Anthropic's API can stand in via ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL, and Merit Order does. The setup command writes these into Claude Code's settings file ($CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR/settings.json, or ~/.claude/settings.json):

Setting Value Why
ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL the gateway Send every request to Merit Order
apiKeyHelper reads ~/.config/meritorder/api_key Your Merit Order key; logging in again rotates it
model auto New sessions let Merit Order choose (--model claude-sonnet-5-5 picks one; --model none leaves Claude Code's choice)
CLAUDE_CODE_MAX_CONTEXT_TOKENS the gateway's window for that model Claude Code would otherwise assume 200,000 tokens for auto and compact early
ANTHROPIC_CUSTOM_MODEL_OPTION, ANTHROPIC_CUSTOM_MODEL_OPTION_NAME auto, auto (Merit Order) Adds "auto (Merit Order)" to the /model picker
CLAUDE_CODE_GATEWAY_HINT_HEADERS 1 Claude Code labels side requests and compaction only when asked (section 2)

With --model set to a Claude model name, it leaves out the window and /model settings (and removes earlier ones): Claude Code already knows those names.

It changes every Claude Code session that uses that settings folder. To keep Merit Order in a separate profile (for example, away from work that uses another account):

meritorder setup claude-code --config-dir ~/.claude-meritorder
CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR=~/.claude-meritorder claude

What to expect:

  • Billing. With the Merit Order key, Claude Code doesn't use your claude.ai login for these requests: subscription limits don't apply, and the cost is per token on the providers' accounts behind the gateway.
  • Non-Claude models. auto can send Claude Code's turns to GPT, Gemini or open models, translated. It works, but Anthropic doesn't support running Claude Code on non-Claude models, so expect rough edges.
  • Cost display. Claude Code's own cost figure guesses prices for a name it doesn't know (a test request it showed as $0.038 cost $0.0096). The gateway's numbers (My usage page, meritorder usage) are the real ones.
  • Reply length. For a model name it doesn't know, Claude Code asks for up to 32,000 output tokens per reply. CLAUDE_CODE_MAX_OUTPUT_TOKENS raises it (to 128,000 at most); Merit Order lowers a request to the chosen model's own maximum when that's smaller.
  • Effort. Claude Code sends its own reasoning effort (its /effort setting), and a client's setting always wins, so the per-level effort (section 6) doesn't apply to its turns.
  • A startup line [claude-code:unrecognized_model] {"model":"auto"} is informational.
  • Subagents each get their own routing thread within the session (section 5), and their own level.

pi gets a "Merit Order" provider listing auto and every model with its context window, sends its session id so sessions stay on the backend that holds their cache, and adds cache markers that survive translation. Codex CLI: meritorder setup codex adds a meritorder provider to ~/.codex/config.toml (or $CODEX_HOME, or --config-dir) on the Responses API over WebSocket, starting on auto with its context window, the key read from the key file. Codex then sends each turn's new items only, and the gateway rebuilds the rest from the connection (04). Other OpenAI-compatible tools need only the base URL (<gateway>/v1) and the key.

13. What auto does today

auto routes by expected total cost (section 5, the default since decision 62, with what a failure puts at stake since decision 67). For a new session on the price list of 12 November 2026, with nothing learned from your outcomes yet and the default $1 person's cost: level 1 goes to GLM-5.3 Flash (or DeepSeek V4.1 Flash on a long prompt), coding level 2 ("write tests", "fix the typo") to DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, general level 2 to Claude Haiku 5.5 (DeepSeek V4.1 Flash for a short one, cheaper than the threshold's pick and just below the level). Ordinary coding (level 3) goes to Claude Haiku 5.5 (DeepSeek V4.1 Flash past about 80,000 tokens), general level 3 to Claude Haiku 5.5 rather than GPT-6.1 Terra, agent work (level 4) to GPT-6.1 Terra, and the hardest coding (level 5) to Gemini 4 Carbon rather than Claude Fable. Below a level, a model goes only where its chance there is at least 60% (10).

With the threshold (model_choice: threshold), the cheapest qualifying model for a typical request at each level, on 11 November 2026:

Level Coding General
1 GLM-5.3 Flash, gpt-oss-20b GLM-5.3 Flash, gpt-oss-20b
2 DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, GPT-6 Luna, Claude Haiku 5.5 Claude Haiku 5.5
3 Claude Haiku 5.5 GPT-6.1 Terra
4 GPT-6.1 Terra Gemini 4 Carbon or GPT-6.1 Sol (the same price; Carbon scores higher, so it goes first)
5 Claude Fable 5.2 only Claude Fable 5.2 only

Level 1 also goes to free models (Gemma 4 31B, Nemotron 3 Ultra) when the opt-in OpenRouter free tier is on (MERITORDER_ALLOW_FREE_MODELS=true).

A Claude Code or Codex task on auto gets the level of its wording: "write tests" or "fix the typo" is coding 2 (DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, GPT-6 Luna or Claude Haiku 5.5), ordinary feature work and bug fixes coding 3 (Claude Haiku 5.5), hard wording ("fix the race condition", "optimize this query") coding 4 (GPT-6.1 Terra), and the hardest ("design a plugin system") coding 5 (Fable), however long the conversation grows. Past about 840,000 tokens a level-4 task moves from Terra (a 922,000-token window, less the margin and Claude Code's 32,000-token replies) to the cheapest level-4 model with a million-token window. Its titles and summaries go to level-1 models, and compaction summaries to level-3 models at most.

That's the threshold. With cost per success (section 5), on the price list of 12 November 2026, ordinary coding (level 3) goes to DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, and level-5 coding to Gemini 4 Carbon: $0.85 per success against Fable's $1.53 for a 90,000-token agent turn with hard wording. General level 2 goes to DeepSeek V4.1 Flash and general level 3 to Claude Haiku 5.5. Level-4 coding stays on GPT-6.1 Terra.

14. Known gaps

  • The level rules are word lists. They're visible (Reports → Levels) and adjustable (Config → Routing), but a listed word sets a coding task's level whatever it's about ("security" in "update the security page's footer" makes it level 4; "rename" in "rename the service across the codebase" would be level 2 but for "across the codebase"), and a task described in other words gets the ordinary level 3. A client that knows better can send X-Route-Floor or X-Route-Hint.
  • A compacted conversation is levelled again from the summary. Claude Code puts its summary of the conversation in a user message, so the summary's words can set the next task's level, often higher than the task had.
  • The learned router learns from weak signals. It's off by default, and in shadow mode changes nothing. Most answers get no signal at all (nobody resends a fine answer, but nobody marks a bad one either), the signals it has are partly about clients rather than the work, and it assumes the rules are right on average, so it can move requests between levels but can't tell that every level is too low (exploration can: below). Coding agents add stronger signals from what the gateway already sees: tests failing after the last edit, a broken build, fix loops, and a "that's wrong" or "revert" in the next prompt. A model is used only if it beats the rules on requests it wasn't trained on, and how well it does on real traffic is what the shadow report is for. Judged labels (opt-in per team) add a label that says "good enough" or not, at a price and by sending sampled prompts to two more models; how well a judge's verdicts match what people do is measured, not assumed, and they've only been tested against mocks.
  • Whether a level is too high or too low is measured only where you explore. Exploration (opt-in per team, off by default) sends about 4% of a team's task starts one level down or up at random, never mid-task, never for a named model or a client's floor, never past the team's models or a nearly spent budget. Reports → Levels compares how often each succeeds, weighted by each arm's chance, and recommends a change once each side has 200 task starts; an admin applies it, or the worker does when the learned router agrees. A model that becomes the cheapest at a level is tried first on a share of the level's work (a canary), and an alert says so. Until a team explores, the report shows the served level only. Tested against mocks.
  • Some scores are estimates. A model without published coding results gets a coding score from its general ability (marked * on the Models page), and published results come from runs at different efforts.
  • Expected total cost rests on assumptions. It's the default; the threshold (the cheapest model at or above the level) is simpler to predict. Its chances at each level are read from the quality scores, not measured level by level, until the fitted layer has learned from your outcomes; failures are taken as independent, though a task one model fails is likely harder for the next; and what a failure puts at stake (a third as much for each level below 5, less under 8,000 tokens) was tuned on the routing simulator, not measured on real failures. The minimum chance (60%) stands in for some of that. Cost per success (opt-in) shares these assumptions and doesn't price a person's time. GPU demand is still counted by the threshold: work a self-hosted model could take below its level doesn't count towards starting its GPUs.
  • Token counts for routing are estimates, corrected per model by its replies (section 7). A model that hasn't answered any long prompts yet, or a conversation unlike its usual ones (a long Korean document in a session of code), can still be off near the limit, and an image given by URL is counted at the largest size. A provider's "too long" is the backstop, and when it says the prompt's real size, that corrects the model's ratio too.
01

Architecture

The processes

Every process is the same meritorder command (and the same image, except the compressor's). The gateway, worker and controller follow the stored configuration in Postgres, so a change saved on the console reaches all of them; the compressor takes only its command-line flags.

Process Command Needs How many
Gateway meritorder serve (port 8080; MERITORDER_PORT) Nothing for a trial (in-memory storage); Postgres and Redis for anything shared As many as you like; --workers N (or MERITORDER_WORKERS) for more processes on one machine, which needs Postgres and Redis
Migrations meritorder migrate Postgres Once per upgrade (Compose's migrate service; the chart's migrate Job, migrations.enabled)
Worker meritorder worker (a cycle every 60 s, --interval; --metrics-port, or MERITORDER_WORKER_METRICS_PORT, for its /metrics) Postgres (it refuses to start without it), Redis One or more: batch jobs and eval runs are claimed with a lease, so several share them
Capacity controller meritorder controller (every 60 s; --interval) Postgres (it refuses to start without it), Redis; SkyPilot or a Kubernetes cluster for the GPUs it runs One active: the others wait on a Postgres advisory lock. Compose's gpu profile; the chart's controller.enabled
Compressor meritorder compressor (port 8090) The compressor extra (LLMLingua-2, torch); its own image Optional. Compose's compressor profile, the chart's compressor.enabled; gateways call it at MERITORDER_COMPRESSOR_URL

Without Postgres there's no worker. A gateway on in-memory storage then checks its own batches every 15 seconds and deletes stored responses past their retention itself.

Inside the gateway

Every request passes through the same pipeline (the code is Gateway.handle and Gateway._handle in proxy.py):

A /v1/responses request is converted to Chat Completions first (in a team's stored mode, rebuilt from the stored chain), so everything after the API surface sees one shape. 02: Request flow follows one request through these steps.

What each box owns

Component Owns Does not own
Harness The conversation, history, compaction (except Responses API clients in a team's stored mode) Which backend serves it
Gateway Auth, policy, routing decisions, prompt shaping, metering; splitting batches across the providers' batch APIs and running GPUs, and joining their results; in a team's opt-in stored mode, the Responses API conversations its clients chain, sealed, for the team's retention Conversation content otherwise (never stored, except in the opt-in response cache, batch uploads until they're submitted, and batch work for GPUs until it runs and its results until retention ends, all sealed, in Postgres or the operator's bucket)
Redis Session metadata, spend and rate-limit counters, published GPU state and controls, each gateway's in-flight counts, backend health, the live feed, compression decisions (by content hash), notes on which GPU replica holds a session's cache, people's Google groups as last read, opt-in response cache Anything that must survive a flush (a missing spend counter is seeded again from the ledger)
Postgres People, keys, SCIM groups, config versions, admin GPU controls, live prices and quality scores, token calibration per model, the ledger (partitioned by month) and hourly rollups, providers' bill lines, GPU cost per hour, GPU activity log, eval runs, the learned router's request features (hashed, no content) and models, batches (their provider jobs and one metadata row a request), stored responses and conversations of teams in the Responses API's stored mode (content sealed with AES-GCM) Hot-path lookups (cached in-process / Redis)
ClickHouse (optional) A copy of the ledger and its hourly rollup, for reports over long ranges and tag breakdowns at very large scale The record: Postgres has every row first, and budgets read Postgres
Worker Rollups for reports, monthly partitions, budget and spike alerts, weekly digests, price refreshes (every 15 min), quality-score refreshes (daily), providers' bills to check the ledger against (every 6 hours), eval runs started on the console, training the learned router (when asked or scheduled), the providers' batch jobs (polled until they end, then settled into the ledger), batch work on running GPUs (in their headroom, at low priority; its own /metrics for the batch requests it settles), stored responses past their team's retention (deleted every minute) and sealing them again after a key rotation, the ledger's copy in ClickHouse (every 30 s, when set up) Requests
Capacity controller "Should model X be running on GPUs right now, and how many replicas?", admin controls, GPU safeguards, GPU cost Per-request routing
Compressor (optional) Running LLMLingua-2 on the tool results a gateway sends it (POST /v1/compress) Which results to compress, and remembering the cuts: the gateway decides and keeps them in Redis
SkyPilot Launching one cluster per replica on any cloud, failing over across regions and clouds for capacity, setting the machine up (image, port, disk, labels), autostop, teardown, catalog prices How many replicas run, which one gets a request, replica health, cost decisions
KServe or llm-d (on your cluster) Running the vLLM pods Merit Order asks for, replacing failed ones How many to run, prices (configured per node type)
KServe's Service, or llm-d's endpoint picker Which replica gets a request when the gateways can't address pods (llm-d's: the one with the most of the prompt cached). SkyPilot replicas have none in front: the gateway picks Which model
Web console Watching and controlling everything (served by the gateway at /ui/) Anything the APIs can't do: it's built only on them
vLLM / SGLang Inference, continuous batching, prefix (KV) cache Anything else
API backends Inference + their own prompt caches; batch jobs and their results until they're deleted Which of them gets a request

Why it's split this way

  • Gateway is stateless so it scales horizontally behind any load balancer and can be restarted freely.
  • Controller is separate because its decisions are slow (minutes) and the gateway's are fast (milliseconds). The controller only changes what exists; the router only chooses among what exists.
  • GPU pool is optional. With no GPUs configured, the system is a cost-aware API gateway, and still useful. A vLLM/SGLang server you already run can be added without SkyPilot (provisioner: static), and a Kubernetes cluster with GPUs can run vLLM through KServe or llm-d (provisioner: kubernetes).

Backend adapters: pass-through first

Merit Order has its own adapter layer instead of depending on LiteLLM (see 09: Decisions, decision 2). It stays small because almost every backend speaks one of two formats:

Format Backends
Anthropic Messages Anthropic, Claude on Bedrock (its Anthropic-compatible endpoint), Claude on Vertex, Claude on Foundry
OpenAI-compatible OpenAI (through its Responses API: api: responses), Azure OpenAI, Gemini on Vertex AI (its OpenAI-compatible endpoint, or Gemini's native API: api: gemini), the Gemini API (native: api: gemini), OpenRouter, xAI, DeepSeek, Mistral, Moonshot, Z.ai, MiniMax, vLLM, SGLang, most others
Later, if needed Bedrock Converse
  • Pass-through keeps fidelity. Fields we don't recognize (cache_control, thinking signatures, encrypted reasoning, provider extras) reach the backend exactly as the harness sent them. That is what keeps prompt caching working.
  • Translation is one pair of converters (OpenAI Chat Completions ⇄ Anthropic Messages), unit-tested in both directions, streams included. The Responses API is converted to and from Chat Completions at the edges: for clients that call /v1/responses, and for OpenAI backends set to api: responses. Gemini's native API is converted the same way, at the backend, for backends set to api: gemini (below).
  • Provider auth uses official libraries: botocore for AWS request signing, google-auth for Vertex, azure-identity for Entra ID (Foundry, Azure OpenAI).
  • Long tail: any OpenAI-compatible endpoint is a valid backend. Anyone who needs a niche provider can run LiteLLM (or anything else) themselves and register it as a backend, out of process.

Gemini's native API

Gemini also answers on OpenAI-compatible endpoints (Vertex AI's, OpenRouter's), but those drop or flatten what Gemini's own API reports. A backend with format: openai and api: gemini calls generateContent and streamGenerateContent?alt=sse instead, while the rest of the gateway keeps seeing Chat Completions (formats/gemini_upstream.py, GeminiBackend in backends/http.py):

Where Config Auth
The Gemini API base_url: https://generativelanguage.googleapis.com/v1beta auth: {type: api_key, header: x-goog-api-key, value_env: GEMINI_API_KEY}
Vertex AI flavor: vertex, project, region (global by default) auth: {type: google}, as for Claude on Vertex

The shipped config has both: gemini, on once GEMINI_API_KEY is set, and vertex-gemini-native, off until MERITORDER_VERTEX_GEMINI_NATIVE=true (on Vertex, the OpenAI-compatible vertex-gemini stays the default for now). A route's model is Gemini's id (gemini-4-carbon); google/… and models/… work too. Prices come from LiteLLM's list (gemini/… for the Gemini API, vertex_ai/… for Vertex), like any direct provider API.

Chat Completions Gemini
system / developer messages systemInstruction
user / assistant messages contents with roles user / model; consecutive turns of one role merged
images, audio, files (data: URLs) inlineData; image URLs become fileData
tools, tool_choice functionDeclarations (the JSON Schema as parametersJsonSchema), toolConfig.functionCallingConfig (AUTO, NONE, ANY, allowed names)
assistant tool_calls, tool messages functionCall and functionResponse parts, matched by id and named after the call they answer
max_tokens, temperature, top_p, stop, seed, penalties generationConfig (maxOutputTokens, temperature, topP, stopSequences, …)
response_format (JSON schema or object) responseMimeType: application/json and responseJsonSchema
reasoning_effort thinkingConfig.thinkingLevel, fitted to the levels each model takes (Gemini 4 Hydrogen alone takes xhigh; Gemini 4 and 3.8 Flash have no minimal; Gemini 3 and 4 can't stop thinking). Gemini 2.5 gets a thinkingBudget. Thought summaries are always asked for (includeThoughts): they cost nothing extra. A model that only thinks when asked (Gemma, Gemini 2.0) gets a level only for an effort other than none

Replies and streams come back as Chat Completions: text, function calls, thought summaries as reasoning_content, and usageMetadata as usage (cached tokens from cachedContentTokenCount; thinking counts as output, and is also shown as reasoning_tokens). Finish reasons:

Gemini says The gateway sees
STOP (tool_calls when the reply calls functions), MAX_TOKENS stop / tool_calls, length
A blocked prompt (promptFeedback.blockReason), or SAFETY, RECITATION, PROHIBITED_CONTENT, BLOCKLIST, SPII, … content_filter with a refusal saying why: a refusal, which auto retries on another model
MALFORMED_FUNCTION_CALL, MALFORMED_RESPONSE An error (502): the request goes to the next source
MISSING_THOUGHT_SIGNATURE An error (400), returned to the client
PUP_LIMITED_DISABLED (the Google account is restricted) 403: the next backend
HTTP 429 (RESOURCE_EXHAUSTED) and 503 (UNAVAILABLE) Capacity: the request moves on, and that model is skipped on that backend for a while (after a 429, for the retryDelay Google gives in the error's details)

Gemini 3 and later return a thought signature with each step's first function call and reject a request whose current-turn call comes back without one. The signature rides on the tool call as extra_content.google.thought_signature, the convention of Google's own OpenAI-compatible endpoint, so a client that sends messages back as it got them keeps Gemini's reasoning between tool calls (an OpenRouter reasoning_details signature is used too). A call with none (a client that rebuilt its history, a translated Anthropic request, a call another model made) is sent with Google's documented bypass value, so the request still works; the model just reasons afresh.

Building blocks

Need What we use Later, maybe
API model prices, context windows and output limits Live: OpenRouter's public catalog and the price list LiteLLM maintains, refreshed by the worker every 15 minutes (fetched as data; no code from either); costs checked against each provider's own cost data
GPU prices SkyPilot's catalog (per cloud, region, instance, spot/on-demand), checked against the AWS, Google Cloud and Azure bills by instance tag; on Kubernetes, a configured price per node type Reconciling Kubernetes GPU time with the cloud bill
