02

Request flow

One turn of a pi session using model="auto" (meritorder setup pi points pi at the OpenAI Chat Completions API).

Hot-path budget

The gateway should add single-digit milliseconds before the first byte goes upstream. Everything on the hot path is in-memory or one Redis round trip:

Step Where it reads from
Key validation In-process cache (60 s), Postgres on miss
Rate limit / budget Redis counters (a missing spend counter is seeded from the Postgres ledger)
Session lookup Redis, in the same round trip as the counters
GPU state and headroom Published to Redis by the controller; each gateway reloads deployment state every 5 s and reads utilization with the session
Token estimate In-memory: one pass over the request's text (sampled above 256K characters, about 5 ms for 4 MB), corrected per model by this process's calibration
Classifier Rules; only on new sessions and task boundaries
Learned router (opt-in) In-memory, pure Python, at the same points: hashing the ends of the latest prompt and six dot products, about 0.4 ms at the p99 on a long agent prompt. Its row (hashed features, no content) is written with the ledger row, after the response
Judged labels (opt-in per team) At the team's sample rate (1%): a reference to the request's body is held, and the answer kept as text once it's complete. After the response, in the background, the replay on a stronger model and the judging run as requests of their own (the team's internal client, judged-labels:<team>); the client never waits. Only the verdict is written (03)
Compression The rules: deterministic and in-memory. Model-based: one Redis round trip for every result's stored decision; a result new on this turn waits for the compressor service at most the team's deadline_ms (1,000), then goes as it is

Writes to Postgres (usage, ledger) are async and never block the response.

What the harness sees

Nothing unusual. Same API it already speaks, streamed tokens, usage numbers. Response headers tell curious users what happened:

x-meritorder-model: qwen3-coder-next          # the model that answered
x-meritorder-backend: gpu-qwen-coder          # where it ran
x-meritorder-floor: coding:3                  # what the classifier decided (auto)
x-meritorder-session: 3f9c…                   # the session it was counted under
x-meritorder-request-id: 6b1e…                # find it in the ledger
x-meritorder-cost-usd: 0.000400               # non-streaming responses: cost,
x-meritorder-baseline-usd: 0.031000           #   what it would have cost without Merit Order,
x-meritorder-savings-usd: 0.030600            #   and the difference
x-meritorder-max-tokens: 128000               # the reply's output allowance,
x-meritorder-max-tokens-source: model         #   and where it came from (client, model, context, …)
x-meritorder-failed-over: openai/gpt-6.1-terra 429   # only when a source failed first
x-meritorder-refused-by: claude-opus          # only when a model refused and another answered
x-meritorder-substituted-for: qwen3-coder     # only when a named model couldn't run (opt-in)
x-meritorder-queued: 1                        # only when it waited in a full GPU deployment's queue
x-meritorder-dropped-tools: web_search        # hosted or server tools this backend went without (Responses, Messages)

x-meritorder-refused-by and x-meritorder-failed-over list every model or source that was tried first, comma separated. A request refused for a budget or the per-session cap (429) carries x-meritorder-limit: budget, so a client can tell it from a rate limit, which carries retry-after instead.

The whole decision, rule by rule, is in 10: How it decides.

A chained Responses API turn (stored mode)

For a team with stored responses on (04, decision 51), a client of OpenAI's Responses API can send only its new input with previous_response_id. This is where the gateway holds conversation content: sealed in Postgres, for the team's retention. The turn is rebuilt into the stateless request it amounts to before anything else happens, so the pipeline above runs on it unchanged.

The client's input is stored as it sent it, before compression, so the next turn rebuilds the same history and compression's stored decisions apply to it the same way. A stream is kept just before its response.completed event goes out, since a client may chain the moment it sees it. If keeping it fails, the client still gets the answer (a non-streamed one says store: false) and meritorder_stored_responses_total{event="failed"} counts it. Conversations (conversation) work the same way, from the conversation's items, and add the turn's input and output to it. background: true keeps the response as queued and answers at once; the same steps run in that gateway, and the client polls GET /v1/responses/{id}.

What Where Until
Each stored response: the object as the client got it, and the input sent with it Postgres (stored_responses), sealed with MERITORDER_RESPONSES_KEY retention_days after the chain's last turn, or the response, its owner, or their team's stored mode is deleted
Each conversation's metadata and items Postgres (stored_conversations, conversation_items), each sealed retention_days after it last changed, or it or its owner is deleted
Owner, chain, status, where it ran, the provider's response id, item ids, sizes the same rows, in the clear with them
A provider's copy (backends with responses_store only) the provider (OpenAI: at least 30 days) deleted there when the gateway deletes its own

A Responses API turn over WebSocket

Codex CLI keeps one WebSocket open to /v1/responses (04, decision 54) and, from its second turn, sends only the new items with previous_response_id. Without stored mode the gateway holds the conversation for the connection only, in memory, and each turn becomes the stateless request it amounts to, so the pipeline above runs on it unchanged.

A previous_response_id that isn't this stream's latest gets previous_response_not_found, and Codex sends everything. In stored mode a stored response chains as in the section above, from any connection. Closing the connection drops what it held and stops a running turn (ledger status 499).

Responses API tools on any backend

A Responses API turn becomes a Chat Completions request inside the gateway, and from there goes to any backend. Plain function tools carry over as they are. The other kinds, which Codex CLI sends, are translated both ways (formats/responses_tools.py, decision 57), as OpenAI's Responses reference and Codex CLI's source (codex-rs, 15 November 2026) define them:

Responses tool On a Chat Completions or Claude backend The model's call comes back as
custom (freeform), e.g. apply_patch with its Lark grammar A function tool with one string argument, input. The description says to put the raw text there, and carries the grammar custom_tool_call with the raw input, streamed as response.custom_tool_call_input.delta and .done
namespace (Codex's collaboration, MCP servers) One function tool per tool inside, named namespace__name (mcp__github__create_issue for a namespace ending in _), the namespace's description first function_call with its namespace and own name
tool_search with execution: "client" A function tool with the same parameters; the tools a search finds join the request's tools from then on tool_search_call with its arguments
local_shell A function tool taking the exec action (command, timeout_ms, working_directory, env, user) local_shell_call with that action
additional_tools input items (Codex's "Responses lite" mode) Tools, merged with tools; a later definition replaces an earlier one as above
Hosted: web_search, image_generation, file_search, ... Claude (not on Bedrock) gets live web search as its own server tool (web_search_20250305, with the allowed domains and the user's location). Everything else is left out, named in x-meritorder-dropped-tools and logged: Codex's default search, cached-only (external_web_access: false), among them Claude's search runs inside its reply; the answer comes back as text

History converts the same way: custom_tool_call, local_shell_call and tool_search_call items become the assistant's tool calls, with their arguments written as compact JSON, and their outputs become tool messages. The same input gives the same bytes on every turn, so the prompt cache reads the conversation's prefix. A tool output's images (Codex's view_image) can't go in a Chat Completions tool message, so they follow the turn's tool results as a user message; Claude wants its tool results first in a turn, so that order suits both. A backend with api: responses gets the tools and the items as the client sent them, additional_tools merged into tools, since the public API takes tools there. Over WebSocket a turn has no response headers: the log line is all that says a tool was left out.

Translating between API formats

When the client and the backend speak the same API, the request passes through untouched. When they don't, formats/translate.py (Chat Completions and Anthropic Messages), formats/responses.py (the Responses API, on top of Chat Completions) and formats/responses_upstream.py (Chat Completions to a backend with api: responses) convert the request and the reply. The tests check each direction against the official openai and anthropic Python SDKs: the streams accumulate in the SDKs' own stream handlers and the objects validate as the SDKs' types (tests/test_api_fidelity.py). Followed: Anthropic's Messages, PDF support, tool use, thinking and preserved thinking docs, and OpenAI's Chat Completions and Responses references, November 2026.

Nothing the request carries is dropped without a word: content goes across in the other API's own form, or the request is refused with a 400 that says why.

Content Anthropic client, OpenAI-format backend OpenAI client, Claude backend
PDF A document (base64 or URL) becomes a file part. A base64 PDF goes as a data:application/pdf URL in file_data; a URL goes as the URL in file_data, which OpenRouter fetches (OpenAI's own API takes only base64 or an uploaded file, and says so with its own 400) A file part becomes a document: a PDF data URL as base64, a URL as a URL source, base64 PDF without a data URL when the filename ends in .pdf, and a plain-text file as a text document. filename becomes the document's title
A file the other provider can't open A document or image from Anthropic's Files API (source.type: file): 400 A file_id (a file uploaded to OpenAI), or a file that isn't a PDF or text: 400
Responses input_file Becomes a file part (file_url goes as file_data), so it reaches Claude as a document; a backend with api: responses gets it back as input_file, with file_url again
Images in a tool result A tool message takes text only: the images and documents follow the run of tool messages as a user message ("Images returned by tool call …"), and the tool message says they follow. The same as a Responses tool output's images (above) Images in a tool message's parts become image blocks in the tool_result
System prompt in blocks Joined with a blank line between blocks, so sections don't run together. On Claude through OpenRouter, blocks with a cache_control marker stay separate parts and keep the marker Text blocks, as they are
cache_control on a block Kept on the part it was on, with the client's lifetime, on Claude through OpenRouter (which reads part-level markers); the gateway then adds no marker of its own. Left out elsewhere, where it would be an unknown field Kept on text parts
Server tools (web search, bash, code execution…) Only Claude runs them: left out, named in x-meritorder-dropped-tools and logged
Forced tool choice any becomes "required", a named tool becomes that function; disable_parallel_tool_use becomes parallel_tool_calls: false "required" becomes {"type": "any"} and a named function {"type": "tool", "name": …}, with parallel_tool_calls: false as disable_parallel_tool_use. Claude Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5, Fable 5.1 and 5.2 and Mythos 5.1 and 5.2 refuse a forced choice on every request, as does any model with manual (enabled) thinking (FORCED_TOOLS_REFUSED). There the choice becomes auto, and a line at the end of the system prompt says to call that tool (or one of the tools), which is what Anthropic suggests for those models. The others, Opus 5 and Haiku 5.5 among them, take the forced choice and answer it without thinking first
Thinking Dropped: no Chat Completions field carries a signed thinking block back

Replies:

Claude backend, OpenAI client OpenAI-format backend, Anthropic client Chat backend, Responses client
Stop reason refusal becomes content_filter, tool_use becomes tool_calls tool_use whenever the reply called tools, also when the provider ended it with stop (Gemini's OpenAI endpoint and some vLLM parsers do). A refusal becomes text with stop_reason: refusal content_filter and length end the response incomplete (content_filter, max_output_tokens)
Refusal A refusal becomes a refusal content part, streamed as response.refusal.delta and .done. A content_filter stop with nothing said gets a refusal part saying the provider's filter stopped the response
Usage Claude's output_tokens_details.thinking_tokens becomes completion_tokens_details.reasoning_tokens input_tokens_details has cached_tokens and cache_write_tokens; output_tokens_details.reasoning_tokens is the provider's count
An error in the stream The error chunk, then [DONE]: no finish chunk after it The error event ends the stream: no message_delta or message_stop after it error, then response.failed with the error; no response.completed

Either way the ledger records the failure (status 400 or more), and a stream that broke off is costed as in 08.

Claude across platforms. Failover can move a session between Anthropic's API, Bedrock and Vertex AI, which all take the same Messages API. The gateway sends thinking blocks back as they came, signatures included, wherever the turn goes: signatures work across platforms, a block the new platform's account or model can't read is dropped by the API for that request without an error and isn't billed, and removing blocks yourself would lose that reasoning for good and can break preserved thinking's prefix check. Blocks from Claude Sonnet 5.5, Haiku 5.5, Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 work only in the account that made them (on Bedrock the AWS account, on Vertex the Google Cloud project), so after such a move the model answers without them. The automatic cache marker (a top-level cache_control) is accepted on all three; only Bedrock's legacy bedrock-runtime integration rejects it for Opus 4.6 and earlier, and the gateway calls Bedrock's Messages API endpoint (bedrock-mantle), not that one.

/v1/messages/count_tokens refuses a model that isn't configured with a 404, as /v1/messages does; auto (or no model) counts for the models the team can use.

Batches: work that can wait

Every provider here charges less for requests that can wait up to 24 hours (about half): summarizing a backlog, labelling a dataset, nightly evals. A GPU deployment that's already running does them for almost nothing while it has room. Clients send them the way they would to the provider, and Merit Order routes each request on its own, splits the batch across providers and GPUs, and joins the results back.

Client Endpoints
OpenAI SDK (Batch API) POST /v1/files (purpose batch, JSONL), GET /v1/files, GET /v1/files/{id}, GET /v1/files/{id}/content, DELETE /v1/files/{id}; POST /v1/batches, GET /v1/batches, GET /v1/batches/{id}, POST /v1/batches/{id}/cancel. Lines may call /v1/chat/completions, /v1/responses or /v1/embeddings
Anthropic SDK (Message Batches) POST /v1/messages/batches, GET /v1/messages/batches, GET /v1/messages/batches/{id}, POST .../{id}/cancel, GET .../{id}/results, DELETE .../{id}
CLI meritorder batch submit FILE [--endpoint URL] [--watch], watch ID, list [--limit N], results ID [--out FILE] [--errors-only], cancel ID, storage (admins)

Both SDKs work unchanged (the tests drive them). Batch objects carry an extra meritorder field: the estimated cost, what's still reserved, what the results cost and saved (the batch discount, and what GPUs took off the batch price), and how many requests went to each provider or GPU; the create call's response also has x-meritorder-estimated-cost-usd. Each line can name a model or use auto. X-Route-Floor, X-Route-Hint and X-MeritOrder-Tags on the create call apply to every line.

Routing a batch

Each request is routed like a live one, with these differences: only routes whose backend has a batch API qualify, and running GPU deployments with room; provider routes are priced at batch prices for that one request (the prompt at the batch input price, plus its max_tokens, or the router's usual reply size when it sets none), and GPU routes at their shadow price for their load now; there's no session to keep warm; and speed doesn't count, since nobody is waiting. So a named model goes to its cheapest route, and auto gives the request its level, takes the models at that level the team may use, and picks the cheapest of their routes. Team policies (allowed_models, allowed_backends), the per-request cost limit (at batch prices) and cost per success apply as they do live. Rate limits and the per-session spend cap don't: they're for live load, and a batch isn't a session. Merit Order adds no cache markers to batch requests (there's no next turn to read them); the client's own are passed on. With the learned router on, a batch request is leveled as a new live task is (the learned level in route mode, when it's sure), but it records nothing for the router to learn from: no retry, raised floor or stopped stream can follow it (03).

A request that nothing allows is refused on its own, with the reason in the batch's error file (or as an errored result), and the rest go ahead; a batch where no request can go is refused outright. Refused requests never reached a provider, so, like a live refusal, they aren't in the ledger. Requests then go into jobs: one per backend, and per model where the provider takes one model a job (OpenAI, Azure, Moonshot, Mistral, OpenRouter, Gemini, Bedrock, Vertex AI), split within each provider's limits. A group smaller than a provider's minimum (Bedrock's 100 records) moves to its requests' next routes. A job a provider refuses moves to its requests' next routes once; what still can't go is refused with every route's reason.

Backend Batch API One job holds Takes embeddings Off the standard price Needs

*.openai.azure.com Azure OpenAI global or data-zone batch on the v1 API (/openai/v1/files, /openai/v1/batches) one deployment, 100,000 requests, 200 MB no (Azure lists no embedding model for its batch deployments) half a Global-Batch or Data-Zone-Batch deployment, named in the route's batch_model
api.mistral.ai Batch jobs: a JSONL file through its Files API, then /v1/batch/jobs one model, 1,000,000 requests, 512 MB yes half nothing more

openrouter.ai Its own: the requests inline, the results on the batch once it's done one model, 200 MB yes about half a model with a batch variant (others are refused, and their requests move to their next route)
The Gemini API (api: gemini) Batch mode: a JSONL file through the Files API, then models/{model}:batchGenerateContent, or for embeddings models/{model}:asyncBatchEmbedContent (one Gemini request per input, joined back into one reply per request) one model, 2 GB yes half nothing more
Bedrock Batch inference (CreateModelInvocationJob) with Claude's InvokeModel bodies one model, 100 to 100,000 records, 1 GB no half batch.bucket: s3://..., batch.role_arn (a role Bedrock assumes to read and write it), AWS credentials (SigV4), and the route's batch_model where batch inference takes another model id

batch.max_requests, max_bytes and min_requests on a backend override these, for a quota that differs; batch.discount changes the discount when the price list has no batch price. DeepSeek, Z.ai, MiniMax and Foundry's Claude have no batch API (DeepSeek's off-peak hours are a lower live price, not a batch API), so their routes are skipped for batches; the console's error for a model with none says why for each route.

Batch work on your GPUs

A GPU deployment that's running is paid for by the hour, whatever it does, so a request that can wait costs it almost nothing while it has room (05, 10). The router prices a batch request on a running deployment at its shadow price for its load now: 2% of the GPU route's price (its API-equivalent rate) while it's below the knee (routing.shadow_knee, 60%), rising toward the full price as it fills. Against the providers' batch prices (about half), a GPU with room wins, for the model the request names, or for auto a model at or above its level (a free upgrade, as live). A deployment that's full, draining, stopped or still starting isn't a route. The request's next route with a provider batch API is kept as its fallback, shaped for that provider at once, so the worker can hand it on without routing it again (Bedrock isn't a fallback: its jobs need 100 requests).

The requests can't wait at a provider, so the gateway holds them, sealed (below), and the worker runs them, a slice of a minute at a time while it holds the job's lease:

  • Only in the headroom. Batch requests fill a deployment up to the knee of max_concurrency × replicas, never past it, counting the gateways' live requests there and other workers' batch requests (each published to Redis every couple of seconds), and none while vLLM's own load, less the batch work it's running, is at the knee. So batch work never makes live traffic pay more than the shadow price's floor. Live routing doesn't count batch requests as load: they give way. A deployment without max_concurrency takes no batch work, since its free slots can't be counted.
  • Live traffic first. Each request goes to vLLM with priority: 20 (batches.gpu.priority; lower runs first), after free upgrades (10) and live requests (0). vLLM's priority scheduler preempts batch requests when live ones need the room.
  • Before the deadline. What hasn't run 12 hours after the batch was made (batches.gpu.handoff_hours) goes to its fallback's batch API (providers finish most batches in minutes to a few hours). So does everything still waiting when the deployment stops, starts draining or leaves the configuration, and a request the GPU refuses (a 4xx) or fails twice. A request with no fallback (a model only on your GPUs) waits for the GPU until the batch's deadline, then expires; one the GPU can't run fails with the GPU's error.
  • The client's deadline holds. A provider gives the handed-on job a fresh 24-hour window, which would end after the client's. So the worker checks a handed-on job again at the batch's deadline at the latest, cancels it there if it's still running, and what the provider hadn't run comes back expired (504), as from a provider whose window closed; what it ran is kept and billed. For that, a GPU's fallback is always a batch API the gateway can cancel: OpenRouter's has no cancel, so it's never one (the next route with a batch API is used, or none). Past the deadline nothing is handed on: what's still waiting for the GPU expires.
  • No GPU starts for it. Batch work doesn't count toward starting or keeping a deployment: the break-even controller sizes GPUs on live demand only, and batch work only uses what that pays for (decision 49).

One request held for a GPU, slice by slice (batches/gpu.py):

Each request settles as soon as it's run: its result is held, then its ledger row is written (service_tier: batch, backend the GPU), priced as live GPU work is, by the GPU time its tokens took at the deployment's hourly price. Its savings split in two: the batch discount, what a provider's batch API would have taken off the model's API price (the fallback's batch price, else the usual half), and self-hosting, what the GPU took off that batch price (negative if the GPU time cost more). What's reserved against budgets is the fallback's estimate, since the request may end up there. The batch object's meritorder.providers counts requests where they are now, so a handed-on request moves from the GPU to its provider.

Prices and spend

A route's batch price is the live price list's (LiteLLM's *_batches prices, cache prices included where listed), else the standard price less the provider's published batch discount (the table above; batch.discount changes it), or a price.batch written on the route for a negotiated rate. Long-prompt tiers move with the input price.

  • Reserved when submitted. The batch's estimated cost must fit every budget it counts against (organization, team, person), counting what's already spent and what running batches have reserved. A batch that doesn't fit is refused with 429, saying which budget and what's left. The estimate is then added to the month's spend counters, so live requests and other batches see it. A counter seeded from the ledger adds what running batches have reserved.
  • Settled from the results. The worker writes one ledger row per request when its job ends (service_tier: batch, batch_id), priced at the batch price the job was submitted at, and moves that request's estimate off the reservation. The row is stamped when it's written, so a job settled late (its results couldn't be read for a while) lands in the month whose spend counters count it, and in the hours the rollups look at again. GPU requests settle one by one, as they run. Failed, cancelled and expired requests get a row with their status (499 cancelled, 504 expired, else the provider's) and no cost. What's left of a reservation is released when the batch ends.
  • Savings. The batch discount is its own cause (savings_batch): the served model at its live API price less the same tokens at its batch price. Routing savings are counted against live prices, as for any request, so the discount never shows up as routing. A client using a provider's batch API directly would get the same discount, which is why it's kept apart. On a GPU, what the GPU took off the batch price is self-hosting's (savings_self_hosting), as for live GPU work.

What the gateway holds, and for how long

What Where Until
An OpenAI-style upload (the JSONL) Postgres (batch_file_chunks), or with batches.storage.bucket one object in your bucket; AES-GCM in 4 MB pieces, keyed by MERITORDER_BATCH_KEY its batch is handed on; or batches.retention_days (7) if no batch uses it
Anthropic-style requests to providers nowhere: they go from the request straight to the providers
Requests for a GPU, with each one's fallback Postgres (batch_blobs) or your bucket (held/), sealed the same way, in pieces of 500 the request runs on the GPU or is handed to a provider
Results of GPU requests the same place, sealed batches.retention_days after the batch ends
Each request's routing: its custom_id, model, backend, level and why, estimated cost, how it ended Postgres (batch_lines), never content as long as the batch's record
Results from providers at the providers (their output files and results), or in the backend's bucket (Bedrock, Vertex AI) batches.retention_days after the batch ends; then the worker deletes them there (OpenAI's files are also set to expire then; Azure's no sooner than its 14-day minimum; xAI has no delete, so its results stay under xAI's own retention)
Results on their way to a client, or into the ledger streamed through, line by line not kept

Without MERITORDER_BATCH_KEY a gateway on Postgres refuses uploads (503, saying why) and sends no batch work to GPUs (it goes to the providers); Anthropic-style batches to providers need no key. An in-memory gateway (development) uses a random key for the life of the process. Deleting an OpenAI batch's output or error file, or an Anthropic batch (DELETE /v1/messages/batches/{id}), deletes its results at the providers (and what's held for its GPU work) at once. Results a provider no longer has (Gemini's files last 48 hours) come back as errors saying so. A batch belongs to the person who made it: others get 404; admins can see and cancel it, but not read or delete its results.

In your bucket. batches.storage.bucket holds uploads and GPU work in an S3 bucket, a Cloud Storage bucket or an Azure Blob Storage container instead of Postgres, sealed all the same: large uploads stay out of the database, and the bucket's own retention and encryption rules apply on top. Requests are signed with the credentials the backends use: those of the backend batches.storage.backend names, else of the first enabled backend that signs in to that cloud (aws_sigv4, google, azure_ad), else that cloud's default credentials (the AWS chain, Application Default Credentials, Entra ID's for https://storage.azure.com/.default). A file uploaded before the setting changed is read from where it was put, as long as that's still the storage bucket (or Postgres); the console says how many are held elsewhere.

Rotating the key while uploads wait. Every sealed piece names the key that sealed it (an 8-byte id derived from the key, not the key). To rotate, set the new key in MERITORDER_BATCH_KEY and the old one in MERITORDER_BATCH_KEY_PREVIOUS (or batches.previous_key_file) on every gateway and worker. New content is sealed with the new key; what the old one sealed stays readable for batches.key_grace_days from when a gateway or worker first used the new key (recorded in the store, so all count from the same moment). The default is the retention period plus two days, the longest anything sealed before the rotation is kept (a batch's window, a fallback provider's, then retention), so nothing is lost if the old key is simply left set that long. After that the old key isn't read: content still sealed with it says so. Reports → Batches and meritorder batch storage show the key ids, until when the old one is read, and how many uploads still need it. Content from before key ids existed is tried with each key.

The worker

Jobs are claimed from Postgres with a lease per job (FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED, as eval runs are), so several workers share them, and one that dies mid-job hands it on when its lease runs out (15 minutes). The first check comes batches.poll_seconds (60) after a job is submitted, and the wait doubles while nothing changes, up to max_poll_seconds (1,800). Provider errors back off the same way, honoring Retry-After, and alert after five in a row. A job the provider no longer knows (404) fails its requests at no cost. The gateway gives a provider 20 minutes to take a job (counted from when it starts sending it, not while it waits its turn), then counts it as refused. A job still "submitting" 30 minutes after that start (the gateway stopped before the provider answered) fails too, and a provider job it may have made isn't tracked. Settling reads the results once, in chunks of 500, each in one transaction with its ledger rows, so a restart picks up where it stopped. A GPU job is worked on a slice at a time and asked again within seconds while it has requests and the deployment has room (15 seconds when it has none); the worker follows the GPUs' state as the gateways do, from what the controller publishes. Without Postgres there's no worker, and the gateway checks on its own batches every 15 seconds.

Metrics. The worker counts each request it settles in Prometheus counters of its own, meritorder_batch_requests_total (by model, backend, the API that ran it, and status), meritorder_batch_tokens_total, meritorder_batch_cost_usd_total, meritorder_batch_baseline_usd_total and meritorder_batch_savings_usd_total (by cause), plus meritorder_batch_gpu_requests_total, meritorder_batch_handoffs_total and meritorder_batch_poll_errors_total, served on MERITORDER_WORKER_METRICS_PORT (meritorder worker --metrics-port; 9464 in Compose and the Helm chart) at /metrics, behind MERITORDER_METRICS_TOKEN when it's set. Nothing is counted twice: a request is counted only by the call that settles it (the database marks it settled in the same transaction), and only in the batch counters, never in the gateways' live ones, so adding the two gives all spend (08). Without Postgres the gateway settles its own batches and serves the same counters on its /metrics.

Batch statuses, in OpenAI's words: in_progress, cancelling, finalizing (the providers are done; results are being settled), completed, cancelled (what ran before it stopped is kept and billed), expired (a provider, or a GPU for a request with no other route, didn't run everything in its window; what ran is kept and billed) and failed (no provider accepted it). Anthropic's processing_status is in_progress, canceling or ended. OpenRouter has no cancel: a cancelled batch there runs to its end, and what ran is billed.

Inside, a batch is in_progress, finalizing or ended with an outcome (batches/poller.py); the OpenAI and Anthropic objects are made from that. A batch whose jobs all end with nothing left to settle goes straight to its outcome.

Configuration

batches:
  retention_days: 7               # then results at the providers, in buckets and held for GPUs are deleted, and unused uploads
  key_env: MERITORDER_BATCH_KEY   # seals uploads and GPU work while they're held (or key_file)
  previous_key_env: MERITORDER_BATCH_KEY_PREVIOUS   # after a rotation, read for key_grace_days (or previous_key_file)
  key_grace_days: 9               # default: retention_days + 2
  poll_seconds: 60                # the first check; the wait doubles while nothing changes
  max_poll_seconds: 1800
  storage:                        # leave out to hold uploads and GPU work in Postgres
    bucket: s3://my-bucket/meritorder   # or gs://..., or https://<account>.blob.core.windows.net/<container>/<prefix>
    backend: bedrock              # whose credentials sign its requests; region: for S3 (default: that backend's)
  gpu:
    enabled: true                 # running GPU deployments with max_concurrency take batch work in their headroom
    handoff_hours: 12             # then what hasn't run goes to its fallback provider's batch API
    priority: 20                  # vLLM priority for batch requests (lower runs first)
backends:
  bedrock:
    batch: {bucket: s3://my-bucket/meritorder, role_arn: arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/bedrock-batch}
  vertex:
    batch: {bucket: gs://my-bucket/meritorder, region: us-east5}
models:
  gpt-terra:
    routes:
      - {backend: azure-openai, model: terra-prod, batch_model: terra-batch}   # its Global-Batch deployment

batch: {enabled: false} takes a backend out of batches (a GPU deployment too); batch.api names its batch API where the address doesn't say. Reports → Batches lists every batch with its status, counts, where its requests went (GPUs marked), estimated and actual cost and savings (admins can cancel there), and for admins where content is held and the key's state; the ledger and every report include batch rows, and Reports → Bills matches the providers' batch-tier lines.

Written from the providers' references, November 2026

Every provider call is tested against fakes shaped like the providers' API references as read on 13 November 2026: Anthropic Message Batches (anthropic-version as the backend sets it, else 2023-06-01), OpenAI's v1 Batch and Files APIs, Azure OpenAI's v1 API, Moonshot's batch guide (platform.kimi.ai), Mistral's batch API (and its Python SDK 3.7.0 for what the reference leaves out), xAI's batch API reference, OpenRouter's batch API guide, the Gemini API v1beta (batch mode and asyncBatchEmbedContent; the Python SDK 3.3.0 still calls batch embeddings experimental), Bedrock's batch inference API, Vertex AI v1, and the S3, Cloud Storage JSON v1 and Azure Blob Storage REST APIs (x-ms-version 2025-11-05). These still need checking with real accounts:

  • Anthropic: the content type of the results download (the SDK asks for application/binary).
  • OpenAI: whether cancelled requests come back in the error file as batch_cancelled (only expired ones are documented), and the exact shape of a request that failed with 4xx or 5xx (both shapes are read).
  • Azure: the batch's endpoint spelling on the v1 API (/chat/completions is sent; lines call /v1/chat/completions), the dotted expires_after.* form fields, Responses API lines, and its timestamps (some examples show ISO strings).
  • Moonshot: whether 24h is accepted as well as 1d (1d is sent), the per-file request limit (none is published), and how files are deleted (OpenAI's DELETE /v1/files/{id} is sent).
  • Mistral: the shape of a failed line in its error file (OpenAI's is read), and DELETE /v1/batch/jobs/{id}, which is in its SDK but not its reference (a 404 or 405 is fine).
  • xAI: which models are discounted (20% is assumed for every route without a listed batch price), and whether a batch with requests still pending after its expire_time reports them as cancelled.
  • OpenRouter: whether a batch variant is named by the plain model id (it's sent as the route's model, or batch_model), and the error type of an expired request.
  • Gemini API: whether output lines echo key, the shape of an error line, how long output files last, and for embeddings which token count a line carries (usageMetadata.promptTokenCount or tokenCount; either is read, else 0).
  • Bedrock: the S3 layout of the outputs (the gateway lists the job's folder), the recordId rules, and whether bedrock-mantle model ids are what batch inference takes (else set batch_model).
  • Vertex AI: Claude's output line format, and whether a Gemini request's labels (where the key rides) are echoed.
  • GPUs: that a vLLM server preempts priority: 20 requests for live ones as its priority scheduler documents (--scheduling-policy priority, which Merit Order's provisioners set; a static server without it refuses the field, and its batch requests go to their fallbacks).
  • Buckets: Azure's x-ms-date with an Entra token, and S3 regions other than the backend's (set batches.storage.region).

Looked at and not built: Bedrock's OpenAI-compatible batch API (on bedrock-runtime, for OpenAI's gpt-oss models only, which no Bedrock route here serves, with the same S3 input as batch inference); Vertex AI has no OpenAI-compatible batch endpoint (its batch prediction for open models takes OpenAI-format input lines, but its output format isn't documented); Azure's embeddings batches (its docs list no embedding model for batch deployments); Z.ai (its international API has no batch API; Zhipu's BigModel in China has one, at a different address), DeepSeek and MiniMax (none).

Not built: embeddings batch work on self-hosted GPUs; re-sealing held content with a new key (the grace period covers everything sealed before a rotation instead); Gemini batch embeddings on Vertex AI.

03

Routing

The router (src/meritorder/router.py) answers: which model, on which backend, for this request? (Every rule and default, as diagrams: 10, How it decides.) What it minimizes is a choice (routing.model_choice, per team too):

Choice Minimizes Counts a failure as
threshold Marginal cost: what this request and the rest of its session add to the bill now, among models whose score meets the task's level nothing: every model at the level is taken as good enough
cost_per_success The expected cost per solved task its tokens, then the work redone on the threshold's pick (below)
expected_cost (the default) The expected total cost to finish the task the person's time the request puts at stake (human_cost_usd for level-5 work, a third as much for each level below, less for small requests), and the next attempt: the same model again or a stronger one from a cold cache, its chance lower after a failure; inside a task, opt-in, escalation when the evidence says so (below)

All three keep the same floors, team policy, budgets and a client's X-Route-Floor, and the same marginal cost of each route (cache rebuild included) is what a try costs.

Decision flow

The quality floor

The classifier (classifier.py) gives each auto request a floor, a task type and a level from 1 to 5, from the work it asks for: the wording of the last two messages from the person (a user message made only of tool results, as in an Anthropic-format agent loop, is passed over), the tools it sends, and the client's X-Route-Floor or X-Route-Hint. The rules are routing.levels (defaults below), shown to everyone under Reports → Levels and edited under Config → Routing → How requests get a level.

Tools say the work is coding; the task's wording sets the level (decision 61). Claude Code and Codex send dozens of tools on every request, whether the task is a typo or a redesign, so a tool count says which client sent it, not how hard the task is. Until decision 61, five tools or more made a request level 4; every coding agent's task landed at 4 or 5, and the cheaper models never got the tests, renames and docstrings that make up much of an agent's day. agent_by_tools: true brings that rule back for a team that wants it.

Rule Setting (default) Floor
Plain text general (2) general:2
…and the whole request under short_tokens (400), no tools short (1) general:1
…with analysis wording analysis (3), analysis_words general:3
Any tools, or code-like text coding (3), coding_words coding:3
…and simple wording, nothing harder: tests, renames, typos, formatting and lint, docstrings and comments, "explain", version bumps simple (2), simple_words coding:2
…and hard wording: race conditions, deadlocks, concurrency, security, migrations, performance, multi-file or cross-cutting changes ("every caller", "behind an interface"), and symptoms of a cause not yet found ("under load", "at random", "on retry", "when two requests…", flaky) hard_raise (1) for each distinct pattern, up to hard_signals (2); hard_words +1 or +2, at most 5
…and the hardest wording: architecture, "design a/the", system design, proofs, large-scale or codebase-wide refactors hardest (5), hardest_words coding:5
…and the newest prompt says the last answer was wrong ("that's wrong", "still not working", "revert", …) correction_raise (1) +1, at most 5
…with at least agent_tools (5) tools, only with agent_by_tools: true agent (4) coding:4, and simple wording doesn't lower it
X-Route-Hint: cheap / smart from the client −1 / +1, kept within 1–5
X-Route-Floor: coding:4 from the client that floor, used as is

When the wording matches more than one list, the hardest wins: "write tests for the deadlock fix" is hard wording (level 4), not simple. Each sign of hard work counts: "the importer deadlocks under load" is two (level 5). Words for how big a person thinks a task is ("quick fix", "small change", "one-liner") aren't on the simple list: on the routing simulator (How we measure routing), hard work described that way failed at level 2. The correction words are the coding outcomes' own list (outcomes.CORRECTIONS, Coding outcomes), read only in the newest message: a new prompt is a task boundary, so that's the only time the level is set again. An empty word list switches its rule off, as does hard_raise: 0 or correction_raise: 0.

The word lists are Python regular expressions matched ignoring case, against the last two messages from the person (their first 20,000 characters). What the harness adds to those messages is left out: Claude Code's system reminders (<system-reminder>, which carry CLAUDE.md, todo lists and notices) and local command output, and Codex CLI's <environment_context> and AGENTS.md instructions (translate.HARNESS_TEXT). They're the same on every task, and a CLAUDE.md that says "run the tests" or "read the architecture doc" would otherwise set every task's level. A message that's only that text is passed over, like one of only tool results. A level outside 1–5, a pattern that doesn't compile or matches empty text (it would match every request), or a misspelt key is refused when the configuration is loaded or saved.

What that gives a Claude Code or Codex session (dozens of tools on every request):

Prompt Level Reason
"write unit tests for the date parser" coding:2 coding: 32 tools; simple task wording (write (unit )?tests): level 2
"fix the typo in the README" coding:2 coding: 32 tools; simple task wording (typo): level 2
"add a --dry-run flag to the deploy command" coding:3 coding: 32 tools
"fix the race condition in the job scheduler" coding:4 coding: 32 tools; hard wording (race condition): +1
"the importer deadlocks under load, fix it" coding:5 coding: 32 tools; hard wording (deadlock, under load): +2
"write tests for the deadlock fix" coding:4 coding: 32 tools; hard wording (deadlock): +1
"design a plugin system for the importers" coding:5 coding: 32 tools; hardest wording (design (a|the)): level 5
"that's wrong, the tests still fail", after "write unit tests…" coding:3 …; simple task wording (…): level 2; the new prompt corrects the last answer (wrong): +1

The level holds for the task. The rules give a level only at a task boundary: a new session, a new human prompt, or a history the harness compacted. Every request in between (tool results going back) keeps the session's model and level outright (Free upgrades), so a level never changes mid-task and the cache stays where it is. A task that turns out harder than its wording is raised at the next boundary, never mid-task, and never by its length: by the person's next prompt (a correction is +1; a new prompt with harder wording gets its own level, and the two-prompt window carries a short follow-up such as "go on" at the level of the prompt before it), by the learned router (below), whose labels include fix loops, failing tests and corrections, and by the outcome report and exploration (Exploration), which move a level whose work fails more than it should.

With the learned router on (below), it predicts its own level next to the rules': in shadow mode that's recorded and changes nothing; in route mode it's used when the model is sure, and the rules decide otherwise.

Length never raises the floor. A long conversation isn't harder work; it needs a model with room for it, so length only rules out the models whose window is too small (see Context windows). A Claude Code session on auto keeps its task's level (coding:2 to write tests, coding:4 to fix a race) however long it grows. Length counts in one place, and only to lower a level: a request under 400 tokens in all is a question on its own, level 1 (decision 38 in 09).

Every request says why. The routing reason starts with the floor and the rules that set it, naming the listed word that matched but never the text around it: classified coding:4 (coding: 32 tools; hard wording (race condition): +1). Mid-task turns repeat the task's reason (mid-task: keeping session model gpt-terra at coding:4 (coding: 32 tools; hard wording …)). A team routing by cost per success gets what was compared at the end: …; cost per success: deepseek-v4.1-flash, expected $0.0051 per success (62% at coding:3) vs $0.0086 (70%) on claude-haiku, the cheapest at the level. A task start a team explores says so: …; exploring: one level down from coding:3 (2.0% of task starts) (Exploration). The ledger keeps it (route_reason), and the console shows it under Reports → Requests and on the Dispatch feed. A team routing by expected total cost gets both models' chances and costs, and an escalation what it compared (Expected total cost).

Named tiers

A caller can ask for a tier by name instead of a model: frontier, standard, cheap and embed by default (decision 72). A chat tier is auto at a fixed level (frontier 5, standard 3, cheap 1), with the task (coding or general) taken from the request unless the tier sets one; an embedding tier is one model, by default the cheapest priced embedding model. The gateway owns the mapping: change tiers in the config and every caller follows. A model with the same name as a tier wins. X-Route-Floor still overrides a tier's level. The ledger records the tier's name as the requested model.

tiers:
  frontier: {level: 5}
  standard: {level: 3}
  cheap: {level: 1}
  embed: {kind: embedding}            # or {kind: embedding, model: text-embedding-3-small}
  review: {level: 4, task: coding}    # your own
  pinned: {model: claude-sonnet}      # a fixed model

GET /v1/routes lists each tier's candidate models and where each can send a request: provider, price, and the data facts in 06.

The cost function

For each candidate backend b, over the session's expected remaining turns:

cost(b) = rebuild(b) + expected_remaining_turns × per_turn(b)

Per-turn cost by backend type

Backend state per_turn(b)
API cached tokens × cache-read price + new tokens × write price + output × output price
Self-hosted, plenty of headroom ≈ 0 (2% of the route's API-equivalent price below 60% utilization: shadow_floor, shadow_knee)
Self-hosted, filling up shadow price rises toward the route's API-equivalent price
Self-hosted, full skipped while another route can take the request; otherwise it waits in vLLM's queue there (up to max_waiting per replica)

Per turn, the router assumes the conversation grew by what it grew since the session's last turn (at least 200 tokens; est_new_tokens_per_turn, 2,000, for a new session) and that the reply is est_output_tokens (600) long. The rest of the prompt is read from cache. The expected remaining turns are the session's turns so far, kept between min_expected_turns (3) and max_expected_turns (30).

The write price is the cache-write price only where caching is explicit: Anthropic-format backends (Anthropic, Bedrock, Vertex, Foundry) and Claude through OpenRouter, which gets a cache marker. Other providers cache automatically and bill new tokens at the input price. A backend set to an hour (cache_ttl_seconds 3600 or more, as the shipped Anthropic, Bedrock, Foundry and Vertex backends are) is priced at Claude's 1-hour write price (cache_write_1h, default twice the input price) from a session's second turn on, which is what the gateway asks for there (04). A session's first turn, and the rebuild that comes with it, is priced at the 5-minute write price, as the gateway sends it: a session counts as new until it has had a turn (turns is 0). One that has come back and moves to such a backend rebuilds at the 1-hour price. So a new Claude session costs the same to start on the direct backends as on OpenRouter, and the hour's premium on the later turns (about 5% over three turns for Claude Haiku 5.5) is set against what the hour saves.

Pauses (decision 60). A later turn that comes 5 to 60 minutes after the one before finds a 5-minute cache gone, and the conversation is written again; an hour's cache is still there. So each later turn on a route whose cache lasts under an hour (cache_ttl_seconds below 3600: OpenRouter, every provider that caches on its own) also carries

pause share × cached tokens × (write price − cache-read price)

the rebuild such a pause costs, times how often one comes. Pauses over an hour rebuild everywhere, so they don't change the comparison, and GPU deployments evict by pressure, not time, so they get none. The pause share is measured (pauses.py): every gateway counts its sessions' later turns, and those that came 5 to 60 minutes after the last, by team, halving the counts every 7 days, and saves them every minute in the store (session_pauses, one entry per gateway, summed by all). A team's share leans on the organization's, and the organization's on a prior of one turn in ten, each by 100 turns' worth:

organization = (paused + 100 × 0.10) ÷ (turns + 100)
team         = (team's paused + 100 × organization) ÷ (team's turns + 100)

At one turn in ten, a new Claude Haiku session at 30,000 tokens costs $0.0060 over three turns on the direct backends and $0.0064 on OpenRouter, so it starts there at the default cost priority. A team whose sessions rarely pause (under about one turn in twenty, at that size) goes back to OpenRouter, where the hour would cost more for nothing. The share in use is the session's team's; batch requests have no session and count none.

Rebuild cost

Situation rebuild(b)
b already holds a warm cache for this session 0
API, cold prefix tokens × (write price − cache-read price)
Self-hosted, cold the same, at the shadow price
Self-hosted, part of the prefix probably evicted the same for the part that's gone: × (1 − share still cached)

On a GPU deployment the cache belongs to one replica, so the share still cached is per replica; how it's known (vLLM's KV events, an estimate from its KV-cache metrics, or the cache TTL) is in 04.

A session only moves off its current backend when the cheapest route beats staying by more than the switch margin: switch_margin_pct (10%) of what staying costs, plus switch_margin_usd ($0.01). Otherwise the reason says staying on <backend> (move would not pay for cache rebuild).

Illustrative, at Claude Sonnet 5.5's list prices in config/prices.json (12 November 2026: $2 input, $0.10 cache read, $2.50 5-minute cache write, $4 1-hour cache write per million tokens): a 120k-token session costs about $0.012 a turn in cache reads to stay. Moving it to another Claude backend set to an hour costs about $0.46 to rewrite the cache (118k tokens × ($4 − $0.10)); to OpenRouter, which writes at the 5-minute price, about $0.28. A move has to save more than that, plus the switch margin, over the rest of the session to be worth it.

Cost per solved task (opt-in)

The threshold treats every model at or above the floor as equally good and every model below it as useless. Quality data says more: each model's chance of solving work at each level. With routing.model_choice: cost_per_success (or a team's model_choice), the router ranks routes by what a solved task is expected to cost:

expected(b) = cost(b) + (1 − chance) × redo
redo        = cost(t) ÷ chance(t)

cost(b) is the cost function above, cache rebuild included. chance is the model's chance of solving work at the request's level. A failed try is still paid for, and the work is then done again on t, the route the threshold would pick (the cheapest that meets the floor), until it succeeds. For t itself that's cost ÷ chance. So a cheaper model below the floor wins when its saving on the try outweighs redoing its extra failures, and a dearer, better model can win when it fails much less.

  • Chances come from each model's score in use: the scale says what a score means on the reference task (FrontierSWE by default), and a model exactly at a level solves that level's work as often as a 5 solves the reference (the anchor: 69.9% for coding). Published scores, overrides, and measured scores applied from evals (with quality.source: config) all get chances; a model without one is judged by the threshold.
  • A minimum (min_success_chance, default 0.6) keeps out any model whose chance at the level is lower, so a nearly free model that usually fails can't look cheap per success. If nothing reaches it, the threshold decides.
  • A client's X-Route-Floor is a minimum it asked for: the threshold decides.
  • Levels don't change. The level still comes from routing.levels; cost per success only changes which models can take a level's work. Reports → Levels lists, under each level, the models below it that are in reach for your team, with their chance.
  • Everything after works on expected cost: the speed premium of the priority, stickiness, the speed checks. A warm cache still counts through cost(b): a session warm on one model doesn't move to a cheaper one that would first pay to rebuild the cache, unless it's still cheaper per success after that.

Example, coding:3 with 30,000 tokens: Claude Haiku 5.5 meets the floor at $0.0060 a try and a 70% chance, so $0.0086 per success. DeepSeek V4.1 Flash scores 2.4, below the floor, but costs $0.0018 a try with a 62% chance: $0.0018 + 38% × $0.0086 = $0.0051 per success, and it wins. Every rule, and more examples: 10, How it decides.

Expected total cost to finish the task

Cheap routing that has to be redone saves nothing, and a redo costs more than tokens: someone notices the answer was wrong, says so and waits. With routing.model_choice: expected_cost (or a team's model_choice), each auto task goes to the model with the lowest expected cost to finish it (decisions 62 and 67, success.py). It's the default since the routing simulator scored it against the threshold (below):

E(m)            = try(m) + (1 − P(m)) × (H × stakes + next attempt)
stakes          = (1/3)^(5 − level) × min(1, prompt tokens / 8,000); level 5 after a correction
next attempt    = min over e of E(e | m failed), from a cold cache, while escalations are planned; else 0
  • try(m) is the cost function above: the rest of the session on that route, cache rebuild, the 1-hour cache and pauses included.
  • H is what a failed attempt at the top of the scale (a level-5 task, a full agent request) costs a person: routing.human_cost_usd, per team teams.<name>.human_cost_usd (Config → Routing → Expected total cost, and Controls). Minutes of their time times their rate; the default, $1, is one minute at $60 an hour. 0 counts only tokens.
  • The stakes (success.stakes, decision 67) are the share of H a failure of this request puts at risk. Each level below 5 puts a third as much at stake (level 4 a third, level 3 a ninth, level 1 1/81): a re-asked question costs a person seconds, a failed agent task minutes of review and a redo, and the benchmark prior, measured at level 5 and read down to level 1 at the same gaps between models, overstates how often a cheap model fails easy work. A request under 8,000 tokens puts proportionally less at stake (coding agents send more than that from their first turn, so this scales questions and short chats). After a correction (the person's newest prompt says the last answer was wrong) the request counts as level 5. So a one-line question puts 1/400 of 1/81 of H at stake, and goes to the cheapest model that meets its level, as the threshold sends it.
  • The next attempt after a failure is the same model again (the person resends, the agent carries on) or a stronger one (a different model with a higher chance) from a cold cache, whichever finishes for less. A task one model failed is harder for the next attempt too: every model's chance on a task moves with a hidden difficulty of the task's own, 1 log-odds wide (SPREAD), so the chance after a failure is conditioned on it. As many more attempts are planned as routing.cascade.max_escalations allows (0 by default: then a failure costs H and nothing more).

The success predictor

P(m) is the chance that m's answer to the task needs no redo. It's built in layers, each used when it's there:

  1. The benchmark prior. Each model's chance at each level (config.apply_chances, the fixed bar of decision 58), read between whole levels in log-odds, at the task's difficulty.
  2. The difficulty. The level the task is routed at. With the learned router in route mode, its difficulty (learned.Prediction.difficulty, moved as the level was by Claude Code's caps, the level map and exploration) and its spread: the chance is averaged over the spread, which pulls it towards a coin toss where the difficulty is unsure.
  3. The fitted layer (routing.success.mode, off by default; Config → Routing → Expected total cost). A logistic model on the learned router's rows, trained with it (meritorder router train, the worker, or Train now):

logit P = prior logit + a + (b − 1) × prior logit + ability(model) + team + repository + project + opening prompt

a and b calibrate the prior to what your outcomes count as success (most answers get no failure signal, so it's usually above the benchmark's chance). ability is each model's own record on your work: exploration's task starts a level down or up (decision 59) are what show a model off its level. The repository is the working directory Claude Code names in its system prompt or Codex in its <cwd>, and the project the client's project tag (X-MeritOrder-Tags), both kept only as keyed hashes of 8 hex characters. The opening prompt's triage features are its word triples (the learned router has the words and pairs) and the paths it mentions (their kind: test, docs, config or core; extension; directories), hashed into 16,384 buckets. Every part has a normal prior at zero, so a model, team or repository with few outcomes keeps the prior. It's fitted by coordinate-wise Newton steps (about 1 second per 10,000 task starts on a laptop), compared with the prior alone on the newest fifth by paired Brier score, and used in route mode only if it was better by more than twice the standard error. In shadow mode its chance is recorded next to the prior, so Reports → Learned router can compare them before it routes anything.

Cold start, with nothing fitted, is the rules' level and the benchmark prior. The benchmark's chances are FrontierSWE's (a model exactly at a level solves 70%), so until the fitted layer calibrates them, failures look likelier than your traffic will show. The stakes keep that from buying strong models for easy work; at levels 4 and 5, where the prior is closest to what it measured, a failure still costs most of H. Hence the recommendation below.

Escalation inside a task

Off by default (routing.cascade.max_escalations: 0): on the simulator it finished 0.1 points more at the same total, counting failed attempts, and a third more model spend (below). Turned on (1 or 2), a task still keeps its model mid-task, and what its tool results show (coding outcomes, below) moves the task model's chance, and the task moves up when continuing costs more than escalating:

Evidence (outcomes.py) Log-odds on the task model's chance
Tests failing after the last edit −0.6
Build or type check broken after it (and no test passed) −0.4
Each failed run in a row after the first (at most 6) −0.3
A fix loop: three edits to one file, each right after a failed run −0.8
Each error tool result in a row after the first (at most 6) −0.15
A correction in the person's next prompt ("that's wrong", "revert", ...) −1.4
Each file touched beyond 5 (at most 8), each core file edited beyond 5 −0.08, −0.05
Tests passing after the last edit +0.5

The gateway reads a team's tool results for this whether or not the learned router is on (only recording them needs it). These are priors set from the outcome labels' weights; Reports → Learned router shows whether the chances they give hold. The bounds: at most cascade.max_escalations (0 by default, at most 2) per task; never down inside a task; never for a named model (decision 23); never past the team's allowed models; never once any budget that applies is 90% spent; never into a refusal by max_request_usd (the request is routed as it would have been). The cache rebuild on the stronger model is in the comparison, at Claude's 1-hour price where that applies (decision 53). An escalated model's chance is its own from then on, and its failures in a row start again.

A human message after a failing run carries the task on only when it's a correction, or when the new prompt, classified first, is the same kind of work at no higher a level than the task's (Router.carries_on): "keep going" does, "now design the multi-region architecture" (coding:5) after a coding:3 task is a new task at its own level.

The routing reason says what was compared, either way. On the shipped price list, a $1 person's cost and the cascade on, a 30,000-token coding:3 task on Claude Haiku: after three failed runs, mid-task: keeping session model claude-haiku at coding:3 (coding: 1 tool); claude-haiku's chance now 41% (was 70%: tests failing after the last edit -0.6, 3 failed runs in a row -0.6); continuing ~$0.10 vs escalating to gpt-terra ~$0.12 (82%, cache rebuild included): continuing (a ninth of H is at stake at level 3); and when the person then says "that's wrong", the request counts as level 5: escalated at the next human message (1 of 1): claude-haiku's chance now 24% (was 70%: tests failing after the last edit -0.6, corrected (wrong) -1.4); continuing ~$1.00 vs escalating to gpt-terra ~$0.28 (82%, cache rebuild included); at coding:3 (coding: 1 tool). A task start's reason ends with both models' chances and costs and what's at stake: classified coding:3 (coding: 1 tool); expected total cost: claude-haiku ~$0.055 to finish: try $0.0060, chance 70% (benchmark), difficulty 3.0 (level 3), a failure costs $0.11 of a person's time (of $1.00: 1/9 at level 3), then claude-haiku again; deepseek-v4.1-flash ~$0.063, chance 62% (benchmark). With the fitted layer routing, each chance also says what moved it: 86% (benchmark 82%; calibration +0.4, model ability +0.1).

What's recorded, and savings

  • The task's route_features row (the learned router has to be on) gets predicted: the chosen model's and the runner-up's chance, the benchmark's, the fitted layer's, the expected total and token costs, the person's cost at stake (human_cost) and its share of H (stakes), and the difficulty; context: the repository and project hashes; and triage_features. At the task's end (the next human prompt that isn't a continuation) its coding column gets what the task cost, its escalations and why.
  • Every request of an escalated task carries the ledger tags escalation (1 or 2) and escalated_from (the model it left), which a client can't set; Reports → Breakdown → Tag → escalation shows what escalating cost.
  • Savings stay honest. The failed attempt wouldn't have been made without Merit Order, so the escalation's first request takes that attempt's baseline cost off its own baseline and its routing savings (a negative routing saving on that row, once: on the answer's row, never a refused attempt's). The gateway knows it from two counters per conversation in Redis (task: for what it cost, task-base: for what it would have cost on the baseline model), read with the budgets in the same round trip.

Reports → Learned router → Expected total cost shows predicted against seen success (a reliability table, the Brier score, by model, and the fitted layer's own), escalations (how often, whether the task then ended without a failure signal, and what was charged), and expected against actual cost per finished task.

Is it the right default?

On the routing simulator (2,000 standard tasks, seed 1, a price of $15 per failed attempt, the level rules of decision 61, docs/routing-eval/scorecard.md), against today's other choices. A failed attempt costs someone time: noticing it, asking again, waiting, cleaning up; here that time has a price per failed attempt, an assumption you can change. The total counts model spend plus failed attempts times that price: it's what the work costs, not time saved.

Strategy Success Model spend per finished task Time lost to failed attempts Total, counting failed attempts (90% interval) Analysis finished
Always Claude Opus 97.7% $1.43 $2.53 $3.95 ($3.57 to $4.35) 89.7%
Always Claude Sonnet 97.4% $0.73 $2.66 $3.40 ($3.08 to $3.76) 87.3%
auto, threshold (the default before decision 62) 97.5% $1.01 $2.62 $3.63 ($3.20 to $4.07) 82.5%
auto, cost per success 96.8% $0.40 $3.07 $3.47 ($3.12 to $3.86) 72.2%
auto, expected total cost, the full person's cost on every request (decision 62) 97.9% $0.51 $2.37 $2.88 ($2.56 to $3.21) 89.7%
auto, expected total cost, the person's cost at stake (the default, decision 67) 97.7% $0.40 $2.67 $3.08 ($2.77 to $3.43) 86.5%
…with its cascade (one escalation) 97.8% $0.54 $2.54 $3.08 ($2.77 to $3.45) 86.5%
Oracle (lower bound) 98.7% $0.17 $1.85 $2.03 93.7%

And what it spends per finished task, class by class, against the threshold (success in brackets):

Class (tasks) Threshold Decision 62 The default (decision 67)
Easy coding (559) $0.053 (100%) $0.094 (100%) $0.027 (100%)
Ordinary coding (740) $0.30 (100%) $0.41 (100%) $0.22 (100%)
Hard coding (128) $13.29 (81.2%) $5.03 (79.7%) $4.90 (80.5%)
Very hard coding (10) $54.12 (60%) $17.77 (60%) $17.55 (60%)
Short questions (159) $0.000026 (100%) $0.0014 (100%) $0.000026 (100%)
Chat (278) $0.0027 (100%) $0.025 (100%) $0.0022 (100%)
Analysis (126) $0.043 (82.5%) $0.095 (89.7%) $0.033 (86.5%)

The default spends 60% less per finished task than the threshold, and no more on any class: the cheapest model that meets the bar on easy work, and less than it on hard work, where at level 5 it picks Gemini 4 Carbon over Claude Fable when Carbon is cheaper to finish with, as cost per success does. It finishes 0.2 points more than the threshold, and in total it costs 15% less than the threshold and 9% less than always using Sonnet (paired, $0.13 to $0.51 less per finished task). Against decision 62, which charged every failure the full person's cost, it spends 20% less but costs $0.20 more per finished task in total (paired, $0.09 to $0.32) and finishes 0.15 points fewer: decision 62 bought analysis's 89.7% by sending every general request to stronger models (chat at 9 times the threshold's spend), since the rules give an analysis and an email the same levels. No setting tried has both (decision 67). It costs least in total at a price of $5 per failed attempt and ties the cascade at $15; at $50 the cascade costs less ($9.00 against $9.31), at $0 cost per success (by 1%). On the sensitivity runs (400 tasks each) it's lowest in total on every mix, at no pause and one turn in ten, within 1% of cost per success when 30% of turns pause, and level with always-Sonnet when the published abilities are off by 3 points.

The cascade escalates 12% of tasks, 62% of them then finish, and it finishes 0.1 points more, at the same total, counting failed attempts, and a third more model spend, so it's off by default. The CI check's baseline now runs 1,000 tasks (seed 7, frozen prices) and the threshold beside the default, and fails if a class spends more than 10% over the threshold (decision 67): decision 62 had $0.457 per finished task and $2.63 in total, counting failed attempts, at 98.0%; the default has $0.358 and $2.86 at 97.7%.

The person's cost the router uses ($1 for level-5 work) is far below the simulator's $15, on purpose: the benchmark's chances are FrontierSWE's (a model exactly at a level solves 70%), more pessimistic than the simulator's work and most traffic, and a new session's try is priced for 3 turns, a tenth of what an agent attempt costs. With the stakes, $2 costs 2% less in total, counting failed attempts, on the simulator but spends 43% more than the threshold on analysis and 30% more on chat; $3 and $5 spend more than the threshold on ordinary coding too; $0.50 costs 3% more. The fitted layer calibrates the chances to your outcomes; raise the person's cost once it routes.

The recommendation: keep the default; turn the learned router and routing.success.mode to shadow, and set success.mode: route once Reports → Learned router shows the fitted layer beat the benchmark prior; try the cascade on one team (cascade.max_escalations: 1) and compare its escalations there.

What only real traffic can tell: how often the in-task evidence means the task will fail, client by client; whether a stronger model finishes what a weaker one couldn't (the hidden difficulty's width); what a person's failed attempt really costs a team; and how much the fitted layer's repository and opening-prompt parts add over the calibration. Request overhead, measured with scripts/bench_load.py (expected-cost against exploration, both with the learned router in shadow mode, on a laptop): a chat request (a new task each time) 0.72 → 0.82 ms of CPU, an agent turn that grows an edit and a test run each request 3.50 → 3.55 ms.

The learned router

The level rules are word lists: a listed word raises a task whatever it's about, and hard work described in other words isn't recognized. The learned router (learned.py, learned_jobs.py, decision 44) learns from this organization's own traffic which requests are harder or easier than the rules say. It's off by default (routing.learned.mode, Config → Routing → Learned router), and the rules stay the default and the fallback.

Mode What happens
off (default) Nothing is recorded or predicted
shadow Gateways record each request's features and what followed its answer, predict a level next to the rules', and change nothing. Reports → Learned router compares the two
route The same, and the learned level is used when the model is at least min_confidence (0.8) sure. Otherwise the rules decide

For one request whose level comes from the rules (a new task without X-Route-Floor):

What it predicts. It corrects the rules' level rather than replacing it:

difficulty    = the rules' level + the weights of the request's features
learned level = difficulty rounded, 1 to 5

It's trained as an item response model, as Epoch places models and tasks on one scale: work of difficulty d sent to a model scoring q (its score for the task type, the one routing uses) shows a failure signal with probability sigmoid(slope × (d − q) + intercept). The slope starts from what Epoch's ability scale implies (about 0.4 a level for failures) and is fitted. The model then needs no traffic on a model to judge it: the scores say how good each model is, the traffic says how hard each kind of request is.

Two things are fixed by construction, because the labels can't tell them apart from how often failures get noticed:

  • The rules stay right on average. Over the training requests of each task type the corrections average to zero, so the model moves requests up or down relative to others the rules put at the same level. It can't raise every level at once, and it can't tell that every level is too low; the scores, cost per success and exploration are for that.
  • The client isn't difficulty. Tags about the client (client:…, format:…) only change how often a failure is noticed (a chat app has a regenerate button, an agent rarely resends), never a request's difficulty.

Where it applies. Only where the rules give a level: a new task (a new session or a new human prompt), or one the harness compacted. Mid-task turns keep the session's model; a session that outgrows its model keeps its level; a client's X-Route-Floor is never second-guessed; Claude Code's caps (request_class_levels) apply to whichever level is used. Requests that name a model are recorded too, for training (a named model shows how a model scoring other than the level does on such work), and never rerouted. A request of a batch is leveled like a new task, so route mode applies to it, but it's never recorded: none of the signals below can follow it (Batches).

What it learns from

Training data is this organization's own traffic. The ledger keeps no prompt text, and neither does this: each task start gets a row in route_features with

Field What it is
Words The words and word pairs of the text the rules read (the last two messages from the person), from its first and last 2,000 characters, hashed into 65,536 buckets with a key. Only bucket numbers are stored
Tags Named facts: the rules' level and which rules fired (rule:simple, rule:hard, rule:hardest, rule:correction, …), the tool count (a band, and rule:agent at agent_tools or more, whatever set the level), the size band, the conversation's length, Claude Code's request class and subagent flag, a client-set effort, structured output, the API format and the client's product name from its User-Agent
Outcome The model that answered and its score, the scores of models that refused, the status, and what followed

The key. MERITORDER_FEATURE_KEY if it's set, else one generated once and kept in the store (learned_router_key). Words are hashed with keyed BLAKE2b (a 128-bit key derived from it). A hash isn't encryption: whoever has the rows and the key can check whether a word they guess was in a request (not read a request back). Set the variable to keep the key out of the database. Changing it makes stored rows and models unusable (they're hashed differently), and the model is reported stale. So are rows and models from before feature version 2 (13 November 2026), whose CRC32 hashing the key didn't hide, and from before version 3 (15 November 2026), whose words came from user messages that were only tool results (so mid-task they often had none), and from before version 4 (decision 61), whose words included Claude Code's system reminders and Codex's AGENTS.md, and whose rules' level for a coding agent came from its tool count. Train again after upgrading.

The labels, and how weak each is:

Signal Seen when Weight How weak
A raised floor The next request of the conversation sends a higher X-Route-Floor (or X-Route-Hint: smart) 1.0 The client said the level was too low. Few clients send it
Sent again The next request has every message unchanged after a successful answer: a regenerated answer 0.6 Some clients resend after a timeout of their own; a retry after an error doesn't count
Stopped The client disconnected while the answer streamed (Esc in Claude Code) 0.4 Often a wrong direction, sometimes the person had read enough
Asked again elsewhere The conversation's last answer, then the same person's first request in a new session within 15 minutes shares at least half its hashed words 0.3 Inferred, not seen; subagents and side requests are left out (their conversations end by design)
Corrected The person's next prompt says the answer was wrong: "that's wrong", "undo", "revert", "you broke", "still failing", "not what I asked" (coding outcomes) 0.7 A rule list over the prompt's first 1,000 characters: "revert the migration" as a new request matches too, and a polite "could you try another way" doesn't
Tests failing at the end The last test run after the task's last edit failed (pytest, jest, vitest, go test, cargo test, npm test, ...) 0.5 Often the agent gave up; sometimes the person took over, or the test was already failing
Build broken at the end The last build or type check after the last edit failed (tsc, mypy, cargo build, go build, make, ...), and no test passed after it 0.4 Agents usually fix their own build errors; one left at the end is the weaker sign
A fix loop Three or more edits to one file, each right after a failed run, and no test passed after them 0.3 Hard work loops too; it says the model struggled, not that it failed
Tests passing at the end The last test run after the last edit passed cancels a broken build and a fix loop The one sign an answer worked; it isn't a label of its own (no signal already counts as no failure)
Turns and tokens to the end of the task Counted per task not a label Shown on the outcome report: what finishing cost
A refusal A model refused and auto moved on 0.2 A policy decision more than a sign the work was too hard
A judged label (opt-in per team) A judge, reading the answer next to a stronger model's, says whether it was good enough: a failure or a success from how well verdicts agree with the signals above A judge's view, not a person's: judged labels
Errors, capacity failovers not a label They say nothing about the work
Epoch scores, eval results the model's side Each served model's score (Epoch's, an override, or eval scores applied as scores) is what a request's difficulty is compared with; the slope starts from Epoch's scale. They aren't per-request labels

Most answers get no signal at all, and a missing signal isn't a success: the labels are rare and noisy, which is why the model is checked against the rules before it's used and shadowed before it routes. A team can add a stronger label, at a price and by sending a sample of its prompts to two more models: judged labels.

Judged labels

Off by default, per team (teams.<name>.judged_labels, Config → Routing → Judged labels; decision 52 in 09). A small sample of the team's task starts is replayed on a stronger model, and a judge model reads the conversation and both answers and says whether each was good enough. The label is whether the answer the request got was good enough, given the stronger one. Unlike the outcome signals, it says so either way.
