What it does Strips terminal codes and trailing spaces, collapses repeated lines, keeps head and tail of huge outputs Drops the least useful words from prose (web pages, docs, long explanations)
Same bytes every turn because It's deterministic Each result is decided once and the decision is stored (below)
Stores Nothing Where each result was cut (character ranges), never the text
Needs Nothing The meritorder compressor service (07)
Turn on compression: {enabled: true} compression: {model: {enabled: true}}, and compressor.url

When both are on, the rules run first and the model gets what they leave.

The rules

  • Only tool results of at least min_chars (4,000) characters.
  • Terminal color codes and trailing spaces go. Three or more blank lines become one. Three or more identical lines in a row become one line and [previous line repeated N more times].
  • Beyond max_chars (24,000), the first 60% (head_fraction) and the last 40% are kept, with a line saying how many lines and characters were left out.
  • Changing the settings mid-session changes the history once (one cache miss).
  • Each process keeps what the rules made of each long result (up to 16 million characters in and out, the oldest dropped first), so a history resent every turn isn't worked through again.

Model-based (LLMLingua-2)

LLMLingua-2 is a token classifier (XLM-RoBERTa large or multilingual BERT, fine-tuned by Microsoft) that labels each word keep or drop. It's much cheaper than an LLM and keeps the words in order, but it isn't deterministic across model versions, library versions or hardware: borderline words can flip. So the gateway never runs it twice on the same result.

  • Decided once. The first gateway to see a new tool result asks the service, by the team's deadline_ms (1,000). The answer is stored in Redis under a hash of the text plus the team, the compressor's model, the rate and the guard's version, with a TTL of compressor.ttl_seconds (6 hours, at least as long as a session stays sticky), renewed each time a turn uses it. Every later turn, on any gateway, applies the stored decision to the original text the harness resends, so the bytes are the same.
  • Late means never. A result the service doesn't finish by the deadline (or can't compress: it's down, or runs another model) is sent as it is, and that choice is stored too, so later turns send it as it is as well. A service that fails isn't called again for 30 seconds.
  • Only new results. A result already sent on an earlier turn without a decision (compression was just turned on, its decision expired, or Redis was emptied) went upstream as it is, so it's stored as left alone. Turning model-based compression on mid-session costs no cache miss; changing its rate or model changes the history once, like the rules.
  • First writer wins. Two gateways that see the same new result at once both ask; each stores its answer only if none is there yet (SET NX in one transaction with the read-back) and uses whatever is stored. Both send the winner's cuts.
  • No content in Redis. The decision is a list of character ranges to drop, or "left alone". The text comes from the harness every turn, as it does without compression. (Only the response cache and the Responses API's stored mode keep content, both opt-in, and batch files are held sealed until a provider or GPU takes them.)
  • Redis down: results are sent as they are; nothing is stored.

The guard. Only prose goes to the model, and some words in it are never cut:

Kept as it is How it's recognized
JSON The whole result parses as JSON, or starts like JSON and nests deeper than the parser goes
Code Fenced blocks, indented lines, lines starting with def, class, import, function, SELECT and similar, lines ending in {, } or ;, lines with many brackets or operators
Errors Lines with error, exception, traceback, fail, fatal, panic, warn, denied, refused, not found, no such, errno, exit code, out of memory, unauthorized, forbidden, undefined, timeout, invalid, cannot, unable and similar anywhere in them, in any case (TypeError, FAILED); stack frames (at …, File "…", #3 …)
File listings Lines starting with a line number (cat -n, Claude Code's Read)
Search results, test ids Lines whose first word holds a path or a place in a file: grep -n and ripgrep (docs/03-routing.md:141:…, Claude Code's Grep), pytest ids (tests/test_x.py::test_y[…] PASSED), compiler and linter output (src/x.c:12:5: …)
Diffs The lines of a unified diff's hunks (after @@ -1,6 +1,6 @@): context, added and removed lines alike; in a result with a diff in it, every line that starts like one (the rules may have cut a huge diff's middle)
Data Tables (|), log lines starting with a timestamp, key: value and key=value lines, headings, quotes, lines that are mostly not letters
Short runs Prose runs under 300 characters, and lines under 20 characters or 5 words
Tools Results of skip_tools (default: read, read_file, view and other file readers), since an agent edits from what it read
Words inside prose Anything with a digit, / or \, _, ::, ->, a hyphen inside it (claude-code, X-Session-Id, and opt-in too), brackets inside a word (configure()), operators, a.b, camelCase, CAPITALS, command-line flags (--device, -d); text in quotes of any kind ("…", '…', “…”, ‘…’) or `backticks`; names (a capitalized word that doesn't start a sentence or a list item: Redis, Zürich, both words of Merit Order); negations (not, no, never, without, unless, …n't) and words that say how much or which (only, all, every, each, always, any, most, some, few, many, more, less, least, both, either, first, last, same)

What it may drop: ordinary words in sentences (articles, most adjectives and adverbs, repeated phrasing), commas, parentheses around prose, and whole sentences' worth of words when the rate is low. Line breaks and sentence ends (., ?, !) are kept, so line numbers still point at the same lines. The text reads like notes. Meaning can still shift (a dropped adjective or verb: "a small team" becomes "team"), and quoting a compressed sentence back won't match the original: leave it off for teams whose agents quote web or document text exactly, or edit prose files read with a shell command (a file reader in skip_tools, or one that prints line numbers, is safe). Names in scripts without capital letters (東京) aren't recognized as names, and the models drop them often.

compressor:
  url: http://compressor:8090      # ${MERITORDER_COMPRESSOR_URL:-} in the shipped config
  model: microsoft/llmlingua-2-xlm-roberta-large-meetingbank
  ttl_seconds: 21600
  api_key_env: MERITORDER_COMPRESSOR_KEY   # optional shared secret
teams:
  docs-team:
    compression:
      enabled: true                # the rules
      model:
        enabled: true
        rate: 0.5                  # keep about half of the prose's tokens (llmlingua's default)
        min_chars: 4000            # shorter results aren't sent to the model
        deadline_ms: 1000          # not done by then: sent as it is, for good
        skip_tools: [read, read_file, view]

The console has the same settings in Config → Teams, with the service's status.

The service. meritorder compressor (the compressor extra: llmlingua 0.2.2, torch, transformers; its own image, never the default one) loads the model and answers POST /v1/compress with the character ranges to drop in each text it gets. It calls llmlingua's PromptCompressor(..., use_llmlingua2=True).compress_prompt(..., return_word_label=True) and matches the labelled words back to the original text, allowing for what the tokenizer normalized (case, accents, ligatures, full-width forms) and skipped (characters it doesn't know). llmlingua's own compressed_prompt isn't used: it's rebuilt from tokenizer pieces, so it puts spaces into 1.2.3 and x.so and loses characters like accents and emoji. llmlingua's <llmlingua, compress=False> spans (structured_compress_prompt) only apply to the original LLMLingua, so the gateway keeps protected text out of the request instead. It forces line breaks and sentence ends (force_tokens) and words with digits (force_reserve_digit). A request's texts (each prose range of each new result) go through the model together, up to --batch-size (50) 512-token chunks at a time, following the steps compress_prompt takes for one text; the labels are the same as one text at a time, and it's 1.7 times faster on a CPU. On a CPU it uses as many threads as the container's CPU limit allows (--threads or MERITORDER_COMPRESSOR_THREADS to choose; torch alone would start one per core of the machine and be throttled). Each process compresses one request at a time; run more replicas for more gateways. Any server that speaks the same API can stand in:

POST /v1/compress  {"model": "...", "rate": 0.5, "force_tokens": ["\n", ".", "?", "!"], "force_digits": true, "texts": ["..."]}
                -> {"model": "...", "version": "...", "results": [{"drop": [[start, end], ...]}, ...]}
GET  /healthz   -> {"ok": true, "model": "...", "version": "...", "device": "cuda"}

Offsets are code points into each text. A request for another model gets 409.

Savings are counted per request the same way for both methods: removed tokens in tool results new on this turn (after the last assistant message) at the input price, removed tokens in older results at the cache-read price. Each method is its own cause, so what the rules cut is never counted as the model's: the ledger's savings_compression is the rules', savings_compression_model what the model took out of what the rules left. Reports, the CSV and the ledger export (JSONL, CSV, Parquet) carry both, as does Prometheus' meritorder_savings_usd_total{cause="compression"} and {cause="compression_model"}. Each compressed request is also tagged compression: rules or compression: model (the model cut something), to filter by: Reports → Breakdown → Tag compression. meritorder_compression_model_results_total{result} counts what happened to each result (compressed, kept, reused, old, late, failed, no_prose, store_error), and meritorder_compressor_duration_seconds how long the service took. The service's own GPU or CPU time isn't charged to requests.

Measured on the published models

Measured on 13 November 2026 with scripts/bench_compressor.py on one laptop: Apple M4 Max (12 performance and 4 efficiency cores, 64 GB), macOS 26.6, llmlingua 0.2.2, transformers 5.22.1, torch 2.15.0, the models at their Hugging Face revisions ebaba9b (XLM-RoBERTa large) and 5f0c827 (multilingual BERT). The service ran on the CPU with 12 threads (torch's choice here), with 2 threads (as in a pod limited to 2 CPUs), and on the laptop's GPU (MPS). No NVIDIA GPU was measured. The laptop was running other work as well: a second CPU run hours later, at a load average of 15 to 30, gave times within about a fifth of these.

The tool outputs come from this repository and the machine, with the repository's path, the home directory and commit authors replaced: pytest -v output, git log --stat and a diff, Python and Markdown files read with cat, ls -R and find listings, JSON responses (the tests' provider replies and the price list), the HTML docs as a fetch tool returns them, web-search-style results, git grep results, the docs as long prose, stack traces (pytest, Python, Node), and prose written to hold everything the guard must keep. Each was measured at 4,000, 16,000 and 48,000 characters.

How much comes out. Tokens removed from the whole tool result at rates 0.33 / 0.5 (the default) / 0.7, and the share of the text the guard sends to the model, over the three sizes:

Tool output Sent to the model XLM-RoBERTa large Multilingual BERT
pytest output, git log, diffs, Python files, listings, JSON, git grep, stack traces 0–1% 0% 0%
Markdown file read with cat 6% 2% / 2% / 1% 3% / 2% / 1%
Web page as text 20% 9% / 6% / 4% 9% / 6% / 4%
Web search results 21% 9% / 6% / 4% 8% / 5% / 3%
Long prose (the docs) 38% 19% / 13% / 7% 17% / 11% / 6%
Prose written for the guard check 48% 25% / 18% / 11% 27% / 21% / 13%

Of the prose it's sent, the model removes about a third of the tokens at 0.5 (28–38%), half at 0.33 and a fifth at 0.7: line breaks, sentence ends and protected words stay whatever the rate. Most tool output an agent sees isn't prose, so the savings come from web pages, docs and search snippets, 5–13% of such a result at the default rate. The guard as it is now keeps about one point more than it did before these measurements (web pages 6.2% instead of 6.9% with XLM-RoBERTa) and no longer cuts search results, test ids and diffs, which it used to take for prose.

How long it takes. The service's time for one tool result (the request a gateway makes for a new result: all its prose ranges at once), p50 / p95, and the share done within the default 1-second deadline. "Prose only" is the worst case: text that is all prose, so every character goes to the model.

Service 4k characters 16k 48k 4k, prose only 16k, prose only 48k, prose only
XLM-RoBERTa large, CPU, 12 threads 0.8 / 1.6 s (66%) 2.5 / 6.7 s (17%) 6.6 / 10.9 s 1.1 / 1.5 s 3.0 / 3.4 s 9.0 / 9.9 s
XLM-RoBERTa large, CPU, 2 threads 1.0 / 2.5 s (50%) 2.9 / 5.9 s (13%) 6.6 / 12.0 s 1.3 / 1.5 s 3.3 / 3.6 s 7.4 / 7.7 s
XLM-RoBERTa large, Apple GPU (MPS) 0.2 / 0.5 s (100%) 0.7 / 1.7 s (71%) 2.2 / 4.0 s 0.3 / 0.3 s 0.8 / 1.0 s 3.1 / 3.3 s
Multilingual BERT, CPU, 12 threads 0.3 / 0.6 s (100%) 0.8 / 1.9 s (69%) 2.2 / 4.0 s 0.3 / 0.4 s 0.9 / 1.1 s 2.4 / 2.5 s
Multilingual BERT, CPU, 2 threads 0.2 / 0.6 s (100%) 1.0 / 1.7 s (47%) 2.3 / 5.3 s 0.3 / 0.3 s 1.1 / 1.2 s 2.8 / 2.9 s
Multilingual BERT, Apple GPU (MPS) 0.1 / 0.2 s (100%) 0.2 / 0.6 s (100%) 0.7 / 1.4 s 0.1 / 0.1 s 0.3 / 0.3 s 1.2 / 1.3 s

Time follows the number of 512-token chunks the model reads, and every prose range is at least one (llmlingua pads each to 512 tokens), so a result with many short prose ranges costs about as much as one with a few long ones. A chunk takes about 0.54 s with XLM-RoBERTa large on this CPU and 0.16 s with multilingual BERT, 0.13 s and 0.04 s on the Apple GPU. Two threads were nearly as fast as twelve on this laptop, whose cores share one unit for matrix work; on an x86 server more cores should help more, and a 2-CPU pod there will be slower than these rows (not measured). The gateway's own part is small: finding the prose in a 48k result takes about 1 ms (up to 3 ms), once per result per process, and applying stored cuts on later turns well under 1 ms.

Memory. At most 4.7 GiB resident for XLM-RoBERTa large and 3.7 GiB for multilingual BERT on the CPU, with the largest request (60 prose ranges, about 50 chunks in one batch, which took 19 s and 6 s); most of it is the batch, so a lower --batch-size uses less. The Helm chart's 4–6 GiB fits either. On the Apple GPU the process held 6.0 and 3.3 GiB, GPU memory included.

The guard, checked. The script finds every path, URL, number, identifier, command-line flag, hyphenated word, quoted string and error line in each input with patterns of its own (not the guard's), about 36,000 of them, and checks at each rate that no cut touches any and that each comes through byte for byte. With the guard as it was, both models cut command-line flags (--device, --config-dir, -d; 55 times with XLM-RoBERTa, 164 with BERT), hyphenated names (claude-code became claude code, x-meritorder-model, gpt-oss, llm-d; 114 and 445 times) and a word in typographic quotes (“deadline”), and shortened lines of git grep results, pytest ids and diffs, which an agent quotes back. The guard now keeps all of these (the table above), and nothing is cut on any kind of output, at any rate, with either model.

Do the facts survive? A proxy only. What a question about a result would ask for (names, numbers, paths), in the prose that went to the model, at the default rate: numbers and paths all survived; names (a capitalized word inside a sentence) 95–96%, the rest being names in a script without capitals (東京); words that say how much or which (only, all, every, same...) all, now that the guard keeps them (the models dropped 74–78% of them before). This checks words, not understanding. It doesn't show that agents still succeed on compressed results: that needs real runs on real tasks, which cost money and haven't been done.

The deadline. The default stays 1 second. It bounds what a new tool result can add to its turn, and a later turn never waits. What it lets through depends on the hardware:

  • CPU, XLM-RoBERTa large (the default model): a chunk takes half a second, so only small results make it (half to three quarters at 4k characters, under a quarter at 16k), and a result that misses it has made its turn wait a second for nothing. Don't run the default model on a CPU.
  • CPU, multilingual BERT: every 4k result and half to five in six 16k ones within a second. On a CPU, use this model (MERITORDER_COMPRESSOR_MODEL and compressor.model, the same on both sides).
  • A GPU: on the Apple GPU, XLM-RoBERTa large does every 4k result and most 16k ones within the deadline, and BERT every 16k one. A data-center NVIDIA GPU has several times this laptop GPU's throughput (the models run in full precision on either, as published), so 48k results should fit too; that hasn't been measured. A GPU is the way to compress large results.
  • Raising deadline_ms compresses larger results on slow hardware at the price of that wait on the turn that brings them: worth it for teams whose agents read long pages and can wait, and set per team.

Stateful APIs

OpenAI's Responses API can keep a conversation on the server: a client sends previous_response_id (or a conversation) and only its new input, and reads responses back later. This is where Merit Order holds conversation content, and only for teams that turn it on. Without it, the gateway is stateless: requests with store: false, or that send the whole conversation, work as always; previous_response_id, conversation, background and item_reference get a 400 saying the team's stored mode is off; and the response object says store: false. Decision 51 has the reasoning. One exception holds nothing past a connection: over the WebSocket transport, a turn can chain from the latest response on its own connection, kept in memory while the connection is open (decision 54).

Stored mode (opt-in per team)

teams:
  research:
    stored_responses:
      enabled: true
      retention_days: 30          # required: there is no default
      readers: []                 # roles that may also read and continue others' responses (team_lead, admin, ...)
response_store:
  key_env: MERITORDER_RESPONSES_KEY        # or key_file: a mounted secret, re-read when it changes
  old_keys_env: MERITORDER_RESPONSES_OLD_KEYS   # while rotating: old keys still read, comma-separated

Config → Teams has the same settings, with what each team holds now (counts and sizes, never content); the Teams page shows it too. In a team with stored mode on, a /v1/responses request is stored unless it says store: false, which is OpenAI's default.

Who holds the conversation: the gateway, not the provider. Each turn that chains is rebuilt from what the gateway stored: every earlier turn's input and output, oldest first (or the conversation's items), then the new input. The rest of the pipeline sees only that rebuilt request, so everything works as for a client that sends the whole conversation each turn:

  • Routing. auto may send turn 2 to another model or provider than turn 1, and a failover mid-chain sends the next route the whole conversation. Instructions are never carried over from an earlier turn (as at OpenAI).
  • Sessions and caching. A chain without a session header stays in the session its first turn got (a conversation in its own), so stickiness, warm caches and prompt-cache keys follow the rebuilt prefix.
  • Compression. The client's input is stored as it was sent, before compression. Rebuilding gives the same history every turn, so the rules cut it the same way and model-based compression finds the decisions it stored for those tool results.
  • Spend and the learned router. Each turn is one ledger row, checked against budgets and limits, and the learned router sees the rebuilt request (a resent turn counts as a retry).

When OpenAI continues its own response. A backend with api: responses and responses_store: true stores stored-mode turns at the provider too (store: true) and records the provider's response id. A next turn that lands on that same backend and model, and chains from that turn with previous_response_id, is sent as the provider's own previous_response_id plus only the new input and the turn's instructions, which keeps OpenAI's reasoning items and its cache. Every other case gets the whole conversation from the gateway: another provider or model, a turn in a conversation, a backend without responses_store, or a provider that no longer has the turn (it answers 400, and the gateway sends everything on the same route). With responses_store the provider holds the content as well, for its own retention (OpenAI: at least 30 days); deleting a response at the gateway deletes the provider's copy. Its prompt counts then include context the gateway didn't send (reasoning items), so they don't calibrate the gateway's token estimate. Off by default.

What's kept, sealed. Each response's object as the client got it and the input sent with it, and each conversation's metadata and items, sealed one by one with AES-256-GCM. The key is any string, the same on every gateway and the worker (MERITORDER_RESPONSES_KEY or response_store.key_file); without one, a gateway on Postgres refuses requests that would be stored (503). Each sealed value names its key by a public id, and is bound to its row and owner: copied into another row, it doesn't open. Owner, chain, status, where it ran and sizes are in the clear, like the ledger. In-memory storage (development) uses a random key for the life of the process.

Rotating the key. Put the new key in MERITORDER_RESPONSES_KEY and the old one in MERITORDER_RESPONSES_OLD_KEYS on every gateway and the worker. New values are sealed with the new key, old ones still open, and the worker seals everything again with the new key, 500 values a minute. Config → Teams says how many values still need an old key, and when none do; then remove it. A value sealed with a key that's on neither list (dropped too soon, or a typo) can't be opened: the worker leaves it out of resealing, so it doesn't hold up the values behind it, and raises one critical alert per such key id. Put the key back in the old keys to read and move those values; otherwise they stay unreadable until their retention deletes them.

Retention. A chain is kept retention_days after its last turn, all of it (continuing a chain renews its earlier turns too, since every turn is rebuilt from them), and a conversation retention_days after it last changed. Past that it's unreadable at once and the worker deletes it within a minute (a gateway on in-memory storage does it itself). Shortening the retention applies at the next pass; turning stored mode off for a team deletes everything it kept at the next pass, the providers' copies too. Teams that aren't in the configuration follow the default team's settings. A background response sent with store: false is kept only 10 minutes after it ends (response_store.background_unstored_seconds), to be polled, and can't be chained from.

Who can read it. A response or conversation belongs to the person and team whose key made it. Nobody else can read, list or chain from it (404), admins included, unless the team lists their role in readers: admins then from any team, the other roles on the same team. Only the owner deletes. Someone moved to another team leaves their stored responses with the old team. Disabling someone on the People page, or deactivating or deleting them through SCIM, deletes everything they stored, and the providers' copies.

The API

As OpenAI's reference defines it (read on 13 November 2026, openai-python 3.42 to 3.50); the official SDK works unchanged.

Endpoint What it does here
POST /v1/responses store (default true in stored mode), previous_response_id, conversation (an id or {id}; not with previous_response_id), background, item_reference items (resolved from the chain, the conversation, or anything else the person stored: the Vercel AI SDK sends earlier turns this way)
GET /v1/responses/{id} The response, with its status. stream=true (resuming a background stream with starting_after) isn't built: background responses don't stream here (decision 51)
DELETE /v1/responses/{id} Deletes it, its content, and the provider's copy. A later turn chaining from anything after it in the chain gets 404
POST /v1/responses/{id}/cancel Background responses only: stops one that's queued or running. Cancelling one that ended returns it as it is
wss://…/v1/responses The WebSocket transport: response.create events, each turn through the same pipeline; chains on the connection with or without stored mode
POST /v1/responses/compact Compaction, written by the gateway with a model the router picks, readable on every backend. Any team; previous_response_id in stored mode
POST /v1/responses/input_tokens The input's size in the model's tokens: the gateway's estimate, calibrated per model by providers' counts. Any team; previous_response_id and conversation in stored mode
GET /v1/responses/{id}/input_items What the response was made from: the earlier turns of its chain (or the conversation's items before it), then its own input; after, limit (1 to 100, default 20), order (default desc)
POST /v1/conversations A conversation, with starting items and metadata (16 pairs)
GET, POST, DELETE /v1/conversations/{id} Read it, change its metadata, delete it. Deleting deletes its items too (OpenAI keeps them); its responses stay
GET, POST /v1/conversations/{id}/items List its items (after, limit, order), add items
GET, DELETE /v1/conversations/{id}/items/{item_id} One item; deleting returns the conversation

A response created with conversation builds on the conversation's items and adds its input and output to them when it's done (with store: false too). Background responses (background: true) are kept as queued and run in the gateway that took them; clients poll GET. While it works on one, the gateway touches its row once a minute (four times per timeout when response_store.background_timeout_seconds is under four minutes), so one that runs for hours is never given up on. A gateway that stops leaves them running; once nothing has touched one for response_store.background_timeout_seconds (an hour) the worker marks it failed. With store: false, the time it's kept for polling counts from when it ends, however long it ran. A background response can't also stream here, so resuming one with starting_after isn't built: it would mean keeping every event of a response, content included, where any gateway could replay it, for what polling already covers.

meritorder_stored_responses_total{event} counts turns rebuilt from stored history, kept, sent as the provider's continuation, and ones that couldn't be kept.

The WebSocket transport

As OpenAI's WebSocket mode guide and event reference have it (read 15 November 2026, openai-python 3.42 to 3.51), and as Codex CLI uses it. A client opens wss://<gateway>/v1/responses with its key in the Authorization header (a bad key is refused at the handshake, 401) and sends {"type": "response.create", ...}: the body of POST /v1/responses, flat. The events come back one per message, the same as the SSE stream's. Each turn runs through the same pipeline as the HTTP endpoint: the key is checked again (a revoked key stops at the next turn), budgets and caps, routing, the session, compression, translation to any backend, one ledger row, and stored mode when the team has it.

Chaining on the connection, without stored mode. For each stream of the connection, the gateway keeps its latest response's whole conversation (the input it was made from and its output) in memory, and nowhere else, until the connection closes. A turn that sends previous_response_id with only its new input is rebuilt from it, so the rest of the pipeline sees what a client resending its conversation sends: auto routes each turn on its own, and the prompt cache and compression treat it the same. This is what OpenAI keeps for store: false, and what Codex CLI counts on: it sends store: false and, from its second turn, only the new items. Chaining from anything else (an older response, one from another connection) gets previous_response_not_found, and Codex then sends the whole conversation. In a team with stored mode, turns it stored chain as over HTTP, from any connection; store: false turns chain on the connection.

Upstream is HTTP. The connection ends at the gateway; each turn goes to the backend chosen for it the way that backend takes requests, OpenAI's included (its HTTP Responses API, continuing its own stored response with responses_store). Decision 54 says why.

The rest of the protocol. generate: false prepares a turn without a model call (Codex warms up with it): no backend, no cost, no ledger row, kept on the connection only. stream_id names a stream; a stream's responses run one at a time, in order, streams side by side, up to 32 named ones (OpenAI's limit). Up to 64 response.create messages wait on one stream (MAX_QUEUED); one past that gets an error event (429, websocket_queue_full) instead of being held. background is refused, as at OpenAI. Codex's response.interrupt stops the running response it names (recorded as a disconnect, 499), as does closing the connection. Steering (response.steer) isn't supported. A connection has no time limit (OpenAI's is 60 minutes). A message can be as large as an HTTP body (MERITORDER_MAX_BODY_MB, 32 MB); the handshake says so in x-codex-websocket-max-message-bytes, and Codex sends anything larger over HTTP. A proxy in front of the gateway must pass WebSocket upgrades through. meritorder_responses_websocket_total{event} counts connections, turns, turns rebuilt from a connection's memory, and warm-ups.

meritorder setup codex points Codex CLI at the gateway with the WebSocket transport on (00).

Codex's tools on any model. Whatever backend a turn lands on, Codex's tools work: its custom (freeform) tools such as apply_patch become function tools with one string argument and come back as custom_tool_call items, its namespaced tools (sub-agents, MCP servers) come back with their namespace, and tool_search and local_shell calls keep their own item types (02, decision 57). History converts to the same bytes each turn, so a session that stays on one model reads its cache every turn. Codex sends apply_patch only for the models its own catalog knows (OpenAI's); on auto and any other name it edits files through its shell (exec_command), which works everywhere. Web search: Codex's default is OpenAI's cached index (web_search = "cached"), which only OpenAI has, so on other models the turn goes without it (x-meritorder-dropped-tools: web_search, and a log line). With web_search = "live" Claude searches with its own server tool, at $10 per 1,000 searches on the ledger.

Compaction

POST /v1/responses/compact takes a conversation (input, or previous_response_id in stored mode) and returns, as OpenAI does, its user messages followed by one compaction item; the client sends that window as the start of its next turn. OpenAI's compaction item is encrypted for OpenAI alone, so behind auto a next turn on any other provider couldn't read it. The gateway writes the summary itself instead: the conversation goes through the pipeline with a prompt to summarize it, routed like Claude Code's compaction requests (auto caps its level at routing.request_class_levels.compaction, 3 by default; a named model is that model), admitted against budgets, and metered as one ledger row tagged compaction: responses. The item's encrypted_content holds the summary, encoded, not encrypted (it's the client's own conversation). A later turn carrying it is read as a user message with the summary, wherever it goes. A compaction item from OpenAI itself is refused (400) rather than dropped, and so is compaction_trigger (OpenAI's compaction inside a turn); Codex CLI compacts by summarizing on its own for a custom provider, which works through the gateway like any turn.

Batches

Batches are the one place requests outlive the call that sent them, and the same rule holds: content passes through, and stays where it has to, for as long as the operator says. An OpenAI-style upload is held encrypted (AES-GCM, MERITORDER_BATCH_KEY) only until its batch is handed on; Anthropic-style requests to providers aren't held at all. Results stay with the providers (or, for Bedrock and Vertex AI, in the operator's bucket) and are read again whenever the client asks, until batches.retention_days after the batch ends, when the worker deletes them there. Batch work for your own GPUs has no provider to hold it, so the gateway does, sealed the same way: each request until it runs (or is handed to a provider), its result until the retention period ends. All of it can live in the operator's bucket (batches.storage.bucket) instead of Postgres, and the key can be rotated while it waits. The gateway keeps only each request's routing metadata besides. Details: 02, Request flow.

Response caching

Exact-match response caching rarely hits for agent traffic (every turn is unique), but helps chatbots, RAG, evals, and repeated pipeline calls.

  • Opt-in: per team (response_cache: {enabled: true, ttl_seconds: 3600}) or per request with X-MeritOrder-Cache: on. off always bypasses it.
  • Scoped: cache keys include the team (or the user, with scope: user), so answers never cross that boundary.
  • One of the two exceptions to "no stored content" (the other is the Responses API's stored mode, above): entries hold the response in Redis until the TTL expires. See decision 13.
  • Hits cost $0 and are recorded with the original cost as savings_response_cache. Streaming requests can be served from the cache (replayed as a stream); only non-streaming responses are written to it. /v1/responses requests don't use it.
05

GPU autoscaling

Only open-weight models (Qwen, DeepSeek, Kimi, GLM, Llama, …) can be self-hosted. Every self-hostable model should also have at least one API route serving the same weights (OpenRouter, the vendor, Bedrock, …). APIs are the floor; GPUs are an optimization. The console warns about models without one before anyone stops their GPUs.

Three provisioners run the GPUs: SkyPilot (one cloud VM per replica, each of which deletes itself if the controller stops renewing its lease), Kubernetes (KServe or llm-d on your cluster), and static (a vLLM server you already run, which Merit Order only routes to). The capacity controller (meritorder controller) decides when each deployment starts, scales and stops. The gateways only route to what it publishes.

What has been run for real. The decision logic, the state machine and every provisioner are tested in CI against stand-ins. The Kubernetes provisioner has also run on a local kind cluster with a stand-in vLLM (Checked on kind). The SkyPilot provisioner has started one replica on a real cloud: one A10 on Lambda, serving gpt-oss-20b on real vLLM. That start found the driver and image problems below and gave the cold start its numbers (Cold starts). Nothing else has run on a real cloud yet: no cluster has been scaled, preempted or drained through Merit Order, no lease has run out on a real machine, and no GPU cost has been compared with a bill. The replica gate and its lease have also run on a laptop, against a stand-in vLLM (tests/test_skypilot.py). scripts/skypilot_check.py is the full check to run next (Checking it on a real cloud).

The full decision logic, with every rule and default, is in 10: How it decides.

Lifecycle of a self-hosted model

Controller loop (every 60 s, --interval)

Only one controller acts at a time: each takes a Postgres advisory lock, and extra copies stand by. The active one checks every cycle that it still holds the lock (a dropped Postgres connection releases it, and a standby may then take it). When it can't confirm that, it stops acting until it holds the lock again. A Redis error while it waits for the next cycle or writes its heartbeat is logged; the controller goes on. It needs Postgres (MERITORDER_DATABASE_URL) and Redis, and picks up config versions saved from the console without a restart. An admin's GPU control wakes it at once instead of at the next cycle.

Each cycle the controller reads every ready replica's /metrics directly (when their addresses are known) rather than the load balancer's, which would answer for one replica only: its load, and its KV cache's size, use and token counters, which gateways estimate warm caches from (04). The deployment's utilization is the replicas' average.

A self-hosted model therefore needs a quality score: one the live quality source doesn't cover counts no auto demand (only requests that name it) until it gets a quality_override.

Why addressable demand: if the controller only counted traffic already sent to a model, a model that isn't running would never look worth starting, because auto routes its traffic elsewhere. So it counts what you currently pay for all traffic this model could serve (its quality meets the request's floor), at API-equivalent prices. That value doesn't drop when the GPUs start serving, so the controller doesn't flap.

The break-even test

demand_per_hour   = addressable API-equivalent spend per hour (max of the 1 h and 4 × 15 min windows)
throughput        = addressable tokens per second (same windows)

by_load           = ceil(throughput / (capacity_tokens_per_second × target_utilization))
keep              = replica_price × (1 + margin)                    what a running replica must cover
start             = keep × (cold_start + hold_minutes) / hold_minutes   what one more replica must cover
kept              = min(running, floor(demand_per_hour / keep))
affordable        = kept + floor((demand_per_hour − kept × keep) / start)   (just kept, if kept < running)
replica_price     = cheapest SkyPilot catalog offer in the allowed clouds/regions,
                    or on Kubernetes the node type's configured price, else gpu_cost_per_hour
desired_replicas  = clamp(min(by_load ≥ 1, affordable), min_replicas, max_replicas)
                    (min_replicas alone when there's no demand at all, whatever the price)

A GPU with no price never starts. On SkyPilot and Kubernetes, a replica whose price is 0 or unknown (SkyPilot's catalog gave none and gpu_cost_per_hour is 0) isn't started, pinned or not: no GPU budget or fleet cap could hold it, and nothing it cost would be counted. The deployment's note says so. A Kubernetes deployment with neither a priced node type nor gpu_cost_per_hour is refused when the configuration is loaded. A static server (your own hardware) may have no price: it has no cloud bill, and it runs while there is demand for it (or min_replicas).

running is the replicas the deployment has now (starting, warm or draining). cold_start is the expected time from the launch request to a ready replica: the average of the deployment's last 10 starts, or serve.cold_start_minutes (12) until one has been measured; 0 for a server you run yourself (static).

Why the cold start counts. A replica bills from its launch, and during the cold start it serves nothing. Once warm, the controller keeps it at least hold_minutes. So a start is worth it only if the demand pays for the cold start as well, over that hold. With the defaults (a 12 minute cold start, a 30 minute hold, a 20% margin), a replica that isn't running needs demand of 1.2 × 42/30 = 1.68 × its price per hour to start, and a running one needs 1.2 × to stay. A burst that would pay for a GPU once it's warm, but not for 12 paid idle minutes on top, leaves its traffic on the APIs. The gap between the two thresholds is also hysteresis: a replica that just started isn't stopped by the same small dip that would have kept it from starting. Each deployment's record shows what a start needs now (start_needs: the dollars an hour, the cold start used and whether it was measured), and the GPUs page shows it under "A start needs".

Defaults, per deployment under serve:: margin 0.2 (demand must pay 1.2 × the replica price), target_utilization 0.7, scale_up_after_minutes 10, hold_minutes 30, drain_minutes 15, provision_timeout_minutes 45, cold_start_minutes 12.

State machine (src/meritorder/gpu.py, pure and unit-tested):

From To When
api_only provisioning desired ≥ 1 continuously for scale_up_after_minutes (or min_replicas > 0)
provisioning warm replicas answer /v1/models
provisioning api_only failed or provision_timeout_minutes passed; 30-minute cooldown
warm warm replica count follows desired
warm draining desired = 0 for scale_up_after_minutes, and warm for at least hold_minutes
warm provisioning replicas stop answering (e.g. spot preemption); traffic goes to APIs until they're back
draining warm demand returns and the replicas are ready
draining api_only after drain_minutes; GPUs released
provisioning api_only the start call fails (SkyPilot can't be run, a region it can't place, the Kubernetes API refuses): whatever it made is torn down first; 30-minute cooldown
provisioning provisioning the start fails and so does the teardown: still tracked (and billed) as starting, and stopped every cycle until that works; then api_only with the cooldown
warm warm a scale call fails: the replicas that ran stay (and are billed), and the scale is tried again next cycle
any unchanged a stop fails: the deployment stays marked as running, and the stop is tried again every cycle
any api_only / draining an admin stops it, Stop all GPUs, or the GPU budget runs out (see Controls)
api_only provisioning an admin pins replicas: at once, skipping the wait and any cooldown (a start that fails while pinned ends the pin and cools down like any other; pinning it again retries at once)

Key details:

  • Free upgrades don't count. Traffic running above its floor because a GPU had headroom is excluded, so idle capacity can't keep itself alive by attracting traffic.
  • Batch work doesn't count either. Requests of a batch use a running deployment's headroom, at low priority, up to the shadow price's knee (02), but they're never part of the demand GPUs are started or kept for: they come in bursts a provider's batch API does at half price within hours, and the ledger sees them only once they're done. When live demand stops paying for a deployment it drains as usual, and its waiting batch work goes to the providers (decision 49).
  • Measured capacity, not benchmarks. capacity_tokens_per_second should be what one replica sustains at your latency target on real agent traffic (prefill-heavy).
  • Hysteresis everywhere. Margins, minimum hold time, the scale-up delay and the cold start a new replica must pay back stop flapping. A 20-minute cold start is expensive to waste.
  • Spot where it's safe. The controller launches a preempted SkyPilot replica again (on a spot node pool, the Kubernetes Deployment replaces it); overflow to the API covers the gap.

Will a GPU ever pay? (Models → GPU break-even)

Before configuring a deployment, the console's GPU break-even tab (Models page; also GET /v1/reports/gpu/breakeven, team leads and up) shows how much traffic one replica needs to pay for itself by the rule above, next to your traffic. Every open-weight model gets a replica sized to it and priced from SkyPilot's catalog:

  • Size. The model's weights as published, from Hugging Face: the size of its safetensors files (one copy, where a repository ships two formats, as Mistral's do), and from their metadata, how many parameters are in 16 bits, 8 bits or packed 4 bits. gpt-oss and Kimi ship MXFP4 and DeepSeek's experts are FP4, stored as bytes; the files' size tells them apart from real 8-bit weights. Kimi K3.1 is 1.56 TB, not the 2.8 TB its parameter count at a byte each would suggest. For a mixture-of-experts model, the parameters each token uses come from its name ("A3B") or are worked out from its config's layer sizes (gpt-oss-120b: 5.1B; Qwen3 Coder Next: 2.9B). A model with files but no metadata is sized from its files and the parameter count in its name; a gated one from its name at 16 bits, or not at all.
  • Weights: As published, FP8 or 4-bit. FP8 serves a 16-bit checkpoint in FP8, as vLLM's --quantization fp8 does (a checkpoint published already quantized is served as published). 4-bit serves every weight above 4 bits in 4, as a 4-bit checkpoint made from the published one would (AWQ, GPTQ, NVFP4): about 4.25 bits a weight with its scales. Quantizing changes what fits and how fast the GPUs compute; it doesn't change the quality scores, which are for the weights as published. The tab warns that a quantized model may score lower (coding usually suffers first), so measure it with an eval before routing on it.
  • Machine. Every machine whose GPUs hold the weights in 70% of their memory (the rest is the KV cache), on 1, 2, 4 or 8 GPUs (how vLLM splits a model), among the data-center GPUs the sizing knows: A10, A10G, L4, L40S, A100 (40 and 80 GB), H100 (and H100 NVL), GH200, H200, B200, B300 and MI300X. Of those, the one that pays from the least traffic: the cheapest per hour whose replica, when full, costs less per token than the API work it takes (plus the margin). The cheapest machine isn't always it: four-bit weights fit on old A100s that can't serve enough to pay, where a Blackwell machine can. When none can pay, the cheapest per token shows (or a cheaper machine within 10% of it), so never means never on any machine on offer. A model that needs more than one machine says so.
  • Price. SkyPilot's catalog, through SkyPilot itself: on-demand or spot prices (a switch on the tab) for every cloud it covers (AWS, GCP, Azure, Lambda, RunPod and Nebius by default, plus your deployments' clouds; the tab can narrow them), with the region and instance. These are prices only: launching on a cloud needs SkyPilot's support for it where the controller runs (Which clouds). When a report finds the prices over 6 hours old (or the model sizes over a week old), it shows the stored ones at once and fetches new ones in the background; the tab says so and updates when they're in (a lookup takes about a minute, two with downloads). Get latest prices has SkyPilot download its catalogs again now. A gateway runs one refresh at a time: a report or button press while one runs waits for it rather than starting another, since lookups at once slow each other down and starve the gateway. A lookup that fails says why (SkyPilot's last error line, or that it ran past 10 minutes), the tab shows that with the age of the prices it still uses, and reports try again after 5 minutes. Lookups never use cloud credentials: prices don't need them.
  • Throughput is an estimate: a share of the GPUs' peak dense compute (10% by default, adjustable) at two operations per active parameter per token, with input read from the prompt cache not computed again. The peak is at the precision the GPUs compute the weights in: FP8 weights at the FP8 rate on GPUs that have it (L4, L40S, H100 and later, MI300X); 4-bit weights at the FP8 rate on Blackwell (B200, B300), whose 4-bit kernels take 8-bit activations, and at 16 bits elsewhere (Hopper's 4-bit kernels dequantize the weights); everything else at 16 bits. A deployment's capacity_tokens_per_second (measure it) replaces the estimate, and its own GPUs, clouds and spot setting replace the sizing (a Kubernetes deployment uses its node type's price, a server you run its configured price).

What the tab shows:

  • Best level you can host, per task type: the open model with the highest score that fits on a machine on offer, its machine and price, and any better one that doesn't fit.
  • By quality level. A replica takes traffic that auto would otherwise send to the cheapest API model good enough for its level, so that model's price is the one to beat. For each level: that model and its price; the open model that qualifies and pays from the least traffic (or, if none can, comes closest), on its machine; the tokens per minute (and about how many requests an hour) that replica needs; and your average and busiest hour at that level. A level where no open model qualifies, or none fits on one machine, says so.
  • By open-weight model. Its size and replica, what the traffic it could serve actually cost per million tokens over the window (the controller's own measure), its own API price, what it needs, and a verdict: pays now, pays from a given traffic, or never.
  • Never means one replica can't get there at any traffic, on any machine on offer: at full load (its target utilization) the GPU costs more per token than the API, plus the margin, so more replicas wouldn't help either.

On 11 November 2026, with spot prices:

  • Level 1 paid with gpt-oss-20b on one L4 ($0.12 an hour on AWS), from about 72,000 tokens a minute.
  • At level 2, the closest was DeepSeek V4.1 Flash on eight B200s ($13.92 an hour on GCP) at $0.054 per million tokens against $0.065 on APIs. That's cheaper, but not by the 20% margin, so it never pays.
  • The best open coder was Kimi K3.1 (coding 2.7). It's published in 4 bits (1.56 TB) and fits on eight B300s ($20.08 an hour on AWS). Level 3 starts at Claude Haiku's 3.0, and no open model reached it, as published or quantized: the strongest open models already ship in 4 bits, so quantizing doesn't let a better one fit.
  • Qwen3 Coder, Qwen3 Coder Next, Devstral 2 and Qwen3 Coder 30B had no published score, so they don't count until they're measured.

Prices are blended for the traffic's mix of input, cached input, cache writes and output (a level or model with at least 20 requests uses its own, otherwise everyone's; with no traffic, an assumed agent-like mix). Free tiers don't count as the price to beat: they're rate-limited and can't take sustained traffic.

Where SkyPilot runs for prices. The gateway asks SkyPilot directly when it has it. The compose stack builds the gateway, worker and migrate images with SkyPilot in its own environment (SKYPILOT_VERSION, 0.14.2 by default; empty leaves it out), and the controller's image always has it. For meritorder run on a laptop, uv tool install "skypilot[aws,gcp,kubernetes,lambda]==0.14.2" puts it on the path. Without it (the Helm chart's gateways run the plain image; only the controller runs the -gpu one), the GPU controller publishes the prices every 6 hours and when someone asks for the latest, and the tab says if no controller is running.

Configuring a self-hosted model

backends:
  gpu-qwen-coder:
    kind: self_hosted
    format: openai
    gpu_cost_per_hour: 16.0          # one replica (here 4× H100)
    capacity_tokens_per_second: 4000
    serve:
      provisioner: skypilot          # or `kubernetes` (your cluster, below), or `static` for a server you already run
      model: qwen3-coder-next        # its hf_id is what vLLM serves
      accelerators: "H100:4"
      use_spot: true
      clouds: [aws, gcp, lambda]
      image: vllm/vllm-openai:v0.32.0-cu129
      vllm_args: "--max-model-len 262144"
      max_replicas: 4

The model also needs a route to the deployment with a price: at the API-equivalent rate: auto skips unpriced routes, and the router scales that price down while the GPUs have room (Overflow). Keep the API route for the same weights next to it:

models:
  qwen3-coder-next:
    hf_id: Qwen/Qwen3-Coder-Next
    routes:
      - {backend: gpu-qwen-coder, model: Qwen/Qwen3-Coder-Next, price: {input: 0.12, output: 0.80, cache_read: 0.07}}
      - {backend: openrouter, model: qwen/qwen3-coder-next}

The SkyPilot provisioner turns this into one SkyPilot cluster per replica (below). It needs SkyPilot and cloud credentials where the controller runs (sky check). Set HF_TOKEN there for gated models: it goes to the machines as a SkyPilot secret. Under serve:, lease_minutes (15) and autostop_minutes (5) bound how long a replica outlives its controller (The lease), port (8000) is the one port each replica opens, and ssh_tunnel (auto) says when to reach it through the controller instead. vllm_args is a list of arguments, read the way a shell splits words (shlex.split: quote a value with spaces), never a shell fragment: each token reaches vLLM as written, quoted in SkyPilot's run script and passed as a list on Kubernetes, so ; or $(...) is text, not a command. It can't turn on vLLM's request logging (--enable-log-requests, --enable-log-outputs, also spelled with underscores or shortened as vLLM's parser allows): it would write prompts to the replica's log. The check runs on the tokens, so quoting can't hide the flag. cold_start_minutes, load_format and weights_cache are about starts: Cold starts.

The image and the NVIDIA driver. The default image is vllm/vllm-openai:v0.32.0-cu129, vLLM 0.32.0 built for CUDA 12.9.1. vLLM's plain tags (v0.32.0, v0.33.0) are CUDA 13.0.2 builds, and v0.33.0 has no CUDA 12.9 build (Docker Hub, November 2026). CUDA 13 images need NVIDIA driver 580 or newer (580.65.06). An older driver runs the CUDA 12 runtime through minor version compatibility, but not everything built against a newer 12.x toolkit: on Lambda's A10, driver 570.148.08 (CUDA 12.8 at most), the CUDA 12.9.1 image failed at startup to load torchcodec's library (checked live, 15 November 2026). So when nvidia-smi reports an older CUDA than the image's, minor versions included, the replica's gate starts vLLM with NVIDIA's forward-compatibility libraries: the image's /usr/local/cuda/compat (vLLM's images install cuda-compat) first on LD_LIBRARY_PATH, and VLLM_ENABLE_CUDA_COMPATIBILITY=1. Forward compatibility works on data-center GPUs (A10, A100, H100, L4 and the like), not GeForce cards. Cloud GPU images often ship a 535, 550 or 570 driver. The gate logs the driver, the image's CUDA and whether it used the compat libraries; when the driver is too old even so, it says so plainly in the replica's failure reason (When a replica fails).

A broken optional package in the image. vLLM v0.32.0-cu129 (torch 2.13.0+cu129) bundles torchcodec 0.17.0 built for CUDA 13: it links libcudart.so.13, which the image doesn't have, so importing it raises an OSError. vLLM's guarded import catches ImportError and RuntimeError only, so vLLM died at startup on every machine (found on Lambda and reproduced in the image on a laptop, 15 November 2026). Before it starts vLLM, the gate imports each optional package vLLM can do without (OPTIONAL_PACKAGES in replica_gate.py: torchcodec, for audio input) and uninstalls one that fails with an OSError, and says so in the replica's log. vLLM then runs without audio input.

Keeping sessions on their replica. Each replica has its own KV cache, so gateways send a session's turns to the replica that served its last one, while it's ready, has room, and isn't so busy that rebuilding the cache on an idle replica costs less (03). SkyPilot replicas have no load balancer in front, so the gateway picks one for every request (the cheapest by the same formula: the least loaded, or the one holding the session's cache), and replica_affinity can't be turned off there. Their addresses come from SkyPilot (each cluster's head IP and port); the gateways must be able to reach them, or go through the controller's SSH tunnel (Reaching the replicas). For a server you run, list each replica:

    serve:
      provisioner: static
      model: qwen3-coder-next
      static_url: http://vllm-lb.internal:8000/v1           # optional: used when no replica answers directly
      static_urls: [http://gpu-a.internal:8000/v1, http://gpu-b.internal:8000/v1]
      replica_affinity: true                                 # default; false lets the load balancer pick
      kv_events: true                                        # follow vLLM's KV events (default false)
      kv_events_port: 5557

With kv_events: true the controller follows each replica's KV-cache events and knows when a session's cached blocks are evicted; SkyPilot and Kubernetes deployments get vLLM's --kv-events-config, and SkyPilot opens the port. Set it only where that port is on a private network: the events carry token ids, the gate doesn't cover them, and SkyPilot opens a port to anyone who can reach the VM (on Lambda, to the whole account). For a static server, start vLLM with --kv-events-config '{"enable_kv_cache_events":true,"publisher":"zmq","endpoint":"tcp://*:5557"}' (vLLM 0.30 or later tags events with the session) and --enable-prompt-tokens-details. Without events, eviction is estimated from each replica's metrics. Details: 04.

How SkyPilot runs a deployment

Not run on a real cloud yet. Everything in this section is what the code does, checked in CI against a stand-in SkyPilot package and a stand-in vLLM (tests/test_skypilot.py). What SkyPilot itself does is from its source and docs, version 0.14.2, read in November 2026. scripts/skypilot_check.py runs the whole cycle on a real cloud (below); until someone has run it, treat this as unverified.

Merit Order runs one plain SkyPilot cluster per replica and does the rest itself (decision 56): the controller decides how many replicas run, the gateways send each request to a replica directly, and the controller probes them. SkyPilot does what it's good at: finding capacity across the allowed clouds and regions (and failing over between them), setting the machine up (the vLLM image, the port, the disk, the labels), its price catalog, autostop and teardown. There's no SkyServe controller VM: nothing runs that isn't a replica, so nothing runs that isn't priced.

Names. Replica n of deployment <backend> is the cluster mo-<install id>-<backend>-<n> (the backend name lowercased, other characters turned into -, at most 24, with 4 characters of its hash when that changed it). The install id is 8 random characters made once and kept in Postgres (gpu_install_id; MERITORDER_INSTALL_ID sets it), so two Merit Order installs on one cloud account never see, let alone tear down, each other's clusters. Every instance also carries the labels meritorder-deployment: <backend> (for matching bills, What GPUs cost) and meritorder-install: <install id>, on the clouds that take labels (AWS tags, GCP labels; not Lambda).

Calls. SkyPilot runs in its own Python, so the controller runs a small script there (or in-process when SkyPilot is importable where the controller runs) that calls the SDK's sky.launch, sky.down and sky.status and answers in JSON. Launches run in the background, so a cycle never waits for one.

When What the controller does
Start, or more replicas sky.launch for each missing cluster, with idle_minutes_to_autostop=autostop_minutes, down=True, wait_for=jobs (and the same in the task's resources.autostop)
Fewer replicas sky.down of the highest-numbered clusters
Stop sky.down of every cluster of the deployment, waited for; a cluster that's already gone counts as stopped
Every cycle sky.status (refreshed from the clouds) of this install's clusters, once for all deployments; then for each wanted cluster that's UP: renew its lease, probe /v1/models, read /metrics
A cluster is on Kubernetes or RunPod sky.endpoints once, for the address its port is mapped to (Reaching the replicas)
A wanted cluster is UP without autodown (a launch cut short before SkyPilot set it, someone's sky autostop) sky.autostop with down=True, wait_for=jobs again, at most every 10 minutes
A cluster is STOPPED (a spot machine preempted on Azure or Nebius, someone's sky stop) sky.down: a stopped machine bills for its disk and can't delete itself
A wanted cluster is missing or stuck in INIT with no launch under way (the controller restarted mid-launch, a spot preemption) Launch it again
A launch fails (no capacity in any allowed place) Read sky logs --tail for why, tear down whatever it made, show why, try that replica again after 10 minutes. If every wanted replica failed, the start has failed: 30-minute cooldown
vLLM exits before it was ever ready (it crashed, the driver is too old for the image) Read why from the gate, tear the cluster down at once, and wait as after a failed launch before launching it again, so a crash loop doesn't keep paying for machines
vLLM exits after it was ready (out of memory under load, a GPU fault) Read why from the gate (its last 40 lines go to the log), tear the cluster down at once rather than leave it idle until autostop, and launch it again. A second such crash within an hour waits 10 minutes, as after a failed launch
A wanted cluster goes away while the deployment drains Not launched again: the deployment is on its way down
A cluster goes away before vLLM was ever ready (the image wouldn't start, the gate exited unseen) The same wait before launching it again

A replica is PROVISIONING while SkyPilot launches it, STARTING until its gate answers and vLLM answers /v1/models, then READY. Its address is http://<head IP>:<port>/v1. When the controller restarts, it takes the replica count from the deployment's last published record, so it wants the same clusters it wanted before; after a config change, each deployment's new provisioner takes over its old one's launches and waits.

The task. What each field comes from:

Field Value
resources.accelerators serve.accelerators (default H100:8)
resources.use_spot serve.use_spot (default false)
resources.any_of With serve.regions: one infra: <cloud>/<region> for each pair SkyPilot's catalog has these GPUs in (at the spot or on-demand price, per use_spot), among serve.clouds if set. So a region goes only with its own cloud, and the launch goes exactly where the expected price came from. Without regions: one infra: <cloud> per cloud in serve.clouds. With neither: left out, and SkyPilot picks the cheapest offer among the clouds sky check enables that can run it (Docker images, autodown and ports: it skips the others)
resources.image_id docker:<serve.image> (default vllm/vllm-openai:v0.32.0-cu129; pin one you have tested)
resources.disk_size serve.disk_size_gb (default 1000; Lambda's disks are fixed by instance type)
resources.ports serve.port (8000), the gate; plus kv_events_port when kv_events is on. Nothing else. Given with each any_of entry, and left out for clouds where SkyPilot can't open ports (Vast, Mithril, Slurm): asking for them there would rule the cloud out, and those replicas are reached over SSH
resources.labels meritorder-deployment: <backend>, meritorder-install: <install id>
resources.autostop {idle_minutes: autostop_minutes, down: true, wait_for: jobs}, always
envs MERITORDER_KEY_SHA256 (the key's hash, not the key), MERITORDER_LEASE_SECONDS, MERITORDER_PORT, MERITORDER_UPSTREAM_PORT
secrets HF_TOKEN, from the controller's environment when it's set (a SkyPilot secret: not in the task file)
run Writes the gate (replica_gate.py) to /tmp and runs python3 /tmp/meritorder_gate.py -- vllm serve <hf_id> --host 127.0.0.1 --port 8001 with the flags in Inside the GPU pool, then vllm_args, each token shell-quoted

The key

Every replica lets in only callers with its deployment's key. The key is an HMAC of this install's secret and the deployment's name, which the controller and every gateway work out for themselves; the secret is made once and kept in Postgres (gpu_replica_secret; MERITORDER_GPU_KEY sets it, the same on every process), like the learned router's hashing key. Gateways send it as Authorization: Bearer to the replicas of every SkyPilot deployment (a backend's own auth doesn't apply there).

The machine never gets the key itself, only its SHA-256. The reason is SkyPilot's API server: it keeps every launch request, the task's environment and secrets included, in its database (~/.sky/api_server/requests.db in 0.14.2). So vLLM doesn't get --api-key either: it listens on the loopback address only, behind the gate, a small standard-library Python program that is the only thing on the open port. The gate checks the key on each connection's first request, on every path (vLLM's own --api-key covers only paths under /v1, leaving /metrics, /tokenize and /invocations open), answers 401 without it, and then passes the connection to vLLM byte for byte. A connection has 5 seconds to send that first request, and at most 256 may be waiting to show the key at once (MAX_UNVERIFIED); past that a new connection is closed straight away, so a scan or a flood of idle connections can't use up the replica's sockets. Connections that showed the key aren't counted. Rotating the secret changes every key; replicas started before then refuse the new one, so stop them first.

Traffic to the replicas is plain HTTP, as before: the key and the prompts cross the network unencrypted. Keep the gateways and the GPUs on a network you trust, or reach them through the SSH tunnel below.

The lease

The gate also holds a lease. The controller renews it every cycle (POST /meritorder/lease with the key) for each cluster it wants. When it isn't renewed for lease_minutes (15 by default; at least 3), the gate stops vLLM (SIGTERM, then SIGKILL after 30 s) and exits. That ends the task, the cluster has nothing running, and SkyPilot's autostop, set with down: true at launch, deletes it autostop_minutes (5) later. The lease starts when the gate does, so a replica whose controller never comes back stops too.

How SkyPilot 0.14.2 decides a cluster is idle (sky/skylet/events.py, StopEvent): every 60 seconds the skylet on the head node counts the cluster's jobs that aren't finished (job_lib.is_cluster_idle) and, with the default wait_for: jobs_and_ssh, open SSH sessions. Merit Order sets wait_for: jobs, so an SSH session (the tunnel below, or someone logged in) doesn't keep a machine alive. When nothing has run for idle_minutes, it tears the cluster down from the machine itself, with the cloud credentials SkyPilot put there at launch. The chain is lease runs out → the gate exits → the job ends → idle → down: all of it on the machine, so it holds when the controller is dead, its laptop sleeps, the network drops, or ~/.sky is lost. A replica therefore costs at most about lease_minutes + autostop_minutes + 2 minutes after the controller last renewed it (22 by default). The same holds when vLLM exits by itself: the gate exits with it, after the controller has read why or 2 minutes have passed (When a replica fails).

The controller warns at startup when its cycle (--interval, 60 s) is so long that three missed cycles outlast the shortest lease.

Leases while things fail. The leases are renewed first thing in each cycle, before the controller reads the ledger, the controls or its own settings, each deployment on its own: a Postgres outage, or one deployment's error, doesn't cut them. When Redis can't say what runs either, the replicas this process already asked for are renewed. Listing the clusters (sky.status) and asking for a replica's address give up after 60 s (STATUS_TIMEOUT); launches and teardowns keep their longer timeouts. When SkyPilot can't be asked (its API server hung or down), the last list it gave stands in for up to an hour (STALE_SECONDS, counted to when the failed call was made), so leases are still renewed meanwhile; after that, each replica stops when its lease runs out.

What the lease doesn't cover. SkyPilot sets autostop after the machine is up and set up (execution.py, the PRE_EXEC stage, after provisioning and the image pull), the same way on every cloud. A launch interrupted before then (the controller's container killed mid-launch, with its local API server) can leave a machine without autostop or a gate. When the controller comes back with its ~/.sky, it launches a wanted one again (which sets autostop), sets autodown again on an UP one that shows none, and the sweep tears down the rest; without ~/.sky too, SkyPilot no longer knows the machine, and you'd find it by its name, mo-<install id>-..., in the cloud's console. Keep ~/.sky on a volume. Two more gaps, per cloud (Which clouds): a spot machine preempted on Azure or Nebius is stopped rather than deleted, and a stopped machine runs no skylet, so only the controller deletes it; and on the clouds Merit Order refuses, there's no autodown at all.

When a replica fails

A failed replica's machine is deleted, and vLLM's output with it, so the controller reads why first.

  • The gate keeps vLLM's last output. vLLM's stdout and stderr go to the task's log as before (sky logs), and the gate also keeps the last 200 lines in memory. It runs nvidia-smi once at start for the driver version, the newest CUDA that driver runs and the GPUs, and reads the image's CUDA version (CUDA_VERSION, else /usr/local/cuda/version.json). GET /meritorder/status, with the deployment's key like the lease, returns all of it with vLLM's state, exit status and uptime. Anything in a line that looks like a key or token (a bearer token, a value named like a key, token, secret or password, hf_/sk-/AWS key ids, a run of 32 or more letters and digits) is replaced by [redacted]. A line from vLLM's request logger, which would hold a prompt, is left out (request logging is off, and vllm_args can't turn it on).
  • The gate stays to say why. When vLLM exits by itself, the gate keeps answering until the controller has read /meritorder/status, for at most 2 minutes (MERITORDER_LINGER_SECONDS) or until the lease runs out. Then it exits as before. When the lease runs out or the gate is asked to stop, it exits at once.
  • The controller reads it. Each cycle the lease renewal says whether vLLM is still running. When it has exited, the controller reads the gate's status once, and tears the replica down at once. A replica that was never ready waits 10 minutes before it's launched again; one that was ready is launched again at once, unless it's the second crash within an hour, which waits the same 10 minutes. Before a failed launch is torn down, and before the controller stops a deployment with failed replicas, it reads the same, or sky logs --tail 40 (sky.tail_logs) when the gate doesn't answer. Reading never holds a teardown up by more than 25 seconds.
  • Where it shows. The failure reason (for example "vLLM exited with status 1 before it was ready: the NVIDIA driver 535.129.03 (CUDA 12.2 at most) is too old for this image's CUDA 13.0.2: CUDA 13 images need driver 580.65.06 or newer") is on the replica and the deployment. The controller's log has it with the driver and CUDA versions and the last 40 lines. The GPU activity log has a replica_failed entry with the same: the console shows the reason and versions, and the lines under Last 40 lines of output. scripts/skypilot_check.py prints them when a start fails.

The sweep

Every controller cycle, and on the first one after it starts, the controller lists every SkyPilot cluster whose name starts with this install's prefix (mo-<install id>-) and tears down each one no deployment wants now: one of a backend that was renamed, removed or switched off, a teardown that failed, a launch that finished after its deployment was stopped, or a scale cut short by a crash. Each is logged, and recorded in the GPU activity log (sweep, with the cluster, its status and where it ran; a teardown that fails is an error, tried again next cycle). Clusters of other installs and anything else on the account are never touched. It runs while a SkyPilot deployment is configured or the last sweep found leftovers, and once at startup either way.

Kubernetes has a sweep of its own (Kubernetes).

Reaching the replicas

Gateways and the controller reach each replica's gate on its open port. Where that isn't possible, the controller opens an SSH tunnel to the gate, ssh -N -L with the SSH config SkyPilot writes for each cluster (~/.sky/generated/ssh/<cluster>), and publishes the tunnel's address as the replica's: MERITORDER_TUNNEL_HOST (default 127.0.0.1; in Compose, controller) on a port of its own. serve.ssh_tunnel decides:

ssh_tunnel When a replica goes through a tunnel
auto (default) Where SkyPilot can't open the port (Vast, Mithril and Slurm, always; Lambda's us-south-1, which has no firewall rules), and when connections to the port time out from the controller for 3 cycles in a row (a firewall that drops them)
always Every replica
never None. A deployment that may launch on Vast, Mithril or Slurm is refused with never

Where the address comes from, without a tunnel: the cluster's head IP and port on most clouds. On Kubernetes (a LoadBalancer service by default, or an ingress) and RunPod (a public port mapped at launch), the port is published somewhere else, so the controller asks SkyPilot (sky.endpoints) once per cluster.

KV events aren't tunneled: follow them only on a private network. A tunnel carries all of the replica's traffic through the controller's host, so it's a fallback, not the way to run a busy fleet.

Which clouds

  • serve.clouds limits where a deployment may launch, and serve.regions where in them. Each region is paired only with the clouds that have these GPUs in it, from SkyPilot's catalog, and the expected price is looked up in exactly those places, so the launch and the price agree. regions without clouds pairs each region with every cloud that has it. A region SkyPilot's catalog can't place (or no catalog at all) fails the start with that reason. Empty clouds: any cloud SkyPilot has credentials for (sky check) and can run a replica on.
  • What the images support. The -gpu image installs SkyPilot 0.14.2 with the extra of every cloud a replica can run on (the SKYPILOT_EXTRAS build argument, below), plus the ssh and rsync clients SkyPilot sets machines up with. Credentials for each: 07.
  • Prices cover more clouds than launches. Catalog prices need no credentials, so the break-even tab can show a cloud you can't launch on yet.
  • The shipped config's gpu-qwen-coder example uses clouds: [aws, gcp, lambda] with spot H100s (so AWS and GCP only: Lambda has no spot), and is off until MERITORDER_SKYPILOT=true. gpu-small (gpt-oss-20b on one A10 on Lambda) is off until MERITORDER_SKYPILOT_SMALL=true.

A replica works the same on every cloud only if three things hold there: SkyPilot runs the vLLM image (image_id: docker:), the machine deletes itself when its task ends (autostop with down, "autodown"), and the controller can reach the gate. The table is what SkyPilot 0.14.2 does on each cloud it supports, read from its source in November 2026 (paths are under sky/ in the installed package; the numbers point to the sources below the table). Nothing here has been run on a real cloud yet.

Where a replica can run. On AWS, GCP, Azure, Lambda, RunPod, Nebius, Kubernetes (CoreWeave included), Vast, Fluidstack, Paperspace, DigitalOcean, Mithril, Seeweb, and Slurm with Pyxis. SkyPilot can't run a Docker image on OCI, Cudo, Shadeform, SCP, vSphere or IBM, and can't make a machine delete itself on Hyperbolic, PrimeIntellect, Verda or Yotta: a deployment that names one of these in serve.clouds is refused when the config loads, with the reason. With clouds empty, SkyPilot skips them by itself, because the launch asks for Docker and autodown and it fails over past clouds that lack a feature it asks for [31].

Cloud (pip extra) How the machine deletes itself, and what credential it holds Ports Stop, and what bills after one Docker image Spot
AWS (aws) The skylet terminates it with the skypilot-v1 IAM instance role SkyPilot attaches: AmazonEC2FullAccess and AmazonS3FullAccess on the account [1]. It drops any AWS keys from its own environment first, so the role is what it uses [2]. With static keys in the controller's ~/.aws/credentials, SkyPilot still copies that file to the machine [3] A security group per cluster, the port open to 0.0.0.0/0; deleted at teardown, or after autodown at the controller's next status refresh [4] Supported for on-demand; EBS volumes bill while stopped Yes Yes. Terminated when interrupted
GCP (gcp) The skylet deletes it with Google's default credentials, which are your copied gcloud files (~/.config/gcloud, with application_default_credentials.json) when there are any [5]. The machine also has the skypilot-v1 service account (compute.admin, storage.admin, iam.serviceAccountUser on the project) [6], used when nothing is copied A firewall rule per cluster, by network tag; deleted at teardown [7] Supported; the persistent disk bills while stopped Yes Yes. instanceTerminationAction: DELETE: a preempted machine is deleted [8]
Azure (azure) The skylet deletes the cluster's resource group with the Azure CLI credential, the only one SkyPilot's Azure client uses [9]: your copied ~/.azure, the az login token cache, good for every tenant and subscription that login reaches. The machine also gets a managed identity, Contributor on its own resource group [10], which 0.14.2 never uses, so keeping the CLI cache off the machine (remote_identity: SERVICE_ACCOUNT or NO_UPLOAD) would leave it unable to delete itself A rule in the cluster's own network security group, deleted with its resource group Supported (deallocate); managed disks bill while deallocated Yes Yes, but the eviction policy is Azure's default, Deallocate: a preempted machine is stopped, its disk billing, until the controller tears it down [11]
Lambda (lambda) The skylet terminates it with the copied ~/.lambda_cloud/lambda_keys: an API key for the whole account [12] One firewall rule for the whole account, the port open to 0.0.0.0/0 for every instance, never removed (other clusters may use it). None in us-south-1, which has no firewall rules: tunneled [13] No stop Yes (Lambda has no custom machine images, but Docker images are a separate feature) No
RunPod (runpod) The copied ~/.runpod/config.toml, a RunPod API key Mapped at launch to a public port on another number; Merit Order asks SkyPilot for it [14] No stop Yes: the pod runs the image itself Yes (interruptible pods)
Nebius (nebius) The copied ~/.nebius/credentials.json, a service-account key (scope it with Nebius IAM), and the tenant id A security group per cluster. Autodown can't delete it (the machine is gone first): SkyPilot does at the controller's next status refresh [15] Supported; disks bill while stopped Yes Yes, with the preemption policy STOP: a preempted machine is stopped, its disk billing [16]
Kubernetes (kubernetes); CoreWeave through it The pod deletes itself, and its services, with SkyPilot's service account, which may do anything in its namespace [17]. Your kubeconfig isn't copied: remote_identity defaults to SERVICE_ACCOUNT there [18] A LoadBalancer service by default (or an ingress, or the pod IP), deleted with the pod [19]; Merit Order asks SkyPilot for the address No stop Yes: the pod's image Only on clusters whose nodes carry a spot label
Vast (vast) The copied ~/.config/vastai/vast_api_key None: 0.14.2 doesn't pass ports when it creates the instance, and forwards only 8080 through Vast's gateway [20]. SSH tunnel, always Supported; storage bills while stopped Yes Yes (interruptible)
Fluidstack (fluidstack) The copied ~/.fluidstack/api_key Every port is open by default [21] No stop Yes No
Paperspace (paperspace) The copied ~/.paperspace/config.json SkyPilot does nothing [22]: reachable if the machine's network allows; ssh_tunnel: auto tunnels after 3 timeouts Supported; storage bills while stopped Yes No
DigitalOcean (do) The copied ~/.config/doctl/config.yaml, an API token (DigitalOcean's custom scopes can limit it to droplets) Every port is open by default [23] Supported; a powered-off droplet bills in full Yes No
Mithril (mithril) The copied ~/.config/mithril/config.yaml SkyPilot can't open ports there [24]: SSH tunnel, always Supported by SkyPilot Yes Yes
Seeweb (seeweb) The copied ~/.seeweb_cloud/seeweb_keys Every port is open by default [25] Supported Yes No
