Slurm (slurm) No cloud credential: down cancels the job. Autodown only for container jobs, on clusters with Pyxis [26] None: SSH tunnel, always Only with Pyxis Only with Pyxis No
OCI (oci), Cudo (cudo), Shadeform (shadeform), SCP (scp), vSphere (vsphere), IBM (ibm) Refused: no Docker images there in 0.14.2 [27] No
Hyperbolic (hyperbolic), PrimeIntellect (primeintellect), Verda (verda), Yotta (yotta) Refused: no autodown there in 0.14.2, so a replica whose controller is gone would bill until someone deleted it [28] No stop

The same on every cloud:

  • Autostop is set after setup. SkyPilot sets it in the PRE_EXEC stage, after provisioning, the image pull and setup, through the skylet, for every cloud alike (Kubernetes also gets it as pod annotations) [30]. That's the gap The lease describes.
  • Down always means delete. The skylet's autostop with down calls the cloud's terminate_instances, never stop_instances [32]; Merit Order launches with down=True, puts down: true in the task, tears down with sky.down (which deletes), sets autodown again on a cluster that shows none, and tears down any cluster it finds STOPPED.
  • Every cloud's credentials go to every machine. SkyPilot copies the credential files of every cloud it finds where the controller runs to every cluster it launches, whichever cloud that is [29]: a Lambda replica gets your AWS keys too, if they're there. The exceptions are the cloud a cluster runs on, when its remote_identity isn't LOCAL_CREDENTIALS, and any cloud whose remote_identity is NO_UPLOAD, both in ~/.sky/config.yaml (for AWS and GCP only there: a task can't set them [33]).

So where self-deletion is safe depends on the cloud. On AWS, and on GCP with remote_identity: SERVICE_ACCOUNT, the machine deletes itself with an identity of its own, nothing to steal but what that role may do (broad: all of EC2 and S3, or compute and storage admin on the project). On every other cloud it deletes itself with a long-lived key that is copied onto it: an account-wide API key on Lambda, RunPod, Vast, Fluidstack, Paperspace, DigitalOcean, Mithril and Seeweb, a service-account key on Nebius, and on Azure your own az login. Anyone who gets onto a replica (vLLM runs in the same container as the gate) can read it. So:

  • Give SkyPilot keys of their own, made for it alone, that you can revoke: a separate Lambda, RunPod or Vast API key; a Nebius service account limited to the project; a DigitalOcean token with only droplet scopes; for Azure, log the controller in with a service principal that is Contributor on one subscription (az login --service-principal), not your own account. The controller warns when the config loads, for each key it finds that SkyPilot will copy.
  • Keep other clouds' keys off the machines: mount only the credentials of the clouds you launch on, and set remote_identity in SkyPilot's config:
# ~/.sky/config.yaml where the controller runs (or the file SKYPILOT_GLOBAL_CONFIG names)
aws:
  remote_identity: NO_UPLOAD        # AWS machines delete themselves with the skypilot-v1 role; no keys copied anywhere
gcp:
  remote_identity: SERVICE_ACCOUNT  # GCP machines use the skypilot-v1 service account; your gcloud files stay here
# and for a cloud whose credentials are here but you don't launch on, e.g.:
# lambda:
#   remote_identity: NO_UPLOAD

Don't set NO_UPLOAD or SERVICE_ACCOUNT for Azure, Lambda, RunPod, Nebius, Vast, Fluidstack, Paperspace, DigitalOcean, Mithril or Seeweb if you launch there: their machines need the key to delete themselves.

Image size. All the extras above make SkyPilot's environment in the -gpu image about 2 GB, up from about 0.8 GB with only aws,gcp,kubernetes,lambda (measured in November 2026: 2.0 and 0.8 GB for Linux x86-64 and Python 3.12, 2.2 and 0.8 GB for Linux arm64 and Python 3.14). Azure's CLI and SDKs are about 1 GB of it. --build-arg SKYPILOT_EXTRAS=aws,gcp,kubernetes,lambda (or any list) builds a smaller one. OCI's SDK would add about 0.5 GB for a cloud Merit Order can't use, so it isn't in the default.

Checking it on a real cloud

scripts/skypilot_check.py runs a full cycle against a running gateway and controller, through Merit Order's API, on any cloud a replica can run on (--cloud, Lambda by default). It picks the cheapest GPU on that cloud that holds the model (gpu-small's gpt-oss-20b: its size from Hugging Face, the price from SkyPilot's catalog as the controller sees it, as the break-even tab sizes replicas; one A10 on Lambda), prints what one replica costs an hour and what the run should cost, and says how to set the deployment to that GPU and cloud if it isn't. Then it starts one replica and waits until it's warm, sends a few requests pinned to it, checks that the replica answers 401 without the key, with a wrong key and on /metrics, scales to zero and checks the cluster is gone, then starts one again, stops the controller, and checks that the machine deletes itself within the lease plus autostop. "Gone" is checked twice: in SkyPilot's list, and in the cloud's own list of instances (sky.provision.query_instances for that cloud, with what SkyPilot recorded about the cluster while it ran; this needs SkyPilot's state where the script asks, so not with a remote API server, and says so). It prints the time and the estimated cost at each step, needs --yes-spend, and always unpins, restarts the controller and tears down anything left in a finally. It asks SkyPilot about the clusters as the controller sees them: in the Compose controller's container by default (--sky local for a controller on the same machine). Usually 45 to 75 minutes of one machine (about $1 to $1.60 on a Lambda A10). When the controller gives up on a start (the deployment goes back to API only, or gets a failure cooldown), the script stops at once: it prints why each replica failed, with the driver and CUDA versions and vLLM's last 40 lines from the GPU activity log, unpins in the finally, and exits with status 1. It has run once, on Lambda: with the CUDA 13 image, vLLM stopped before it was ready, and the cause was lost with the machine.

SkyPilot's state

SkyPilot keeps its state in ~/.sky of the user the controller runs as (its local API server, the SSH keys and per-cluster SSH configs it makes, and its record of the clusters it launched) and reads cloud credentials from the usual places (~/.lambda_cloud, ~/.aws, ~/.config/gcloud, and so on). Losing ~/.sky doesn't leave a GPU running for long: each replica stops when its lease runs out. But a controller that keeps it sees and stops its clusters at once, so keep it on a volume.

  • Compose: mount ~/.sky (a named volume, sky-state) and the credentials into the controller service (the lines are commented out in compose.yaml; 07).
  • Helm: controller.skypilot gives the controller a writable home (a claim the chart makes, one of yours, or an emptyDir) and mounts credential Secrets inside it (07).

Cold starts

The first real start on Lambda (one A10, gpt-oss-20b, vllm/vllm-openai:v0.32.0-cu129, November 2026) took about 11 minutes from the launch to a warm replica: about 8 for the machine to boot, SkyPilot to set it up and Docker to pull the ~10 GB image, and about 3 to download ~13 GB of weights from Hugging Face and load them. Those 11 minutes bill without serving, which is why the break-even counts them (The break-even test).

What a start is made of

Every SkyPilot replica's start is timed in phases. The controller marks when it asked SkyPilot for the launch and when SkyPilot's launch returned; the replica's gate marks the rest on the machine (startup in the gate's /meritorder/status and in every lease reply):

Phase From To What happens
machine boots launch requested (controller) machine booted (/proc/uptime) the cloud finds capacity and boots the VM
image pull machine booted container started (PID 1 in /proc) SkyPilot sets up Docker's GPU runtime, pulls the image, starts the container
SkyPilot setup container started SkyPilot's launch returned (controller) SkyPilot's runtime in the container, the task submitted
task start launch returned gate started usually zero: the task starts as the launch returns
GPU check gate started vLLM started nvidia-smi, the broken-package check
weights download vLLM started vLLM logs Time spent downloading weights Hugging Face download (vLLM prints it only when it took over 0.5 s)
weights load download vLLM logs Model loading took … seconds (or Loading weights took) the weights into GPU memory
engine start weights loaded vLLM's port takes a connection memory profiling, torch.compile, CUDA graphs, the KV cache
first ready probe listening the controller's probe of /v1/models answers up to one controller cycle (60 s)

A mark that isn't known (no download line on a warm cache, an older gate) merges its phase into the next one ("weights download + weights load"). The controller's marks and the machine's are on two clocks, both normally kept by NTP, so a phase across them is clamped at zero; the phases add up to the total. Only a launch the controller made itself, in this process, is timed: after a restart, when it was asked for isn't known, and nothing is made up.

When a replica is first ready, the controller logs its phases, writes a replica_ready entry to the GPU activity log (the phases, the total, and vLLM's own download and load seconds), and adds the total to the deployment's rolling average (cold_start in its record: the last 10 starts, their average and the last one's phases). The break-even uses that average. On Kubernetes the start is timed as a whole, from the controller's start to the first ready replica. The GPUs page shows each replica's start under its status ("started in 11.2 min", the phases on hover), the last start and what a start needs in the deployment's cost column, and the replica_ready entries in the activity log. scripts/skypilot_check.py prints the phases each time the replica is warm.

Faster starts

What each change saves is an estimate for the Lambda A10 run above, not measured yet.

Change On by default Expected saving Trade-off
Xet high-performance downloads (HF_XET_HIGH_PERFORMANCE=1) yes, every replica none over vLLM 0.32's own default (it sets this itself when unset); it keeps the fast path with other images uses every core and the whole link while it downloads
serve.load_format (runai_streamer, fastsafetensors) no (auto) perhaps 10 to 60 s of the load for a 13 GB model; more for large models not checked with every model (gpt-oss's MXFP4 weights are unconfirmed); a model that fails to load shows in its replica_failed entry
serve.weights_cache: volume no most of the ~3 minute download after the first start, plus part of the engine start (vLLM's compile cache is on the volume too) only on Kubernetes and RunPod; bills every month; see below
A copy of the image near the GPUs (SKYPILOT_DOCKER_*) no part of the ~10 GB pull; depends on the registry and the cloud you keep the copy up to date
Pre-baked machine images not built the whole image pull, and the download if the weights are baked in too see below

Hugging Face downloads. The Hub now serves files through Xet, and huggingface_hub 1.x (vLLM 0.32 needs 1.31 or later) ignores HF_HUB_ENABLE_HF_TRANSFER: hf_transfer "can't be used anymore", and the vLLM image doesn't ship it. Xet's high-performance mode is its successor. vLLM 0.32 turns it on itself when the variable isn't set (model_executor/model_loader/weight_utils.py, enable_xet_high_performance); the task sets it anyway so it holds for other images. Nothing is installed at boot.

Load formats. serve.load_format is passed to vLLM as --load-format (every provisioner); auto (the default) is vLLM's own loader, which every model works with. vLLM v0.32.0's image includes runai-model-streamer (with its S3, GCS and Azure extras) and fastsafetensors (a CUDA requirement), so both work without installing anything. Both read safetensors faster than the default, but both download a Hugging Face repo first and then read the local copy, so they don't shorten the download. runai_streamer takes --model-loader-extra-config '{"concurrency":16}' (or memory_limit) in vllm_args. fastsafetensors runs without GPUDirect Storage (it falls back by itself, and turns it off for tensor parallel). Neither is confirmed with every quantization; try one on the model with scripts/skypilot_check.py before you leave it on. vLLM's source at tag v0.32.0: vllm/config/load.py, model_loader/runai_streamer_loader.py, model_loader/weight_utils.py.

The image pull. SkyPilot 0.14.2 has no setting that makes the pull itself faster: it runs a plain docker pull before it starts the container (sky/provision/docker_utils.py), on every launch. What it does offer is a registry login: with SKYPILOT_DOCKER_USERNAME, SKYPILOT_DOCKER_PASSWORD and SKYPILOT_DOCKER_SERVER all set where the controller runs, each launch takes them as SkyPilot secrets and the machine logs in before it pulls. Copy the vLLM image to ECR or Artifact Registry in the region the GPUs run in and point serve.image at the copy, and the pull stays inside that cloud. For ECR the password may be empty: the machine logs in with its IAM role. This helps on AWS and GCP; on Lambda and other GPU clouds there's no registry next to the GPUs, and Docker Hub is as close as any.

The weights cache volume

serve.weights_cache: volume (default none) keeps the Hugging Face cache on a SkyPilot volume where the GPUs run. The first start fills it; later starts find the weights there and skip the download. vLLM's compile cache (VLLM_CACHE_ROOT) goes on it as well, so a later start can load compiled graphs instead of compiling them.

    serve:
      provisioner: skypilot
      clouds: [runpod]
      regions: [CA]                            # optional; must be the volume's region if set
      weights_cache: volume
      weights_cache_infra: runpod/CA/CA-MTL-1  # runpod/<region>/<data center>, or kubernetes[/<context>]
      weights_cache_gb: 50                     # the weights and some room: you pay for every GB a month
      weights_cache_usd_per_gb_month: null     # null: RunPod's published price; set it for a Kubernetes PVC

Where it works. SkyPilot 0.14.2 has volumes on two clouds only (sky/utils/volume.py, VolumeType):

  • Kubernetes: a PersistentVolumeClaim (k8s-pvc). With max_replicas above 1 it's asked for as ReadWriteMany, so every replica can mount it at once, and your storage class must allow that; with one replica, ReadWriteOnce.
  • RunPod: a network volume in one data center (runpod-network-volume, at least 10 GB).

Not on Lambda, AWS, GCP, Azure or the other clouds. AWS, GCP and Azure have only the disks a machine is launched with (resources.volumes), which go with the machine. Lambda has persistent filesystems, but SkyPilot 0.14.2 doesn't attach them (its Lambda launch sends none: sky/provision/lambda_cloud/instance.py). A config that asks for a volume anywhere else is refused when it loads, and so is one whose clouds or regions would let a replica run away from its volume (SkyPilot refuses such a task too: Task.resolve_and_validate_volumes).

How it's made. The volume is mo-<install id>-<deployment>-hf. Before a deployment's first launch in a controller process, the controller makes it with sky.volumes.apply if SkyPilot doesn't list it; the launch then mounts it at /mnt/meritorder-cache with HF_HOME and VLLM_CACHE_ROOT under it. A volume that can't be made fails the launch like any other (a replica_failed entry, the usual retry after 10 minutes). Several replicas writing the same cache at once rely on huggingface_hub's file locks, which work on most shared filesystems.

What it costs. A volume bills every hour it exists, GPUs running or not. RunPod's network volumes cost $0.07 a GB a month for the first TB and $0.05 beyond (docs.runpod.io, November 2026); 50 GB is about $3.50 a month. A PVC costs what your storage class does, which Merit Order doesn't know unless weights_cache_usd_per_gb_month says. The config load logs the monthly estimate. The controller records each volume it makes (the gpu_volumes setting, and a volume entry in the GPU activity log), and every cycle adds its price for the time since the last cycle to the deployment's GPU spend (730 hours a month), so it counts against the GPU budget and shows in "GPU spend this month". It isn't part of the burn rate or the fleet's dollars-an-hour limit, which are about machines. A volume without a known price isn't counted. The GPUs page lists the volumes and their monthly cost under "GPU cost by deployment".

Cleaning up. Nothing deletes a volume by itself: not the sweep (it lists and tears down clusters only), not a teardown, not switching weights_cache back to none, not removing the deployment. It bills until you delete it, where the controller runs (SkyPilot and the database):

meritorder gpu volumes                                  # this install's volumes, what they cost, what uses them
meritorder gpu volumes delete mo-ab12cd34-gpu-small-hf --yes

Deleting is refused while a replica uses the volume. It's recorded in the GPU activity log (volume_deleted), and the volume stops counting in GPU spend. If the deployment still asks for a volume, its next start makes a new, empty one.

Pre-baked images (not built)

On AWS, GCP and Azure a launch can start from your own machine image (image_id with an AMI, a GCP image or an Azure image instead of docker:). SkyPilot takes one or the other, so the image would hold vLLM itself (its Python environment, the CUDA libraries the driver needs) and the model's weights in its Hugging Face cache, and the task would run vLLM on the machine rather than in a container. That skips both the image pull and the download: on the run above, most of the 11 minutes but the boot. It isn't built, because it means one image per model, region and cloud, rebuilt for every new vLLM or model version, with its own storage cost, and a second way of running vLLM beside the container, with its own driver checks. Lambda and most GPU clouds don't take custom images in SkyPilot 0.14.2 (IMAGE_ID is unsupported there), so it would help only the large clouds.

Kubernetes

Teams with GPUs in their own cluster can have the controller run vLLM there (provisioner: kubernetes), through KServe or llm-d. The controller drives it like SkyPilot: the same break-even test, controls, safeguards, activity log and cost accounting.

KServe (api: kserve, the default) llm-d (api: llm-d)
Merit Order creates An InferenceService (serving.kserve.io/v1beta1) per deployment, in KServe's Standard mode with its autoscaler off (serving.kserve.io/autoscalerClass: none) and minReplicas = maxReplicas = what the controller wants A Deployment of vLLM pods per deployment, with the labels of an InferencePool you installed with llm-d's router, listening on the pool's target port
You install first KServe in Standard mode (Knative isn't needed) llm-d's router: a Gateway, the InferencePool (inference.networking.k8s.io/v1; v1alpha2 for older llm-d) and its endpoint picker
Which replica gets a request The gateway, which keeps a session on the pod holding its cache (below; gateways must run in the cluster to reach pods), else KServe's Service llm-d's endpoint picker: the replica with the most of the prompt in its cache and a short queue. Gateway affinity is off unless replica_affinity: true
Endpoint gateways use endpoint:, else the InferenceService's cluster address (status.address.url) + /v1 endpoint: (required): the Gateway's /v1 URL
Stop The InferenceService is deleted The Deployment is deleted; the router and pool stay

Both run the same vLLM as SkyPilot: serve.image, vllm serve <hf_id> with prefix caching and priority scheduling, tensor parallel across the replica's GPUs, then vllm_args. Each pod asks for the GPU count in accelerators (H100:4 is nvidia.com/gpu: 4; gpu_resource: amd.com/gpu for AMD), tolerates that resource's taint, gets shared memory at /dev/shm and a Hugging Face cache (cache_pvc, else an emptyDir, so every start downloads the weights again), and has a readiness probe on /health. A pod removed by a scale-down gets termination_grace_seconds (120) to finish its requests. cpu and memory become the container's requests and limits beside its GPUs. KServe deployments need both: KServe gives a predictor without them its own defaults, 1 CPU and 2 GiB (KServe 0.21, seen on kind), too little for vLLM to load a model, so the configuration is refused without them. llm-d's are optional (blank: no limit).

kubernetes:                          # the cluster
  namespace: gpus                    # blank: MERITORDER_GPU_NAMESPACE (the Helm chart sets it), else the controller's own
  node_types:                        # a cluster has no price catalog: what one node costs you an hour (example rates)
    a3-highgpu-8g: {usd_per_hour: 88.0, gpus: 8, spot_usd_per_hour: 30.0}
    g6.12xlarge: {usd_per_hour: 4.60, gpus: 4}

backends:
  gpu-qwen-k8s:
    kind: self_hosted
    format: openai
    gpu_cost_per_hour: 44.0          # only when the node type has no price
    capacity_tokens_per_second: 4000
    serve:
      provisioner: kubernetes
      model: qwen3-coder-next
      accelerators: "H100:4"
      image: vllm/vllm-openai:v0.32.0-cu129
      vllm_args: "--max-model-len 262144"
      max_replicas: 4
      kubernetes:
        api: kserve                  # or llm-d, with inference_pool and endpoint
        node_type: a3-highgpu-8g     # a nodeSelector on kubernetes.node_type_label (node.kubernetes.io/instance-type), and the price
        hf_token_secret: hf-token    # a Secret in the namespace with an HF_TOKEN key, for gated models
        cpu: "90"                    # what one replica may use on its node: required for KServe
        memory: 900Gi
        cache_pvc: hf-cache          # optional
        # Also: namespace, node_selector, tolerations, labels, annotations, endpoint, gpu_resource.
        # llm-d: inference_pool: qwen-pool, endpoint: http://llm-d-gateway.gpus.svc.cluster.local/v1

The model needs a priced route to the backend, as with SkyPilot. The endpoint must be reachable from the gateways and the controller: KServe's cluster address works when they run in the same cluster; from elsewhere, set endpoint:. For an older KServe that calls Standard mode RawDeployment, set annotations: {serving.kserve.io/deploymentMode: RawDeployment}.

Prices. A replica costs its share of its node: the node type's price × its GPUs / the node's GPUs (four GPUs of an $88 eight-GPU node: $44 an hour), or the spot rate with use_spot. The break-even test, the fleet caps and the GPU budget use that price, and the console shows it as the node type's rate, with how it was worked out. While running, each pod is priced for the node it landed on: that node's type, and its spot rate when the node has a spot label (Karpenter, EKS, GKE or AKS). Reading nodes needs a cluster-wide permission (controller.kubernetes.readNodes in the Helm chart); without it, pods are priced at the configured node type. A pod with no node yet costs nothing. With no node type or no price for it, gpu_cost_per_hour is the price; with neither, the configuration is refused, since an unpriced GPU can't be held by the GPU budget or the fleet caps. These are your rates, so they are only as right as the table.

Readiness and failures. A deployment is ready when at least one pod is Ready and the endpoint answers /v1/models. While it starts, the console's card and the activity log say what holds it up:

What Kubernetes reports What the controller does
A pod waits for a node (Unschedulable, e.g. Insufficient nvidia.com/gpu) Waits: a cluster autoscaler may be adding one. The 45-minute provisioning timeout still applies
Pods can't be created (ReplicaFailure: an exceeded quota, PodSecurity, a webhook) Fails: deletes it, 30-minute cooldown
The image can't be pulled (not found, unauthorized, an invalid name) Fails. A pull error that may pass (a registry timeout) waits
CreateContainerConfigError, e.g. the HF token Secret is missing Fails
vLLM crash-loops 3 times (OOMKilled, a bad argument) Fails
The Kubernetes API doesn't answer, or refuses Replicas that still answer stay warm; a start keeps waiting. With no credentials or no permission, and nothing answering: fails
The resource was deleted by someone else Fails: traffic moves to APIs, 30-minute cooldown
The resource is already there (a controller restarted mid-run) Replaced with the current spec, unless another install's label is on it: then the start fails
A stop The resource is deleted, and the stop waits until it and its pods are gone (their grace period, plus 60 s at most), which is billed too. Pods still there after that: the stop failed, the deployment stays running (and billed), and it's tried again next cycle

Stopping what's no longer configured, and the sweep. A deployment switched off, removed, renamed (its backend or its model) or moved (another namespace, KServe instead of llm-d) while it runs is stopped as soon as the controller loads that configuration. On top of that, every cycle while a Kubernetes deployment is configured (or the last sweep found leftovers), the controller lists the InferenceServices and Deployments in its GPU namespaces labelled app.kubernetes.io/managed-by: meritorder and meritorder.dev/install: <install id>, and deletes each one no running deployment owns: one removed while the controller was down, or what's left of a stop that failed. Each is logged, and recorded in the GPU activity log (sweep; a delete that fails is an error, tried again next cycle). The install label keeps two installs sharing a namespace out of each other's resources; anything KServe made (it has an owner) and resources made before the install label existed are left alone.

Utilization. Each pod's address is in its replica entry, so the controller reads vLLM's /metrics from each ready pod (it runs in the cluster), as for SkyPilot replicas, not through the Service, which would answer for one pod at random. With kv_events, it follows each pod's KV events the same way.

Draining is the gateways' job, as with SkyPilot: no new sessions go to the deployment while warm ones finish, and the pods stay until it's drained. Then the resource is deleted.

The Kubernetes API is called over plain HTTPS with httpx, no client library. In the cluster the controller uses its service account (the token is read again when it rotates). For development it reads a kubeconfig (kubernetes.kubeconfig, KUBECONFIG or ~/.kube/config, with kubernetes.context): a token, token file, client certificate, or exec plugin (aws eks get-token, gke-gcloud-auth-plugin, kubelogin). Setup and permissions: 07: GPUs on your Kubernetes cluster.

Checked on kind

On 2026-11-14, with scripts/kind/ (07): kind 0.33 running Kubernetes 1.36.1, KServe 0.21.0 from its own charts (minimal CRDs, Standard mode), the Gateway API Inference Extension 1.6.2's InferencePool CRD, cert-manager 1.21.3, and Merit Order from its Helm chart (Helm 4.3.1) with the controller in the cluster under the chart's Role. The node advertised eight fake nvidia.com/gpu, and the model servers were scripts/fake_vllm.py, which takes vllm serve's command line and serves vLLM's endpoints and metric names. Times are with a 10-second controller cycle (60 by default) and the image already on the node.

Verified on kind Still needs real GPUs, llm-d's router, or a cloud
KServe: an InferenceService in Standard mode with autoscalerClass: none; KServe makes the predictor Deployment (labeled serving.kserve.io/inferenceservice) and Service, and status.address.url (port 80) reaches the container's port 8000; spec.predictor.labels reach the pods; scaling by patching minReplicas and maxReplicas vLLM itself: downloading and loading weights, its time to ready, host memory and /dev/shm for tensor parallelism, and shutting down within termination_grace_seconds (the stand-in stops at once)
KServe fills in a predictor's missing cpu and memory with 1 CPU and 2 GiB: a KServe deployment now has to set both GPU nodes: the device plugin, GPU taints, and a cluster autoscaler adding a node for a pod that waits
llm-d: model server pods with the InferencePool's labels and target port, the pool read from inference.networking.k8s.io/v1 llm-d's Gateway and endpoint picker routing to the pods (a plain Service stood in for the Gateway), and /v1/models through it as the readiness check
Up, warm (12 to 22 s), requests through the gateway pinned to the deployment, each pod's metrics, its address, node type, zone and price from the node's labels (readNodes), scaling up and down (12 to 22 s), draining (pods stay for drain_minutes, then go), stopping at once KV events from real vLLM, replica affinity on real replicas
Failures: a missing HF token Secret (failed in 12 s), an image that doesn't exist (12 s), vLLM crash-looping (3 restarts, 42 to 52 s), a GPU quota of 0 (ReplicaFailure, 12 s); each deleted and cooled down. A pinned start cools down too. More GPUs than a node has: it waits NetworkPolicies between the controller and the pods
The chart's Role, narrowed to the calls the controller makes (no list on InferenceServices, no get on pods): no request was refused Exec-plugin kubeconfigs against EKS, GKE and AKS; workload identity
The controller on the plain image (no SkyPilot): it now says once, not every cycle, that catalog prices can't be fetched Prices against a real cluster's bill

Controls and safeguards

The console's GPUs page shows, for every deployment: where each replica runs (cloud, region, zone, instance, spot or on-demand, from SkyPilot; on Kubernetes the pod's node, zone and node type), how long it has been up, its load, how many sessions sit on it and how many are probably still warm there, its burn rate, what this run and this month have cost, what demand would pay for it at API prices, and why the controller is doing what it's doing. A Cache affinity line says whether sessions are kept on their replica and what warm caches are known from (KV events, an estimate from KV-cache metrics, or the cache TTL), and Sessions on its replicas lists the recent ones: replica, last turn, context size, and the share of the prefix probably cached now (admins see every session, team leads their team's). An activity log records every state change, scale, and admin action with who did it, what holds up a start (on Kubernetes no GPU node free or an image that won't pull; on SkyPilot a launch that failed, or a replica whose gate doesn't answer yet), every SkyPilot replica that failed with its last output and driver (When a replica fails), and every cluster the sweep tore down. On SkyPilot each replica's status also shows its cluster's name, how long its lease has left, and whether it's reached through an SSH tunnel.

Admins can override the controller:

Control Effect
Stop (drain first) No new sessions; warm ones finish for up to drain_minutes, then the replicas go down. Skips the usual hold time
Stop now Replicas go down at once; their sessions continue on APIs (caches rebuild there)
Pin N replicas Runs N (up to max_replicas) regardless of demand, skipping the scale-up wait and any failure cooldown. If a start then fails, the pin ends (an activity log entry by the controller says why) and the deployment cools down for 30 minutes, then follows demand. A pin that outlived its failure would launch the same broken deployment (an image the driver can't run, a missing secret) again after every cooldown, for as long as nobody looks. Pin it again to retry at once
Back to automatic Demand decides again
Stop all GPUs Every deployment stops (at once, or after draining) and none start until someone resumes the fleet

Stops and pins can expire after a set number of hours (up to 90 days) and can carry a reason, which the activity log and the alert show. Gateways stop routing to a stopped deployment within seconds, before the controller acts; the controller wakes up as soon as a control changes. For a static server, Merit Order can only stop sending it traffic.

Organization safeguards apply on top, to pins as well (06): a monthly GPU budget, a fleet burn-rate cap, and a replica cap. The burn-rate cap counts each running replica at what it really burns when that's more than the expected price. A pin that ends because its start failed removes only itself from the controls: a Stop all GPUs or another pin saved while that cycle ran stays.

What GPUs cost

Prices come from SkyPilot's catalog, the same list prices its optimizer uses to pick a cloud:

  • Before launching, the break-even test uses the cheapest catalog offer for the deployment's accelerators within its allowed clouds and regions (spot or on-demand, per use_spot).
  • While running, each replica is priced for its actual cloud, region, instance type, and spot/on-demand, so a replica that lands in a pricier region costs what it really costs.
  • On Kubernetes there's no catalog: prices are configured per node type, and a replica pays its share of its node (Kubernetes). The console labels which price it used.
  • gpu_cost_per_hour is only a fallback, used for static servers (your own hardware), a Kubernetes deployment whose node type has no price, and when SkyPilot isn't installed where the controller runs. On SkyPilot and Kubernetes, a replica with no price at all is never started (The break-even test).

Cost is accrued every cycle from the moment provisioning starts until the replicas are down (a stop counts until it returns), and stored per hour (gpu_usage). After a gap in the controller's cycles (it was down, or Postgres was), the whole gap is counted on Kubernetes and for static servers, which run on without the controller, and for the weights cache volumes. A SkyPilot replica stops itself lease_minutes after its last lease renewal and is deleted autostop_minutes later, so its gap is counted up to then; when the last renewal isn't known, the whole gap.

Self-hosted tokens are charged back at the same live price: each request on a GPU carries its share (its tokens at capacity_tokens_per_second), which is what its team and person are charged. The organization's spend counts the accrued time instead, idle and starting included, and the GPU time no request paid for comes off the self-hosting savings (08, decision 64). A GPU that runs for little traffic shows as a loss, not as nearly free.

These are list prices, not your bill: they don't include negotiated discounts, reservations, or credits, and they leave out disks and egress. Every machine SkyPilot runs for Merit Order is a replica, so all of them are priced, in the ledger, the GPU budget and the fleet caps: on SkyPilot the burn rate counts every cluster of the deployment that exists or is being launched (one being torn down too) at its own catalog price. Spot prices in the catalog are refreshed periodically, not live. SkyPilot tags every instance with meritorder-deployment: <backend>, and Reports → Bills compares the recorded GPU cost with what AWS, Google Cloud and Azure billed for instances with that tag (08). Kubernetes GPU time isn't in that comparison: its nodes are shared and carry no such tag, and its prices are the rates you configured.

SkyPilot runs in its own Python environment (/opt/skypilot in the -gpu image, built with --build-arg SKYPILOT=0.14.2), so its dependencies never mix with the gateway's. Merit Order calls its SDK in SkyPilot's Python (MERITORDER_SKY_PYTHON, found from the sky command when unset), or in-process when SkyPilot is importable where Merit Order runs. Launches, teardowns and status get the controller's environment (its cloud credentials); price lookups run without them: no AWS variable but the region, and no AWS config or credentials file, reaches them.

If the controller stops running while GPUs are up, the console flags it: nothing would scale them down. SkyPilot replicas then stop by themselves when their lease runs out (The lease); Kubernetes ones stay until the controller is back (which stops and sweeps what no longer runs, Kubernetes). If a stop fails at the cloud, the deployment stays marked as running and the controller keeps retrying, so a GPU that may still be billing is never shown as off; so does a start that failed halfway whose teardown failed too. A SkyPilot cluster that slipped through anyway is torn down by the sweep.

Overflow

Up to 60% load (routing.shadow_knee), a self-hosted token is priced at 2% of its route's price (routing.shadow_floor). Above that the shadow price rises toward the full price, so new sessions drift to APIs before the GPU is full. At 100%, nothing new goes there while any other route can take it; sessions already there move too. A saturated GPU that's a model's only route still takes requests, which wait in vLLM, until max_waiting (default 32) per replica are waiting. Set max_concurrency so gateways see saturation within seconds instead of at the controller's next sample. Details: When a GPU is full.

Inside the GPU pool

  • Continuous batching is the engine's job (vLLM / SGLang). The gateway sends concurrently and never serializes requests per replica.
  • Replica choice is the gateway's when it can address the replicas: a session goes back to the replica that holds its KV cache unless that replica is gone, full, draining, or busy enough that rebuilding the cache elsewhere costs less (03). Otherwise (or with replica_affinity: false) KServe's Service, or your load balancer, picks. SkyPilot has none: the gateway always picks. On Kubernetes the gateway addresses pods directly, so it must run in the cluster. Behind llm-d, affinity is off unless set: llm-d's endpoint picker already sends each request to the replica with the most of its prompt cached.
  • Eviction is seen in vLLM's KV events (kv_events: true) or estimated from each replica's KV-cache metrics, so a session whose cache is gone isn't treated as warm (04).
  • Priority scheduling: free-upgrade requests go to vLLM with priority: 10 (lower runs first), so traffic at its own floor goes ahead of them.
  • The vLLM command is the same on SkyPilot and Kubernetes: vllm serve <hf_id> --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8000 (behind llm-d, the pool's target port; on SkyPilot --host 127.0.0.1 --port 8001, behind the gate) --served-model-name <the route's model id> --tensor-parallel-size <GPUs in accelerators> --enable-prefix-caching --scheduling-policy priority --enable-prompt-tokens-details, plus --kv-events-config with kv_events, then vllm_args. served_model_name overrides the name.
  • Engine knobs go in vllm_args (e.g. --max-model-len, --max-num-seqs, --max-num-batched-tokens, speculative decoding). Prefix caching and priority scheduling are always on.
06

Auth & spend

This doc covers who can call the gateway (keys, sign-in, teams and roles) and how spend is limited (budgets, caps, safeguards) and recorded (the ledger).

What's been checked. Token verification runs in CI with a real signing key: expired, forged, wrong audience or issuer, algorithm confusion, and tokens shaped like Google's. Budgets, limits and safeguards are tested in CI against both in-memory storage and real Redis and Postgres. Sign-in, group mapping and SCIM have not been run against a real Entra tenant, and Google sign-in and Google Groups have not been run against a real Workspace domain. Those calls are written from the providers' docs and tested against mocks.

Getting a key into pi and Claude Code

Harnesses can't do interactive SSO, so people log in once with the CLI and get a short-lived virtual key tied to their identity. The harness sends it like any API key.

meritorder login --gateway https://llm.example.com    # or: meritorder use-key <key from an admin>
meritorder setup pi            # adds a "meritorder" provider to ~/.pi/agent/models.json
meritorder setup claude-code   # points Claude Code at the gateway, starting sessions on auto
meritorder setup claude-code --config-dir ~/.claude-meritorder   # …in a separate Claude Code profile

The key is saved to ~/.config/meritorder/api_key (under $XDG_CONFIG_HOME when that's set), with mode 600, next to credentials.json, which also records the gateway URL. Both harness configs read the key file at request time (!cat ... for pi, apiKeyHelper for Claude Code), so logging in again rotates the key without touching them. pi is configured to send its session ID as x-session-id and to add cache breakpoints, which Merit Order uses for sticky routing and caching. setup pi keeps the previous models.json as models.json.bak.

setup claude-code writes to Claude Code's settings file: $CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR/settings.json when that's set, else ~/.claude/settings.json, or the folder given with --config-dir (then start Claude Code with CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR=<folder> claude). It sets:

Setting Value
env.ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL the gateway
apiKeyHelper cat ~/.config/meritorder/api_key
model auto (--model <name> for another model /v1/models lists for your key; --model none leaves Claude Code's choice)
env.CLAUDE_CODE_MAX_CONTEXT_TOKENS the gateway's context window for that model (from /v1/models; for auto, the largest among the models auto can pick for your key), so Claude Code doesn't assume 200,000 for a name it doesn't know
env.ANTHROPIC_CUSTOM_MODEL_OPTION, …_NAME auto, "auto (Merit Order)": adds it to the /model picker
env.CLAUDE_CODE_GATEWAY_HINT_HEADERS 1: Claude Code labels side requests and compaction summaries only when asked; Merit Order caps their level (routing.request_class_levels)

For a Claude model name (claude-…) the window and picker entries are left out (Claude Code knows those models) and removed if an earlier setup added them. The previous file is kept as settings.json.bak. With the Merit Order key, Claude Code's requests don't use a claude.ai login: subscription limits don't apply, and spend is counted here like any other key's.

How the gateway knows who's calling: every request carries a key (Authorization: Bearer or x-api-key). The gateway hashes it, looks it up (cached for a minute), and gets the user, team, and role, which drive budgets, policy, and reports. Unknown, revoked, or expired keys get a 401.

Client Auth
People in the console Their account: a password kept here, or SSO (below)
People with harnesses meritorder login → virtual key (above)
Services / apps An Entra token directly as the bearer token, or a key from meritorder keys create
Local dev / quickstart MERITORDER_DEV_KEY (static admin key from the environment), until the first admin account exists

Sign-in switches on when MERITORDER_OIDC_ISSUER and MERITORDER_OIDC_CLIENT_ID are set. With Entra, map group IDs to teams and roles in auth.oidc in the config; SCIM provisioning (below) disables people when they leave. Google needs a little more: see Signing in with Google, and Google Groups to map Google groups the same way.

Signing in to the console

People sign in to the console as themselves and get a session; keys are for harnesses, CI and services (decision 69).

Small team, no identity provider Organization with Entra or Google
How people sign in Email address and a password Merit Order keeps; meritorder login asks for them The console's "Sign in with Microsoft / Google / your organization" button; meritorder login (device code)
How they join An invite link from an admin or team lead (People → Invite someone) The first time they sign in (or SCIM provisions them)
Forgotten password An admin's or lead's reset link (People → Password link) Their identity provider
Leaving Disable them on the People page Disable or remove them in the identity provider (with SCIM, at once)
Turning passwords off auth.local.enabled: false

SSO in the browser

With auth.oidc set, the console's sign-in page shows a "Sign in with …" button. It uses OIDC's authorization-code flow with PKCE: the gateway sends the browser to your identity provider, takes the code back at /auth/sso/callback, checks the ID token (signature, issuer, audience, expiry, the nonce it sent, and for Google the Workspace domain), and opens a session for the person, created or updated from the same sign-in mappings as meritorder login. A disabled person is refused. The answer is tied to the browser that asked (a short-lived mo_sso cookie) and each sign-in attempt works once, within ten minutes.

Provider What to register
Entra In the same app registration: Authentication → Add a platform → Web, redirect URI https://<gateway>/auth/sso/callback, and a client secret (Certificates & secrets) in MERITORDER_OIDC_BROWSER_CLIENT_SECRET. Or, without a secret, the redirect URI under Mobile and desktop applications (a public client; "Allow public client flows" is already on for meritorder login)
Google A second OAuth client of type Web application (the device-login client can't do this), with that redirect URI as an authorized redirect URI. Its ID in MERITORDER_OIDC_BROWSER_CLIENT_ID, its secret in MERITORDER_OIDC_BROWSER_CLIENT_SECRET. Until both are set, the console doesn't show the button
Other OIDC providers A client allowed the authorization-code flow with that redirect URI; its secret if it's confidential

The gateway builds the redirect URI from the address the browser used (with X-Forwarded-Proto and X-Forwarded-Host behind a proxy); set auth.oidc.redirect_uri if that isn't what you registered. auth.oidc.browser: false hides the button. Where everyone should use SSO, set auth.local.enabled: false: the password form and invite links go away, and keys still work for harnesses and services.

meritorder login signs in with the device-code flow where SSO is set up, and asks for the email address and password where it isn't (or with --password); either way it saves a short-lived key for the harnesses.

The first admin. On a new install, either sign in once with the setup key (MERITORDER_DEV_KEY in .env: "Sign in with an API key instead") and invite yourself and others from the People page, or create the account directly:

docker compose exec gateway meritorder accounts create you@example.com --role admin   # asks for a password
docker compose exec gateway meritorder accounts create pat@example.com --link --url http://localhost:8080   # prints an invite link
docker compose exec gateway meritorder accounts reset pat@example.com --url http://localhost:8080          # prints a reset link

A static admin key from the environment or the config file keeps working after that. Outside a laptop, take it out once people have their own accounts and restart the gateway: anyone who has it can do anything.

Sessions. A session is a random token in an HttpOnly, SameSite=Strict cookie: mo_session over plain HTTP, and over HTTPS (directly or through a proxy that sets X-Forwarded-Proto) __Host-mo_session, marked Secure, which no other subdomain can set, so a sibling site can't sign your browser in to an account of its choosing. The gateway keeps only its hash. It lasts auth.session_hours (12 by default). Like a key, it acts as the person's record as it is now, at most a minute old, so moving, demoting or disabling someone applies to their console sessions too. Signing out ends the session on the gateway, not only in that browser. When a session ends while the console is open, its next call takes it back to the sign-in page, which says why; signing in again returns to the page you were on. Changing your password (account menu → Change password) ends your other sessions; a reset link ends all of them.

Invite and reset links work once, for auth.local.invite_hours (72 by default). Each person has at most one open link; making a new one withdraws the old, and so does changing their team, role or access. Merit Order doesn't send email: the person who makes the link sends it. Who may make one follows the rule for keys: an admin for anyone, a team lead for new people and people on their own team with the user role. A password set through a team lead's link acts at most as a user: if the person is promoted later, it stops signing in and they need an admin's link, so whoever chose it can't follow them up. Open links are listed on the People page, where they can be withdrawn. The link's token goes in the request body, never a URL, so access logs don't record it.

Passwords are only for people invited by email. Someone who signs in with SSO, or who only has a key, can't be given one (People → Password link refuses, and so does inviting an address an SSO person already has), so removing them in the identity provider or revoking their key is enough. Inviting someone by email in an organization that also has SSO gives them a separate, local account; set auth.local.enabled: false where that shouldn't happen.

Passwords need at least 12 characters (auth.local.min_password_length) and no particular mix of characters: length is what makes a password hard to guess. They're kept as scrypt hashes. Each attempt counts before it's checked (a right one is taken back off), so after 10 failed sign-ins for one address in 15 minutes, or 30 from one client in a minute, the gateway answers 429 until the window ends, however many attempts arrive at once. A wrong address gets the same answer as a wrong password. The per-address limit means anyone can lock a known address out for 15 minutes; that's the trade for stopping guessing. Behind a proxy, the gateway sees every client as the proxy's address unless the proxy is trusted (FORWARDED_ALLOW_IPS, 07): then the per-client limit applies to everyone at once. Resetting or changing a password also revokes the keys meritorder login got with the old one.

Two-factor sign-in

People with a password here can turn on two-factor (account menu → Two-factor sign-in): signing in then also takes a six-digit code from an authenticator app (1Password, Apple Passwords, Google Authenticator, Authy and others), on the console and in meritorder login (decision 73). People who sign in with SSO get two-factor from their identity provider instead.

  • Turning it on: the console shows a QR code to scan, an otpauth:// link (opening it on the phone or Mac with the app adds the account) and the key to type in; entering the code the app shows turns it on, ends your other sessions, and shows ten recovery codes, once. Each recovery code signs you in once in place of a code.
  • Codes: the standard time-based kind (SHA-1, 6 digits, 30 seconds), accepted one step either side for clock drift; each code works once. A wrong code counts against the sign-in limit like a wrong password.
  • A forgotten password doesn't turn it off: a reset link sets a new password, and the code is still asked for.
  • A lost device: a recovery code, or an admin's Reset two-factor on the People page, which turns it off and ends the person's sessions. Team leads can't.
  • Storage: the authenticator secret has to be read to check a code, so it's sealed (AES-256-GCM, tied to its person) with MERITORDER_AUTH_KEY when that's set, and stored as it is otherwise; recovery codes are stored as hashes.

Keys in the console. "Sign in with an API key instead" still works: the gateway checks the key and opens a session tied to it, so the browser never stores the key, and revoking the key ends the session. A console that kept a key from an earlier version trades it for a session the next time it opens, and forgets it.

Requests the cookie can make. A browser sends the cookie on its own, so a request made with it that changes something (anything but GET) must also carry the console's x-meritorder-console header and, when the browser says where it came from (Origin), come from the gateway's own address. Other sites can't send that header, and SameSite=Strict already keeps the cookie off requests other sites start. Behind a proxy that changes the host name, have it send X-Forwarded-Host. Requests with a key in the Authorization header don't need either, and the proxy's own APIs (/v1/chat/completions, /v1/messages, …) never accept the cookie.

Setting Default
auth.local.enabled true Password sign-in and invite links. Off: SSO and keys only
auth.local.min_password_length 12 8 to 128
auth.local.invite_hours 72 How long an invite or reset link works
auth.session_hours 12 How long a console sign-in lasts
auth.oidc.browser true The console's SSO button
auth.oidc.browser_client_id client_id The client the browser signs in with (Google: the Web application client)
auth.oidc.browser_client_secret_env The environment variable holding that client's secret (MERITORDER_OIDC_BROWSER_CLIENT_SECRET in the shipped config)
auth.oidc.redirect_uri the browser's address + /auth/sso/callback Set it if a proxy hides the gateway's public address

Data policy

Each backend says who receives what's sent to it and what your agreement with that provider says, so a caller can keep some data away from some providers (decision 72).

Backend setting
provider Who receives the data. Default: from the address (anthropic, bedrock, azure_openai, foundry, vertex, gemini, openai, openrouter, mistral, deepseek, xai, moonshot, zai, minimax); your own GPUs are self_hosted; anything else is the backend's name
zero_retention true if the provider keeps no prompts or outputs under your agreement (for example Anthropic's or OpenAI's zero-data-retention terms, if you have them); false if it keeps them; unset is unknown
trains_on_data Whether the provider may train on what's sent; unset is unknown

Merit Order never guesses these: retention depends on your contract, not on the provider's name. Your own GPUs keep nothing and train on nothing.

A request can carry the caller's policy:

X-MeritOrder-Allowed-Providers: anthropic, bedrock
X-MeritOrder-Zero-Retention: required

Routes to other providers, or (with zero retention required) to providers not stated as zero-retention, are left out of the choice, as a team's allowed_backends would be. If nothing is left, the request is refused with 403 and a message starting data_policy: that names each route's reason. Embeddings follow the same rules. GET /v1/routes shows each tier's candidates with their provider, price and these facts (with source: config, self_hosted or unknown), so a caller can check its policy before sending; GET /v1/capabilities says both are offered.

Request screening

Agents read web pages, run commands and edit files on someone's machine, and the gateway sees every tool call they make and every result they send back. Request screening reads those and records what a security team would want to know. It's per team (screening.mode: shadow, off by default) and, for now, shadow only: nothing is blocked or changed, so it can run on real traffic to show what it would catch and how often it would be wrong before anything acts on it (decision 71).

Each request is read once: only what's new since the session's last turn, so an agent's tool calls and their results are each looked at as they arrive. Fixed rules, no model; it takes well under a millisecond (meritorder_screening_seconds).

Kind What it means
unicode_tags Unicode tag characters: invisible to people, read by models ("ASCII smuggling")
unicode_bidi, unicode_invisible Bidirectional overrides; zero-width characters (not the joiner emoji use)
secret_in_tool_call A provider-prefixed key (sk-ant-, ghp_, AKIA, private key blocks and others) in a tool call the model made: it may be sending it somewhere
secret_in_prompt Such a key in text going to the provider: a prompt or a tool result
pipe_to_shell A download piped into a shell or interpreter (curl … \| sh)
upload Data sent out: curl -d/-F/-T, wget --post-*, nc host port
dns_exfil ping, dig, nslookup… with command substitution: a known way to leak data through DNS
credential_read Reading .env, SSH keys, ~/.aws/credentials, .netrc, .git-credentials, kube or Docker config
config_write Writing agent, editor, git-hook, CI workflow or shell start-up configuration (.claude/settings*.json, .mcp.json, .cursor/mcp.json, .git/hooks/*, ~/.zshrc…)
md_image_url An image link with a query string in the model's own text: a way to leak data when a client renders it
after_untrusted One of the risky kinds above after the session read untrusted content: the shape of a prompt injection

Untrusted content is a result from a web fetch or search tool (WebFetch, web_search, browser tools, MCP fetch tools). Once a session has read some, its requests carry screen_untrusted: 1.

Where it shows. Each request with findings gets a screen ledger tag (the kinds, joined with +, for example after_untrusted+credential_read), so Reports → Breakdown → Tag → screen lists them and the Requests view filters by tag=screen. meritorder_screening_findings_total counts each kind by team for alerts. Only kinds and counts are kept: never the text, the command, the path or the key. A finding about a tool call lands on the request after it, which is when the gateway first sees the call. Clients and keys can't set or clear these tags.

What it doesn't do yet. Block or redact anything; detect injections in prose (published detectors miss most injections against agents and flag up to a third of ordinary tool output, decision 71); read base64 or other encodings; scan responses as they stream. Each is a later step, and blocking will start from what shadow mode shows on your traffic.

People and teams

What Where it's managed
Who exists, and their group membership Your identity provider (Entra or Google). People are created in Merit Order the first time they sign in with meritorder login, when they're issued a key, or when Entra provisions them through SCIM.
Teams, with budgets, limits, and model policy Merit Order: Config → Teams. An IdP has no notion of "$5,000 a month, these models only".
Which team and role someone gets Entra groups, or with Google, Google groups (read by the gateway) and verified email addresses and domains, mapped to teams and roles in Config → Access. Re-read at each sign-in; Google groups also while people use the gateway.
Exceptions The People page: an admin can move someone or change their role (either pins team and role, so later sign-ins and SCIM don't override them), hand them back to the sign-in mappings (Follow sign-in), set a monthly limit, or disable them.

The user record decides a person's team, and it can lower what a key acts as but never raise it: a key acts as the lower of the role it was issued with and the role on its person's record (ROLE_RANK: user, team lead, finance, admin). Moving, demoting or disabling someone takes effect within a minute on every gateway, including keys they already have and static keys from the config file. Promoting someone applies to keys issued after it: their next meritorder login, or a key an admin issues. So a user key a team lead issued for someone who hasn't signed in yet stays a user key when that person turns out to be an admin. The Keys page shows each key's role and, where the person's record outranks it, what the key acts as.

A team lead issues and revokes keys only for themselves, for new people, or for people on their own team with the user role; keys for anyone else (another team, a lead, an admin) need an admin. Their keys expire within expires_days (default 90, at most 3650); only an admin can issue a key that never expires. A disabled person can't sign in: POST /auth/exchange answers 403 and issues no key.

Role Sees Can change
user Their own usage Nothing (meritorder login gets them a new key)
team lead Their team: reports, requests, ledger export Keys on their team (they issue only user keys)
finance Every team, aggregated: no per-request rows, exports or live request feed (/v1/reports/requests and /v1/console/feed answer 403) Nothing
admin Everything, except the content of other people's stored responses Everything

No role reads another person's stored responses (below) unless their team lists that role in stored_responses.readers.

SCIM provisioning (/scim/v2, enabled by MERITORDER_SCIM_TOKEN): Entra pushes people and group changes as they happen. Group membership recomputes team and role with the same mappings as sign-in (an admin's pin still wins), and anyone deactivated or removed in Entra is disabled at once: their keys stop working within a minute (spend history is kept), and anything they kept in the Responses API's stored mode is deleted. SCIM's active flag works both ways: if Entra later sends the person as active again, they are enabled again, even if an admin disabled them on the People page. To keep someone out, disable or remove them in Entra too.

Entra group overage. A person in more than 200 groups gets a token without the groups claim (Entra puts a pointer to Microsoft Graph in _claim_names instead). The gateway doesn't call Graph, so their group mappings don't apply: they get the email mappings and default_team, and the gateway logs a warning naming them. Configure the app registration to send only groups assigned to the application ("Groups assigned to the application" in Token configuration), or map them by email, or provision them with SCIM. Setup: Entra → Enterprise applications → your app → Provisioning → Automatic; Tenant URL https://<gateway>/scim/v2, Secret token = MERITORDER_SCIM_TOKEN.

Signing in with Google

Google sign-in uses the same meritorder login (device code) and the same /auth/exchange as Entra. Google's tokens and login flow differ in a few ways, and the gateway handles each:

Entra Google
Who can get a token Members of your tenant: the issuer is per tenant Anyone with a Google account: one issuer for everyone. hosted_domains limits sign-in to your Workspace domains, checked against the token's hd claim. It's required: the gateway won't start with the Google issuer and no domains
Groups in the token Yes (groups) None. The gateway can read them from Google (Google Groups); verified addresses and whole domains map too (team_from_emails, role_from_emails), and exceptions go on the People page
Email preferred_username; not verified, so never used for mapping email with email_verified. A token whose address isn't verified is refused
Who the person is oid sub (Google says addresses can change and be reused; sub never is)
Device login A public client with no secret An OAuth client of type "TVs and Limited Input devices". Its secret goes with every poll; Google treats it as public for that client type, so the gateway hands it to meritorder login
Scopes openid profile email offline_access openid email profile, set automatically (Google refuses offline_access, and its device login allows only these)
Issuer in tokens As discovered https://accounts.google.com or accounts.google.com; both are accepted

Setup:

  1. In the Google Cloud console, open Google Auth Platform (APIs & Services → OAuth consent screen) and set the audience to Internal, so only accounts in your Workspace can sign in at all.
  2. Clients → Create client, application type TVs and Limited Input devices. Copy the client ID and secret.
  3. On the gateways (.env, or the Helm secret):

bash MERITORDER_OIDC_ISSUER=https://accounts.google.com MERITORDER_OIDC_CLIENT_ID=123456789012-abc.apps.googleusercontent.com MERITORDER_OIDC_CLIENT_SECRET=GOCSPX-... MERITORDER_OIDC_HOSTED_DOMAINS=example.com # comma-separated if you have several

The shipped config reads all four. If your configuration was already saved from the console before these fields existed, fill in the client secret and domains on Config → Access. The secret must stay a reference (${MERITORDER_OIDC_CLIENT_SECRET}), since secrets aren't stored.

  1. Map teams and roles in auth.oidc (or Config → Access):

yaml auth: oidc: team_from_emails: "@example.com": platform # everyone in the domain "@research.example.com": research "bob@example.com": data-science # one person role_from_emails: "carol@example.com": admin "dana@example.com": finance key_ttl_days: 7 # see "Leavers" below

A key with @ in the middle is one address; @example.com or example.com is a whole domain. Team: the entry for the exact address, else a mapped group (Google Groups), else the address's domain, else default_team. Role: the highest any of them gives; everyone else is a user. Matching ignores case. These lists apply only to an email the token marks verified, which Google's are and Entra's aren't: with Entra, map groups.

  1. People run meritorder login. It prints https://www.google.com/device and a code; they sign in with their Workspace account, and the gateway issues a key as with Entra.

Refusals: an account outside hosted_domains (a personal Gmail account, say) gets 403 "sign-in is limited to accounts in example.com", and an unverified address gets 403 "this account's email address isn't verified". Both checks also apply to a Google ID token sent directly as a bearer token. A Google service account's ID token has no hd, so services use a key from meritorder keys create. If the issuer is written another way (https://accounts.google.com:443, say) the start-up check doesn't see Google, so the gateway also refuses every token Google's issuer signed while hosted_domains is empty.

Leavers. Google Workspace doesn't provision custom apps over SCIM, so a suspended account isn't disabled here at once. It can't sign in again, and its keys stop when they expire (key_ttl_days, 30 by default; 7 is a reasonable choice with Google). To cut someone off now, disable them on the People page. With Google Groups on, taking someone out of their groups also takes away the team and role those groups gave, at the next refresh, while their keys still work.

Google Groups

Google's ID tokens never include groups, so the gateway can read them itself from Google's Cloud Identity Groups API (v1, as documented in November 2026) and map them as it maps Entra groups: team_from_groups and role_from_groups, keyed by the group's address.

auth:
  oidc:
    issuer: https://accounts.google.com
    # client_id, public_client_secret, hosted_domains as above
    google_groups:
      enabled: true          # the shipped config: MERITORDER_GOOGLE_GROUPS=true
      credentials_env: MERITORDER_GOOGLE_GROUPS_CREDENTIALS   # the service account's JSON key (or credentials_file)
    team_from_groups:        # the first group in this list someone is in sets their team
      "platform-team@example.com": platform
      "research@example.com": research
    role_from_groups:
      "gateway-admins@example.com": admin
      "finance@example.com": finance
    team_from_emails:
      "bob@example.com": data-science   # an exact address still wins over a group
      "@example.com": general           # the domain catches everyone in no mapped group

Which mapping wins. The team comes from, in order:

  1. the person's exact address in team_from_emails;
  2. the first group in team_from_groups they're in, directly or through nested groups;
  3. their domain in team_from_emails;
  4. default_team.

The role is the highest that any of their groups, their address or their domain gives; everyone else is a user. Addresses match ignoring case. A team or role an admin set on the People page wins over all of them. Map only groups whose membership your admins control: a group anyone in the organization can join, mapped to a role, lets anyone take that role.

Setup. You need a Google Cloud project and a Google Workspace super admin.

  1. Google Cloud console → APIs & Services → Library → Cloud Identity API → Enable.
  2. IAM & Admin → Service Accounts → Create service account, for example meritorder-groups. It needs no IAM roles in the project. Copy its email address.
  3. Give the gateways a way to act as it, one of:

  4. GKE Workload Identity (no key to keep): let the gateways' Kubernetes service account act as it,

    bash gcloud iam service-accounts add-iam-policy-binding meritorder-groups@PROJECT.iam.gserviceaccount.com \ --role roles/iam.workloadIdentityUser --member "serviceAccount:PROJECT.svc.id.goog[NAMESPACE/KSA]"

    and annotate it in the Helm values: serviceAccount.annotations: {iam.gke.io/gcp-service-account: meritorder-groups@PROJECT.iam.gserviceaccount.com}. Leave MERITORDER_GOOGLE_GROUPS_CREDENTIALS unset. A pod has one Google identity, so if the gateways already use a service account for Vertex, give that one the role in step 4 instead. Compute Engine and Cloud Run work the same way, through the service account attached to the VM or service. - A key: the service account → Keys → Add key → Create new key → JSON. Put the file's contents on one line (jq -c . key.json) in MERITORDER_GOOGLE_GROUPS_CREDENTIALS, in .env or the gateways' Secret. With secrets.mountAsFiles in Helm, also set credentials_file: /run/secrets/meritorder/MERITORDER_GOOGLE_GROUPS_CREDENTIALS, so a rotated key is used without a restart. If your organization blocks key creation (iam.disableServiceAccountKeyCreation), use Workload Identity. 4. In the Google Admin console (admin.google.com), signed in as a super admin: Menu → Account → Admin roles. Point to Groups Reader, click Assign admin, then Assign service accounts. Enter the service account's email address, click Add, then Assign role. To limit the role to security groups, choose that while assigning it and set security_groups_only: true. If multi-party approval is on for role changes, another admin approves it. 5. Set MERITORDER_GOOGLE_GROUPS=true (or switch on Read Google Groups on Config → Access) and map groups by address. meritorder check shows which key or identity the gateway will call Google as, without calling it; the first sign-in shows whether Google answers (People page, and an alert if not).

That's all: no domain-wide delegation and no scopes to authorize in the Admin console. The gateway asks Google for one read-only scope, https://www.googleapis.com/auth/cloud-identity.groups.readonly. If the metadata server gives a token with the broader cloud-platform scope instead (GKE Workload Identity does), the Cloud Identity API accepts that too, and the service account can still only read groups: that's all its role allows. Keys and tokens are never logged or stored.

When groups are read. At sign-in, and again for people using the gateway: anyone who made a request since their groups were last read is read again once refresh_seconds (60) have passed, by one gateway at a time. A removal reaches the user record then, and every gateway's key cache within a minute after, as when SCIM brings an Entra group change: about two minutes in all by default. People who stop using the gateway aren't read until they're back. Each reading is one call to Google per person (and a page per 1,000 groups). People who signed in with Google before groups were turned on are read the first time they use the gateway after that.

Nested groups. Google's transitive search (searchTransitiveGroups) lists every group someone is in, through nested groups too, in one call. Google offers it on Workspace Enterprise Standard and Plus, Enterprise for Education, and Cloud Identity Premium; other editions get a 403. The gateway then lists direct groups (searchDirectGroups) and follows the nesting itself, one call per group, keeping each group's parents for a refresh period. A group the service account can't see into (another organization's, say) is left out and logged.

When Google can't be reached. Each person keeps the groups last read for them for keep_last_known_hours (24). After that, their team and role come from the email and domain rules alone, until Google answers again. Each step raises an alert on the console's attention list and the webhook: Google Groups unavailable (for a setup problem, such as a missing role, scope or API, the alert says what to fix), the fallback to the email rules, and the recovery. The last groups read live in Redis with the rest of the gateways' shared state.

On the People page, a Google groups column shows each person's mapped groups (the one that set their team filled, nested ones marked), the rest on hover, which mapping set their team and role, and whether Google answered last time. Team leads see only the groups the mappings use. Follow sign-in reads the person's groups at once and applies them.

Stored responses: who holds them and who can read them

A team can turn on stored mode for OpenAI's Responses API (Config → Teams → Stored responses; 04, decision 51). Then the gateway holds conversation content: each response's input and output, and each conversation's items, sealed with MERITORDER_RESPONSES_KEY, for the retention_days the operator set (required; there is no default). Elsewhere the gateway keeps none.

Who Can
The person whose key made it, on the team it was made in Read it, list its input items, chain from it, cancel it (background), delete it
A role listed in the team's stored_responses.readers Read and chain from it: admins from any team, the other roles on the same team. Not delete it
Anyone else, admins included Nothing: it's 404 to them, as if it didn't exist
  • A response belongs to its person and team. Someone moved to another team can't read or chain from what they stored on the old one; it expires with the old team's retention.
  • Removing someone deletes what they stored. Disabling them on the People page, or deactivating or deleting them through SCIM, deletes their stored responses and conversations at once, and the providers' copies (backends with responses_store). Enabling them again doesn't bring them back. Their ledger rows stay, as for anyone.
  • Spend is as for any request. Each stored turn is one ledger row, checked against the organization, team, person and session budgets, rate limits and the per-request cost limit before it's sent. A chained turn is priced on the whole conversation it's rebuilt into, which is what the provider bills.
  • The console shows sizes, never content. Config → Teams and the Teams page show, per team, how many responses, conversations and items are stored, their sealed size, for how many people, and since when. No page shows what they say.

Secrets in a saved configuration

An admin who saves a configuration from the console chooses both where a backend's key comes from and the backend's base_url, and the backend sends its key to that URL. So a saved configuration may read only what the operator allows (the YAML file on disk is the operator's and isn't checked; configstore.secret_problems):

Field May read
A backend's or bill source's auth.value_env, or ${NAME} in its auth.value A provider's key variable the shipped configs use (ANTHROPIC_API_KEY, OPENAI_API_KEY, OPENROUTER_API_KEY, GEMINI_API_KEY, AZURE_OPENAI_API_KEY, AZURE_FOUNDRY_API_KEY, XAI_API_KEY, DEEPSEEK_API_KEY, MISTRAL_API_KEY, MOONSHOT_API_KEY, ZAI_API_KEY, MINIMAX_API_KEY, ANTHROPIC_ADMIN_KEY, OPENAI_ADMIN_KEY, AZURE_EXPORT_SAS), or any MERITORDER_BACKEND_<NAME>
The gateway's own secret fields Only their own variable: reporting.clickhouse.auth MERITORDER_CLICKHOUSE_PASSWORD, compressor.api_key_env MERITORDER_COMPRESSOR_KEY, auth.oidc.google_groups.credentials_env MERITORDER_GOOGLE_GROUPS_CREDENTIALS, auth.oidc.public_client_secret MERITORDER_OIDC_CLIENT_SECRET, batches.key_env MERITORDER_BATCH_KEY (and _PREVIOUS), response_store.key_env MERITORDER_RESPONSES_KEY (and _OLD_KEYS). A static key's key_env may name any variable: its value is only compared with callers' keys
Any *_file field (value_file, key_file, credentials_file, ...) A file inside MERITORDER_SECRETS_DIR (default /run/secrets/meritorder, the chart's secrets.mountAsFiles), with .. refused and symlinks resolved, named for a variable the field may read
${NAME} anywhere else (a base_url, a region, a budget) Only the variables the shipped config uses there (AZURE_OPENAI_ENDPOINT, AWS_REGION, MERITORDER_ORG_BUDGET_USD, ...; configstore.PLAIN_ENVS)

Anything else (MERITORDER_DATABASE_URL, MERITORDER_SCIM_TOKEN, MERITORDER_ALERT_WEBHOOK_URL, any file elsewhere) is refused with a message saying what the field may read. The operator adds names in the gateways' environment: MERITORDER_CONFIG_SECRET_ENVS for secret fields and MERITORDER_CONFIG_ENVS for ${NAME} elsewhere (comma-separated, a trailing * for a prefix). Restoring an old version applies the same rules.

Where budgets and limits are set

Every budget and limit below is a field in the configuration. There are two places a configuration can come from, and only one is in effect at a time:

  1. The YAML file, config/meritorder.yaml (or MERITORDER_CONFIG), with its include: files. It is in effect only until someone saves a configuration from the console.
  2. The newest version saved in Postgres. The console saves one when an admin saves on the Controls page (Save as new config version) or the Config page (Save and apply), restores an old version (Config → History), or applies an eval run's scores. Once any version exists, every gateway, the worker and the controller use the newest one and ignore the YAML file. Editing the file after that has no effect, so make later changes on the console (the Config page's YAML tab takes the whole document).

Two saves never undo each other. Every save names the version it was made to (base_version: the version that GET /v1/admin/config/source returned, null while the file is in effect). If someone saved another version since, the gateway refuses with 409 ("someone else saved the configuration (version N) since you opened version M; reload to see their change, then make yours again") and saves nothing. The check and the insert are one step in Postgres (an advisory lock), so of two admins saving together exactly one wins. Every console save sends it: Config (Save and apply, Restore in History) and Controls. Changes the gateway or the worker writes for you (an eval run's scores, a level from the outcome report, the worker's auto_apply) are made to the newest version, read just before saving, and checked the same way; the worker skips a recommendation that loses the race and tries it on its next pass. base_version is optional on PUT /v1/admin/config and POST /v1/admin/config/versions/{id}/restore: a script that leaves it out saves over whatever version is newest, as before.

The first save copies the whole running document into Postgres (the file with its include: files merged in), with the fields you changed set to their new values. ${NAME} references are copied as written, not as their values. Each process fills them in from its own environment every time it loads the configuration.

So the environment variables in the shipped file (MERITORDER_ORG_BUDGET_USD and the others under Organization-wide safeguards) set a field only while that field still holds its ${...} reference. That is true of the file, and of stored versions in which nobody has changed that field. When an admin sets the field on the Controls page, the saved version holds the number instead, and the variable no longer has any effect on it. Clearing a field on the Controls page removes it from the document, which means no limit, not the variable's value.

Saving needs Postgres (MERITORDER_DATABASE_URL). Without it the console can edit and validate, but not save, and the YAML file stays in effect. If a stored version can't be loaded when a gateway starts, the gateway logs the error and runs on the YAML file. The worker and the controller log it and keep the configuration they already had (the YAML file, if they had just started).

Setting Where to change it
Organization budget, GPU budget, GPU burn rate and replica caps, per-request cost limit Controls page (admins; finance can view it), or safeguards: in the file
Team budget, per-person default, per-session cap Controls page or Config → Teams, or teams: in the file
Rate limits, model and backend policy, exploration Config → Teams, or teams: in the file
A level moved by the outcome report (routing.level_map) Reports → Levels → Apply (admins), Config → YAML, or routing: in the file
One person's own monthly limit People page, or PATCH /v1/admin/users/{id}. Kept on the user record in Postgres, not in the configuration

Each save is a new version with its author, time and comment. Config → History lists them and restores any of them, which saves it again as the newest version.

Budgets
