A key in localStorage is readable by any script that runs on the page and works everywhere the key does, not only in the console. Signing out only forgot it in one browser. And a small team with no identity provider had no way for people to sign in as themselves: an admin had to mint and hand out keys. Merit Order has to work for both ends: a few people running it on one machine, and an organization with Entra or Google and SCIM (decision 8).

How: Two kinds of credential, each for what it's good at.

  • People sign in to the console and get a session: a random token in an HttpOnly, SameSite=Strict cookie (Secure over HTTPS), stored on the gateway only as its SHA-256 hash (console_sessions). It lasts auth.session_hours (12 by default). Each request reads the person's record as it is now (at most a minute old, like keys), so moving, demoting or disabling someone applies to their sessions too. Signing out ends the session on the gateway.
  • Local accounts, for teams without an identity provider: an email address and a password, kept as a scrypt hash (N=2^17, r=8, p=1, OWASP's setting; hashlib, so no new dependency) in local_credentials. People join by a one-time invite link an admin or team lead makes on the People page (or meritorder accounts create --link); the same rule as for keys decides who may invite whom. An admin's reset link replaces a forgotten password and ends the person's sessions; changing your own password ends your other sessions. Passwords need 12 characters (auth.local.min_password_length) and no composition rules, as NIST SP 800-63B advises. Failed sign-ins are limited per address (10 in 15 minutes) and per client (30 a minute), a wrong address answers exactly like a wrong password, and at most four hashes run at once so a burst can't take the gateway's memory. auth.local.enabled: false turns passwords off where everyone must use SSO.
  • Keys are for machines: harnesses, CI, services and Blackstart. The console still takes one ("Sign in with an API key instead"), but the gateway trades it for a session tied to the key (key_hash on the session), so the browser never stores it and revoking the key ends the session. A console that kept a key in localStorage from before trades it for a session once and deletes it.
  • The first admin of a new install: meritorder accounts create you@example.com --role admin asks for a password, or the setup key (MERITORDER_DEV_KEY, MERITORDER_BOOTSTRAP_ADMIN_KEY) signs in once to invite people. The setup key keeps working until it's taken out of the environment; the docs say to do that outside a laptop. (A console banner warning about it was tried and dropped: on a laptop the dev key is wanted, and the banner was noise.)
  • Cross-site requests: the cookie is sent by the browser on its own, so a request made with it that changes something must carry the console's x-meritorder-console header and, when the browser names an Origin, come from the gateway's own host. No other site can send that header (the gateway allows no cross-origin requests), and SameSite=Strict already keeps the cookie off requests started from other sites. /auth/login and the other /auth changes need the header too. Requests with a key in the Authorization header are unaffected: harnesses never see the cookie, and the proxy's APIs (/v1/chat/completions, /v1/messages and the rest) don't accept it.

  • GET /auth/session answers 200 whether or not the browser is signed in, so a signed-out console logs no error.

  • SSO in the browser: a "Sign in with Microsoft / Google / your organization" button, for any OIDC provider, using the authorization-code flow with PKCE (S256), a nonce, and a single-use state kept in Redis for ten minutes. A short-lived SameSite=Lax cookie ties the provider's answer to the browser that started it, so a link someone else started can't sign you in as them. The ID token is checked as the device login's is (decision 8), with the browser client as its audience, and the person's record is created or refreshed from the same mappings; a disabled person is refused. Entra uses the same app registration (a Web redirect URI with a secret, or a public Mobile and desktop one); Google needs a separate Web application client, because its device client can't do this flow. auth.local.enabled: false makes SSO the only way in for people.

  • meritorder login keeps the device-code flow where SSO is set up (no redirect URI on the laptop needed) and asks for the email address and password where it isn't, or with --password; either way it saves a short-lived key.

After a security review (19 Nov 2026), before any release: passwords and links only for accounts invited by email (an SSO person or a key-only person never gets a password, so the identity provider and key revocation stay the way out); a team lead's link checks, when it's used, that the person is still on the lead's team with the user role, and the password it sets (and the sessions it opens) act at most as a user, so a later promotion doesn't promote whoever chose it; changing someone's team, role or access withdraws their open link; a reset or change revokes the keys meritorder login got with the old password; each sign-in attempt counts before the hash, so parallel attempts can't pass the limit; link tokens travel in request bodies, not URLs; the provider's error text never reaches the console, only its error code; the session cookie is __Host- over HTTPS; at most 64 sign-ins wait for a hashing slot.

Not chosen: Keep the key in localStorage and add password sign-in beside it: two ways in, and the weaker one stays. A JWT in the cookie instead of a server-side session: it can't be ended at sign-out or when someone is disabled without a lookup anyway, and a lookup is what a session is. argon2id: the better hash on paper, but a native dependency for every install; scrypt at OWASP's setting is the stated alternative and ships with Python. Composition rules (a digit, a symbol): NIST advises against them; length and a rate limit do more. Email for invites and resets: Merit Order would need an SMTP setting and a sender reputation; the person who makes a link sends it. Two-factor for local accounts in this change: an organization that needs it has SSO, where its identity provider already enforces MFA; TOTP or passkeys for local accounts can follow. SAML: most identity providers speak OIDC, which the gateway already verifies; SAML can come if someone needs it.

Revisit if: people want two-factor on local accounts (TOTP or passkeys), someone needs SAML, sessions should be listed and ended per device, or invites should send email.

70. Attribution is tags: Claude Code's agent labels recorded as tags, 32 tags a request, and a capabilities answer for services

Why: Two kinds of caller want cost split finer than a person and a team. Claude Code runs subagents and side requests in one session, and people want to know which of them cost what. Services built on the gateway, Blackstart first, attribute every call to an org, project, story, run, step and subagent role, keep their own cost ledger and reconcile it against ours; Blackstart's facade asks the upstream at connect what it offers (a capability handshake).

How: No new mechanism: tags already reach the ledger, every report and every export. - Claude Code's labels become tags: x-claude-code-agent-id → cc_agent, x-claude-code-parent-agent-id → cc_parent_agent, and with its hint headers (which meritorder setup claude-code turns on) x-claude-code-agent-type → cc_agent_type and x-claude-code-request-class → cc_request_class. The client's X-MeritOrder-Tags and the key's tags win over them, as the key's win over the client's. Routing already used the request class to cap side requests (routing.request_class_levels); this adds the record. - A request may carry 32 tags instead of 10: Blackstart's attribution alone is about eleven fields. - GET /v1/capabilities (any key) answers what Blackstart's handshake reads: usage in every response; cost in the x-meritorder-cost-usd header on replies that aren't streamed, and for streams a lookup by request id or tag; the tags header and its limits; x-session-id for cache affinity; the embedding models; /readyz. Route listing with providers, prices and retention, and enforcing a caller's data policy, are stated as not offered, so the facade falls back as its contract says.

Not chosen: A separate attribution header or a JSON body field (metadata): a second way to say what tags already say, and Blackstart's facade strips caller metadata anyway. Cost for streams in a final SSE event: an extra event can break strict clients; the ledger lookup works for every format. Making the cc_ tags reserved: a client that wants other names for them should be able to set them.

Revisit if: Blackstart needs route listing or data-policy enforcement from the gateway (then a routes endpoint with providers, prices and retention flags), streamed cost is needed inline, or 32 tags isn't enough.

71. Request screening starts in shadow, with fixed rules on what agents do, not a detector

Why: The planned request-security layers (secret scanning, normalization, injection signals, moderation, audit) needed an order and a first step. Research on what works against agent attacks (19 Nov 2026) found that prompt-injection detectors are weak as gates: the best detector on one benchmark caught 2% of AgentDojo injections at a 1% false-positive rate, several flagged about a third of ordinary tool output, and adaptive attacks beat most published defenses more than 90% of the time. Character tricks (emoji and Unicode tag smuggling) evaded every guardrail one study tested. What a gateway does have is a view of every tool call before the agent's next turn, and real incidents (DNS exfiltration in Claude Code, a malicious MCP config write in Cursor, markdown image leaks) have shapes fixed rules can see.

How: screening.py, per team (screening.mode: off by default, or shadow), on the messages new since the session's last turn, as outcomes.py reads them: hidden Unicode (tag characters, bidi overrides, zero-width), keys with known prefixes in tool calls and in prompts, shell rules (download piped to a shell, uploads, DNS lookups with command substitution, credential reads, config writes), edits to agent, editor, hook, CI and shell configuration, image links with data in the model's text, and untrusted content (web fetch and search results) that marks the session so later risky calls also count as after_untrusted. Findings are ledger tags (screen, screen_untrusted, reserved) and meritorder_screening_findings_total; only kinds and counts, never content. Shadow first so its false-alarm rate is measured on real traffic before anything blocks.

Not chosen: A hosted injection detector in the request path: the numbers above, plus latency and sending every tool result to another provider; it may come as a sampled, asynchronous audit. A local classifier (Prompt Guard and the like): the owner's rule is no local model in the request path. Entropy rules for secrets: agent traffic is full of hashes and base64, so they'd mostly be noise. Blocking from day one: a rule that's wrong blocks real work, and nobody yet knows how often these are wrong here. Spotlighting or encoding tool results: it would break agents' verbatim edits and the prompt cache.

Revisit if: shadow data shows a kind is rarely wrong (then block it, holding back the tool call while text still streams), a hosted detector shows good numbers on agent traffic, or encodings (base64, hex) start hiding the shapes.

72. Named tiers, a route listing, and a caller's data policy

Why: Blackstart asks for a tier (frontier, standard, cheap, embed), never a model, and expects the gateway to own what each tier sends to. Its data policy decides which providers may receive which classes of data, and whether only zero-retention endpoints may; it needs to see where each tier can send data and to have the gateway keep a request to what the policy allows. GET /v1/capabilities (decision 70) reported both as missing, so Blackstart would have treated every route's provider as unknown.

How: - tiers in the config: a chat tier is auto at a fixed level (frontier 5, standard 3, cheap 1 by default), the task from the request unless the tier sets one; a fixed tier or an embedding tier is one model (by default the cheapest priced embedding model). A model's own name wins over a tier's. The ledger keeps the tier's name as the requested model. - Each backend has a provider (from its address unless set) and the operator's zero_retention and trains_on_data from their agreement; unset is unknown, never guessed. Your own GPUs are zero-retention by nature. - X-MeritOrder-Allowed-Providers and X-MeritOrder-Zero-Retention: required on a request leave out routes the policy forbids, for chat and embeddings; nothing left is 403 data_policy with each route's reason. - GET /v1/routes lists each tier's candidate models, each route's provider, price, data facts (with their source) and whether it's available now, within the caller's team's allowed models and backends.

Not chosen: Guessing retention from the provider (it depends on the contract: Anthropic and OpenAI offer zero data retention only by agreement). A policy stored in the gateway per team: the caller already has one, and passing it per request keeps one source of truth; a team setting can come later. Tiers as model aliases: an alias names one model, and a tier's point is that the gateway chooses.

Revisit if: callers want policy per team in the gateway, data classes need different providers within one request, or providers publish machine-readable retention terms.

73. Two-factor sign-in for local accounts: authenticator codes and recovery codes

Why: Decision 69 left two-factor for later: an organization with SSO gets it from its identity provider, but a small team on local accounts had only passwords.

How: Authenticator-app codes (TOTP, RFC 6238: SHA-1, 6 digits, 30 seconds, one step of drift either side), turned on by each person from the account menu, confirmed with a first code, and asked for at every password sign-in, in the console and in meritorder login. Each step's code works once (a two-minute Redis key). Ten one-time recovery codes, stored as hashes, are shown when it's turned on. A reset link keeps two-factor on, so holding a link isn't enough to take an account over; a lost device means a recovery code or an admin's reset. The secret is sealed with MERITORDER_AUTH_KEY (AES-256-GCM, sealing.py, with the person's id as associated data) when it's set, and stored as it is otherwise: then whoever can read the database still needs the person's password, which is hashed. Turning it on ends the person's other sessions.

Not chosen: Passkeys (WebAuthn) first: better against phishing, but they need a relying-party setup tied to the gateway's host name and a server library; they can come next. SMS or email codes: Merit Order sends neither, and SMS is the weakest second factor. A required MERITORDER_AUTH_KEY: one more secret before anyone can turn two-factor on; the password hash already stands between a database copy and a sign-in. The QR code comes from qrcode-generator (MIT, no dependencies), drawn as SVG squares so nothing is injected into the page.

Revisit if: people want passkeys, or an organization wants two-factor required for everyone with a password.

74. Cheaper models as a budget runs out, not only a refusal at 100%

Why: A budget that's used up stops a team's agents mid-month with a 429. Most of their work would still get done on cheaper models, and other gateways (Cloudflare's, for one) move to them as a limit nears instead of refusing.

How: teams.<name>.budget_step_down (off unless set): once any budget that applies to a request (the organization's, the team's, the person's, the session's) is at spent, new auto and tier tasks are capped at level (an explicit floor, above a client's X-Route-Floor too, and never explored up). A named model is served as asked: the client chose it. A task under way keeps its model until its next task, so its prompt cache isn't thrown away. Requests it covers are tagged budget_step_down. At 100% the refusal stays, unless grace_share lets stepped-down requests go on past the team's and the person's budgets by that share; the organization's budget and the session limit never bend.

Not chosen: Stepping down named models too: a client that names a model has reasons (tools, format) the gateway can't see. Moving tasks already under way: the cache rebuild can cost more than the step saves. Grace by default: a budget should mean what it says unless the team decides otherwise.

Revisit if: teams want named models stepped down to the nearest cheaper model, or a second step (level 2 at 80%, level 1 at 95%).

10

How it decides

Every decision Merit Order makes, in the order it makes them, with the exact rules and defaults. Each rule names the setting that controls it. The code is the source of truth: proxy.py (request pipeline), router.py (model and backend choice), classifier.py (levels), learned.py and learned_jobs.py (the opt-in learned router), success.py (expected total cost: the success predictor and the cascade), tokens.py (prompt sizes), config.py (each model's chance of success at each level), backends/base.py (skipping failing backends), affinity.py (which GPU replica holds a session's cache), gpu.py and controller.py (GPU scaling), batches/gpu.py (batch work on running GPUs).

  • A request, start to finish
  • Which model
  • Which backend: GPU or API
  • When a backend fails or a model refuses
  • When GPUs start, scale, and stop
  • When a GPU is full
  • What happens when…
  • Every threshold in one table

A request, start to finish

Checks run in this order. The first one that fails ends the request with the error shown.

Which model

The classifier (rules, no model call; routing.levels, Config → Routing → How requests get a level, shown to everyone under Reports → Levels):

Request Floor Setting
Has tools or code-like text (code fences, def, import, file names, "refactor", "bug", SQL, …) coding:3 coding, coding_words
…and simple wording, nothing harder (write tests, rename, typo, lint, docstring, explain, bump, …) coding:2 simple, simple_words
…and "hard" wording (race condition, security, performance, migration, multi-file, "under load", flaky, …) +1 for each distinct match, up to 2; at most 5 hard_raise, hard_signals, hard_words
…and the hardest wording (architecture, "design a", system design, prove, codebase-wide, …) coding:5 hardest, hardest_words
…and the newest prompt says the last answer was wrong ("that's wrong", "revert", …) +1, at most 5 correction_raise
…with 5+ tools, only with agent_by_tools: true (off: tools say it's coding, not how hard) coding:4, simple wording ignored agent_by_tools, agent, agent_tools
Anything else general:2 general
…the whole request under 400 tokens (no tools) general:1 short, short_tokens
…analysis wording (analyze, compare, trade-offs, plan, …) general:3 analysis, analysis_words
X-Route-Hint: cheap / smart −1 / +1
Claude Code side request (x-claude-code-request-class: auxiliary) at most 1 request_class_levels
Claude Code compaction summary (compaction), and the summary the gateway writes for POST /v1/responses/compact at most 3 request_class_levels
X-Route-Floor: coding:4 exactly that, skipping the rules (never capped)
The learned router, in route mode, at least min_confidence (0.8) sure its level instead of the rules' (Claude Code's caps still apply) routing.learned

Wording is looked for in the last two messages from the person: tool results aren't read, and a user message made only of tool results (Anthropic's agent loops send one per step) is passed over, so the prompt behind a task counts mid-task. What the harness adds is left out too: Claude Code's system reminders (CLAUDE.md) and Codex's AGENTS.md and environment context. Where lists overlap, the hardest wins. Coding agents send dozens of tools on every request, so the tool count no longer sets the level (decision 61): "write tests" from Claude Code is coding:2, "fix the race condition" coding:4, "design a plugin system" coding:5. The level is set at a task boundary and held until the next one. The word lists are Python regular expressions, matched ignoring case; a pattern that doesn't compile, or matches empty text and so every request, is refused when the configuration is saved, as is a level outside 1–5.

Length never raises the floor. It only rules out models whose window can't hold the prompt plus the reply (the flowchart above, and the table under Which backend). The one length rule left, the short question, can only lower a level. The routing reason, kept in the ledger and shown under Reports → Requests, names the rules that set the floor and the models ruled out by their windows.

The Claude Code caps are routing.request_class_levels (Config → Routing → Claude Code request types); other classes (main, subagent, workflow) aren't capped. Claude Code sends the header to a gateway only with CLAUDE_CODE_GATEWAY_HINT_HEADERS=1, which meritorder setup claude-code sets. The Responses API's compaction endpoint routes its summary as a compaction request, whichever client called it (04).

The learned router (routing.learned, off by default; 03, Routing) predicts a level next to the rules' wherever they give one, from the request's hashed words and named facts, trained on what followed earlier answers. In shadow mode that's recorded with what it would have picked, and nothing changes; in route mode it's used when it's sure. The rules decide whenever there's no model, the model is stale (older than max_age_days, the level rules changed, or the feature key did), it's under min_confidence, or it fails; a client's X-Route-Floor is never second-guessed. The routing reason says what it predicted, how sure it was, its version, and why it was or wasn't used. It's asked only when an auto request is classified (a new task); a request that names its model only has its features recorded, as training data.

Quality scores (1–5 per task type) come from published benchmarks, refreshed daily (quality:; see 00, How it all works). A model the source doesn't cover isn't a candidate for auto unless it has a quality_override.

What the client can force

Client sends Effect
A model name That model; only the backend varies
reasoning_effort / output_config.effort Passed through, translated across formats (an Anthropic client's effort reaches an OpenAI-format model at the nearest level it accepts). Merit Order only picks an effort for auto requests that don't set one
X-Route-Floor, X-Route-Hint Changes the floor for auto when it classifies (mid-task, the session's floor stands)
X-MeritOrder-Priority: cost / balanced / speed How much more a faster route may cost (below); anything else is a 400
X-MeritOrder-Backend Pins the backend (admins and eval-run keys only; anyone else gets a 403)
X-MeritOrder-Cache: on / off Uses the response cache even where the team has it off, or skips it
X-Session-Id (or X-MeritOrder-Session) Names the session; otherwise it's inferred from the conversation
x-claude-code-session-id, x-claude-code-agent-id The session, and a subagent's own thread within it (own model, level, cache; spend still counts the session)
Codex CLI's session-id, and thread-id with x-codex-parent-thread-id The same, for Codex: the session, and a subagent's own thread

Team policy (allowed models and backends) applies before any of this, so nothing above can escape it.

Threshold or cost per success

routing.model_choice (or a team's model_choice) sets how auto chooses among models for a new task:

Choice Picks
threshold The cheapest route of a model whose score is at least the level
cost_per_success The lowest expected cost per solved task, among models whose chance of solving work at the level is at least min_success_chance (0.6), whatever their score
expected_cost (default) The lowest expected total cost to finish the task, among the same models: the try, plus the chance of failing times what a failure costs (the person's time the request puts at stake, human_cost_usd scaled by its level and size, and the next attempt); and escalation inside the task (below)

A model's chance at each level comes from its score in use (apply_chances in config.py). The scale says what a score means on the reference work (absolute, the default: 5 × the model's chance ÷ the anchor; best: ÷ the best model's), so a score read back gives its chance there, and a level gives the chance of a model scoring exactly that level. Level-L work is taken to be as much easier than the reference as a model scoring L is weaker than a 5: a model exactly at a level solves that level's work as often as a 5 solves the reference work (the anchor: 69.9% for coding and 76.9% for general, what Claude Fable 5.2 solved of FrontierSWE-hard tasks on 12 November 2026). Every other model sits by its distance from the level on Epoch's logistic ability scale:

chance at level L = sigmoid( logit(chance of its score) − logit(chance of a score of L) + logit(chance of a 5) )

Level 5 is the reference work itself. For coding, that gives:

Model Coding score Level 1 2 3 4 5
Claude Fable 5.2 5.0 97% 93% 88% 81% 70%
Gemini 4 Carbon 4.4 96% 91% 84% 75% 62%
GPT-6.1 Terra 4.2 95% 90% 82% 72% 59%
Claude Sonnet 5.5 3.9 94% 88% 79% 69% 55%
Claude Haiku 5.5 3.0 91% 81% 70% 57% 42%
DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 2.4 88% 75% 62% 48% 34%
GPT-6 Luna 2.3 87% 74% 60% 46% 32%
gpt-oss-20b 1.0 70% 49% 34% 23% 14%

Reading the chance from the score rather than from the published chance keeps the threshold's own rules: an override counts, and the floor of 1 still makes every model fit for level-1 work. Where the chances come from:

Quality source What a 5 solves Scores that get chances
epoch quality.anchor (scale absolute), or the best configured model's published chance on the reference (best) The source's own, and overrides
config quality.measured_best_rate: the best measured model's pass rate on hard eval tasks, written when an eval run's scores are applied as quality The configured scores, and overrides
artificial_analysis Nothing: the index isn't a chance None

A model without a chance (a mock, a score written in the config while a live source is in use, a task type with no measured rate) is judged by the threshold: it's a candidate only at or above the level, and counts at the chance of a model exactly at it. With no chances for the task type at all, the threshold decides.

Expected cost per success. One try costs the route's estimate (below: the session from here, with its warm cache or rebuild) and succeeds with the model's chance at the level. A failed try is still paid for, and the work is then done again on the redo route: the one the threshold would pick (the cheapest route of a model that meets the level; if none does, the most likely to succeed), tried until it succeeds.

redo     = redo route's cost ÷ its chance
expected = cost + (1 − chance) × redo

For the redo route itself that's its cost ÷ its chance. A model below the level wins only when the try it saves on costs less than redoing its extra failures: cost < chance × redo. Failures are assumed independent, and the time a person spends noticing one isn't counted; the minimum chance is what guards against both.

The rules around it:

  • The minimum holds for every model with a chance, at the level too. A model exactly at the level has 70% for coding, so the default 0.6 only rules out models below the level; a minimum above 70% leaves only models above it.
  • The threshold steps in when no model reaches the minimum, or none that does can run right now.
  • A level the client sets (X-Route-Floor, also how a named model is substituted) is a minimum it asked for: the threshold decides.
  • Mid-task the session keeps its model, as always. Cost per success changes where a new task goes, and where a session that outgrew its model moves.
  • Everything after compares expected costs per success: the priority's premium (2%, 20%, 100%), stickiness (a move must save 10% + $0.01), and the speed checks. Cache warmth counts through each route's cost: a warm session's rebuild is zero, so a cheaper model elsewhere has to beat it after paying to rebuild there.
  • Effort and the output limit follow the level, whichever model wins.
  • Teams set their own model_choice and min_success_chance; blank uses the organization's.
  • Levels are untouched: routing.levels still sets them. Reports → Levels shows, for a team routing by cost per success, the models below each level that are in reach, with their chance there.

The routing reason (the ledger's route_reason, shown on Reports → Requests) ends with what it compared: classified coding:3 (coding: 1 tool); cost per success: deepseek-v4.1-flash, expected $0.0051 per success (62% at coding:3) vs $0.0086 (70%) on claude-haiku, the cheapest at the level. When the threshold decides instead, it says why (cost per success: no chances of success for coding, so the threshold decides).

What it changes, for new sessions on the shipped configuration and price list of 12 November 2026 (minimum 0.6), with pauses on one later turn in ten (the prior, below):

Request Threshold Cost per success
coding:3, 30,000 tokens Claude Haiku 5.5 (Anthropic): $0.0060 a try, 70%, so $0.0086 per success DeepSeek V4.1 Flash: $0.0018, 62%, $0.0051
coding:4 (hard wording), 40,000 tokens GPT-6.1 Terra: $0.064, 72%, $0.089 the same (Gemini 4 Carbon: $0.15)
coding:5 (the hardest wording), 90,000 tokens Claude Fable 5.2 (Anthropic): $1.07, 70%, $1.53 Gemini 4 Carbon: $0.26, 62%, $0.85
general:2, 2,000 tokens Claude Haiku 5.5: $0.0016, 78%, $0.0021 DeepSeek V4.1 Flash: $0.0009, 67%, $0.0015
general:3, 3,000 tokens GPT-6.1 Terra: $0.016, 84%, $0.019 Claude Haiku 5.5: $0.0018, 65%, $0.0086

Expected total cost

With model_choice: expected_cost (decisions 62 and 67; 03), the models in reach are the same as cost per success's, and each route is ranked by

E(m)         = try(m) + (1 − P(m)) × (H × stakes + next attempt)
stakes       = (1/3)^(5 − level) × min(1, prompt tokens / 8,000); counted at level 5 after a correction
next attempt = the cheapest of: m again, or a stronger model e (a higher chance) from a cold cache,
               each E(· | m failed) with one attempt fewer left; nothing once max_escalations are planned
Part What it is Setting (default)
try(m) The route's cost for the rest of the session, as above (warm cache or rebuild, the 1-hour cache, pauses)
H What a failed attempt at the top of the scale (a level-5 agent task) costs the person: their minutes times their rate routing.human_cost_usd ($1); team human_cost_usd; Config → Routing → Expected total cost, Controls
stakes The share of H a failure of this request puts at risk: a third for each level below 5 (level 3: 1/9, level 1: 1/81), times the prompt's size up to 8,000 tokens; the whole level-5 share after a correction ("that's wrong", "revert") fixed (success.STAKES_LEVEL, STAKES_TOKENS)
P(m) The benchmark prior at the task's difficulty, read between levels; widened by the learned router's spread in route mode; the fitted layer in its place once it's routing and beat the prior routing.success.mode (off)
A failure's effect on the next attempt Each model's chance on the task moves with a hidden difficulty 1 log-odds wide, so a task one model failed is harder for the next too fixed (success.SPREAD)
Attempts planned after the first None by default: a failure costs the person's time; with the cascade on, as many as it may escalate routing.cascade.max_escalations (0; up to 2)

Inside a task, with the cascade on (routing.cascade.max_escalations 1 or 2; off by default, since on the routing simulator it saved nothing in total, counting failed attempts at a price per failed attempt, for a third more model spend), a team routing by expected_cost may escalate:

When What's compared
Mid-task, after failures_now (3) failures in a row (failed test or build runs, or error tool results) Continuing: the rest of the task on its model, at its chance now (its chance at the task's start moved by the evidence, table in 03), a failure there escalating later. Escalating: the rest of the task on a stronger model from a cold cache, one escalation fewer left. Escalates when that's cheaper by more than switch_margin_usd ($0.01)
At a human message that carries on the task: a correction, or the code left failing (the last run after the last edit failed) and a prompt that, classified first, is the same kind of work at no higher a level than the task's The same; the task, its row and its evidence go on. A correction puts the level-5 share of H at stake, so it's where an escalation most often pays
At any other human message A new task, chosen afresh: the only way a task goes back down

Never for a named model, never past the team's models, never once a budget is 90% spent, never more than max_escalations per task, never into a refusal by max_request_usd. Every request of an escalated task is tagged escalation and escalated_from; its first request (the answer's row, once) takes the failed attempt's baseline cost off its routing savings.

The reason says what was compared, and what's at stake: classified coding:3 (coding: 1 tool); expected total cost: claude-haiku ~$0.055 to finish: try $0.0060, chance 70% (benchmark), difficulty 3.0 (level 3), a failure costs $0.11 of a person's time (of $1.00: 1/9 at level 3), then claude-haiku again; deepseek-v4.1-flash ~$0.063, chance 62% (benchmark), and for an escalation (cascade on), at the person's "that's wrong" after a failing run: escalated at the next human message (1 of 1): claude-haiku's chance now 24% (was 70%: tests failing after the last edit -0.6, corrected (wrong) -1.4); continuing ~$1.00 vs escalating to gpt-terra ~$0.28 (82%, cache rebuild included); at coding:3 (coding: 1 tool).

What it picks for new sessions on the shipped configuration and price list of 12 November 2026, with the benchmark prior alone (nothing fitted yet; a try's cost and the model's chance at the level):

Request Threshold Expected total cost, H = $0.25 H = $1 (default) H = $5
general:1, 20 tokens ("What's the capital of Portugal?") GLM-5.3 Flash, $0.00038, 77% GLM-5.3 Flash GLM-5.3 Flash GLM-5.3 Flash
coding:2, 20,000 tokens ("write unit tests", an agent) DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, $0.0015, 75% DeepSeek V4.1 Flash DeepSeek V4.1 Flash Claude Haiku 5.5, $0.0046, 81%
coding:3, 30,000 tokens Claude Haiku 5.5, $0.0060, 70% DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, $0.0018, 62% Claude Haiku 5.5 GPT-6.1 Terra, $0.051, 82%
coding:4 (agent), 40,000 tokens GPT-6.1 Terra, $0.064, 72% GPT-6.1 Terra GPT-6.1 Terra GPT-6.1 Terra
coding:5 (agent, hard wording), 90,000 tokens Claude Fable 5.2, $1.07, 70% Gemini 4 Carbon, $0.26, 62% Gemini 4 Carbon Gemini 4 Carbon
general:2, 2,000 tokens Claude Haiku 5.5, $0.0016, 78% DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, $0.00085, 67% Claude Haiku 5.5 Claude Haiku 5.5
general:3, 3,000 tokens GPT-6.1 Terra, $0.016, 84% Claude Haiku 5.5, $0.0018, 65% Claude Haiku 5.5 GPT-6.1 Terra

Under decision 62 alone (the full H on every request) the default sent the first three rows and both general rows to GPT-6.1 Terra or Gemini 4 Carbon, at 2 to 40 times the threshold's try. The benchmark's chances are FrontierSWE-scaled, more pessimistic than most traffic, and the stakes keep that from buying strong models for easy work; at levels 4 and 5 a failure still costs most of H. On the routing simulator the default $1 spends no more than the threshold on any task class; $2 and up spend more on analysis and chat (03). Turn routing.success.mode to shadow (with the learned router on), and to route once Reports → Learned router shows the fitted layer beat the prior.

Exploration and the level map

A team that explores (teams.<name>.exploration, off by default) has a few of its task starts routed a level down or up from the level they'd get, at random, so Reports → Levels can say whether each level is too high or too low for the work (03). Before that, a level the outcome report's recommendation moved is applied (routing.level_map, e.g. {"coding:3": 2}).

Arm Its chance (default share 4%, a canary's 20%) Recorded
served 96% (with a canary at the level: 76.8%) arm served, propensity
down, up 2% each (with a canary: 1.6%); at level 1 or 5 the whole 4% one way; up's half stays served near a budget arm, arm_from, propensity, ledger tags explore, explore_from
canary 20% of the level's task starts, until it has 30 there or 14 days pass arm canary

The report weights each task start by 1 ÷ its arm's chance, so arms and teams with different shares compare fairly. A recommendation ("coding level 3: level 2 does as well in 98% (n=412 explored, 9,870 served); consider lowering") needs 200 task starts on each side and a difference clear at 90%; it raises an alert once, and an admin applies it (or the worker, with routing.benchmark.auto_apply, when the learned router's model in use beat the rules and leans the same way).

Which backend: GPU or API

Each candidate model lists its routes (backends that serve it). A route is dropped when:

Dropped when Why
The backend isn't enabled (no key, no URL) or the team may not use it Policy and credentials
The backend is being skipped after failures (see When a backend fails) Bad credentials or a network-level outage: the whole backend. Retried when the wait is up
This model is being skipped on this backend: over capacity (429/503/529), its deployment doesn't exist there (404), or it failed 3 times in a row (408/409/425/500) Only that model there; the backend's other models are unaffected. A busy route is kept as a last resort if nothing else can take the request
It's a GPU deployment that isn't warm (not started, starting, or stopped now) Nothing to send to
It's draining and this session has no warm cache there (on any of its replicas) Draining only finishes sessions already there
It's a GPU at 100% (see When a GPU is full) Saturated: new work spills to other routes. Kept as a last resort if nothing else can take the request
It's a saturated GPU whose queue is also full No room to wait either
auto and the route has no known price An unknown price must never look free
The model's context window is too small (prompt plus the client's max_tokens > 95% of it) and other models fit Avoid a guaranteed error. Mid-task too: a session that outgrows its model moves to one with room, at the same floor. When nothing at the floor fits, only the largest window is kept and the provider decides
auto and it's a mock backend while real ones exist Mocks are for trying things out
A batch request, and the backend has no batch API; or it's a GPU that's full or draining, or batches.gpu.enabled is off Batch work only goes where it can wait at batch prices

The rest are ranked by what this session will cost from here:

cost = rebuild + expected_remaining_turns × per_turn
rebuild   = cached context × (cache-write − cache-read price) × the share of it the backend no longer holds
            (0 when it holds this session's cache; on a GPU, the share is the replica's, see below)
per_turn  = cached context × cache-read + new tokens × cache-write + ~600 output tokens × output price
            (new tokens: ~2,000, or for a known session what the prompt grew since its last turn, at least 200;
             cached context: the rest of the prompt.
             cache-write is the input price except where caching is explicit and writes cost extra:
             Anthropic-format backends (Claude on Anthropic, Bedrock, Vertex, Foundry) and Claude through
             OpenRouter, which gets a cache marker; on a backend whose cache_ttl_seconds is 3600 or more,
             the 1-hour write price. Elsewhere caching is automatic.)
          + after the first turn, where the cache lasts under an hour (cache_ttl_seconds < 3600):
            pause share × cached context × (cache-write − cache-read)
            (a pause of 5 to 60 minutes rebuilds a 5-minute cache, not an hour's; the share is the team's own,
             leaning on the organization's and a prior of 1 in 10, from pauses.py; GPUs get none)
turns     = turns so far, clamped to 3…30 (a long session is expected to keep going)
prices    = the route's live price (or its `price:` override) at this prompt's length (long-prompt tiers apply)

A GPU's price is a shadow price: what one token "costs" given how busy the GPU is. It scales the price: written on the GPU route, which is set to the model's API-equivalent rate (GPUs have no live price list); a GPU route without one is never used by auto.

So GPUs win whenever they have room, even for a better model than the task needs (a "free upgrade", sent at low vLLM priority so traffic that needs that model goes first). As they fill up, APIs win again.

Batch requests are priced the same way against the providers' batch prices (about half): a running GPU with room wins, at its shadow price for its load now. The worker then runs them only in the headroom below the knee (60% of max_concurrency × replicas, less live requests), at vLLM priority 20, below free upgrades, and hands what hasn't run after 12 hours to the request's provider batch route (02).

Then the tie-breakers:

  1. Close on price, then quality and speed. The same model often costs the same everywhere (Claude on Anthropic, Bedrock, Foundry and OpenRouter), so price alone can't choose. Routes that cost at most the priority's premium more than the cheapest compete on speed instead:
Priority A faster route may cost up to Within that range
cost (default) 2% more (a tie) the higher-quality model (auto), then the faster route
balanced 20% more the faster route, then the higher-quality model
speed 100% more the faster route, then the higher-quality model

With expected total cost the range is the premium of the cheapest route's money (the tokens in its expected total), not of its total with the person's time, so a 2% tie stays 2% of what's spent (decision 67). The organization default is routing.priority; a team can set its own (priority), and a request can send X-MeritOrder-Priority: cost|balanced|speed. Speed is the expected time for a typical reply (routing.est_output_tokens, 600 tokens): time to the first token plus the writing time, both moving averages of real replies on that route (backend + upstream model). Timing starts when the route is called, so a route that took over after a failure isn't charged for it. A route is trusted after 2 replies; until then it ranks after measured ones, keeping cost order. 2. Measuring the alternatives. Otherwise the first route measured would win forever. Every 10th new session (routing.speed_check_every; 0 turns it off) can go to a route in that price range that hasn't been measured, or not in the last 10 minutes. Never mid-session, so no cache is lost. 3. Stickiness: a session stays on its current backend unless the cheapest one saves more than 10% + $0.01 over the rest of the session (with expected total cost, the difference in expected totals has to beat 10% of the current route's money plus $0.01), which is usually only true once its cache has expired (as long as the request's last cache marker asked: 5 minutes, or an hour for the gateway's own markers from a session's second turn on the shipped Claude backends; cache_ttl_seconds per backend). That's what stops a session bouncing between Bedrock and Anthropic and paying to rebuild its cache each time. Speed never moves a session either: a warm cache is cheaper, and usually faster, than any other route.

Each gateway process learns speeds from its own traffic. The console's Backends page shows them per model (first token, tokens per second).

Which replica of a GPU deployment. Each replica has its own KV cache. When the gateway can reach replicas one by one (SkyPilot's clusters, Kubernetes pods, or a static server's static_urls), it prices each with the same formula, at that replica's load and with the share of the session's prefix that replica probably still holds, and sends the request to the cheapest:

The share still held comes from vLLM's KV events (serve.kv_events), else an estimate from the replica's KV-cache metrics (what it has written since the session's last turn against what it had free), else the cache TTL (04). Behind a load balancer that doesn't know sessions, it's divided by the number of replicas. A replica the gateway can't connect to is skipped for 60 s, and the deployment's endpoint is used.

When a backend fails or a model refuses

The gateway reads the start of every stream, up to its first content, before passing it on. So an error that arrives after a 200 still goes to the next source, and nothing reaches the client twice. Once content has started, an error is passed through: switching then would repeat output. The ledger records that request with the provider's error and status, and the tokens it billed. A too-long prompt isn't counted against the backend, and with X-MeritOrder-Backend set it isn't re-decided.

How long a failing backend or model is skipped:

Failure Skipped For
Over capacity (429, 503, 529) That model on that backend The provider's Retry-After if it sends one, else 10 s doubling; at most 5 min either way. Still tried as a last resort
Model or deployment not found (404) That model on that backend 5 min, doubling to 1 hour while it stays missing (a model not deployed there yet is checked less and less often). Turn a backend off in .env (MERITORDER_BEDROCK=false, MERITORDER_FOUNDRY_CLAUDE=false) until its models exist
Credentials rejected (401, 403) The backend 1 min doubling to 10 min
Anything else (5xx, timeouts, network) The model (408, 409, 425, 500) or the backend (402, 502, 504, network) After 3 in a row: 5 s doubling to 60 s. A Retry-After on a retryable error (not 402) applies at once, up to 5 min

When something starts being skipped, an alert goes to the console's "needs attention" list, the log, and MERITORDER_ALERT_WEBHOOK_URL. It says why and where its traffic goes meanwhile. That's at most once per backend and model every 30 minutes, with a second alert when it works again. The Backends page shows what's skipped and for how long. meritorder_failovers_total{backend,status} counts every failed attempt except bad requests (other 4xx and too-long prompts), and responses served after one carry X-MeritOrder-Failed-Over: backend/model status (or prompt too long).

A request gets at most max_attempts (3) tries in all: failovers, moves to a bigger window, and refusal retries count; asking a route again for what its credit covers (HTTP 402) doesn't, and neither does sending a request to a deployment's endpoint after its replica couldn't be reached. Once a stream has started sending content to the client, a failure can't be retried: the client gets an error event, and the partial usage is still recorded.

When GPUs start, scale, and stop

The capacity controller (meritorder controller) runs every 60 s and wakes within 2 s when an admin changes a GPU control. It needs Postgres, and only one is active at a time (a Postgres advisory lock); a second one stands by.

The state machine (per deployment):

Transition Exactly when
start Wanted ≥ 1 continuously for 10 min and not in a cooldown. At once when an admin pins replicas (ignoring any cooldown from before the pin) or min_replicas > 0 (once any cooldown is over)
ready The replicas answer /v1/models
failed, timed out The start call fails, every replica's SkyPilot launch fails (or a cluster dies before vLLM was ever ready), Kubernetes refuses the pods for good (a quota or policy, an image that can't be pulled, a missing Secret, vLLM crashing three times, credentials the cluster rejects, the resource deleted outside Merit Order), or 45 min pass; the replicas are shut down and the deployment cools down for 30 min. A start whose teardown fails too stays tracked as starting (and billing), and the teardown is tried again every cycle. The reason is in the activity log
stopped (while starting) An admin stop, Stop all GPUs, the GPU budget, or a fleet cap: provisioning is cancelled at once
scale Wanted changes while warm: on SkyPilot a cluster launched or torn down per replica, on Kubernetes a patch of the replica count. A scale that fails keeps the replicas that ran, and is tried again next cycle
demand gone Wanted = 0 for 10 min, and the deployment has been warm at least 30 min
stop (drain) An admin stop with "drain first", the GPU budget, or a fleet cap. Skips the 30-minute hold
stop now An admin stop with "stop now", or Stop all GPUs (unless set to drain)
lost readiness Replicas stop answering (e.g. a spot preemption: the controller launches the SkyPilot cluster again, or Kubernetes replaces the pod); traffic goes to APIs until they're back
demand returns Wanted ≥ 1 again while draining, unless it was stopped
drained 15 min after draining started
State Gets traffic? Billing?
api_only No; its models' traffic goes to APIs (or other models for auto) No
provisioning No Yes, from the moment the provisioner starts it (the SkyPilot launches, or the Kubernetes resource is created)
warm Yes, first choice while it has headroom Yes
draining Only sessions whose cache is already there Yes

When a GPU is full

How "full" is measured. Two signals; a backend is saturated when either reaches 100%:

Signal Source How fresh
vLLM's own load: KV-cache use, pushed to 100% by ~10 waiting requests The controller reads /metrics once per cycle Up to one cycle (60 s) old
Requests in flight ÷ (max_concurrency × replicas) Every gateway counts its own requests to the backend and publishes the count to Redis every 2 s Live for this gateway, ≤ 2 s for others

The second signal only exists when the backend sets max_concurrency (vLLM's --max-num-seqs, or what its KV cache fits). Without it, a burst can pile up in vLLM for up to a minute before the gateways notice. Set it.

Where requests wait. Merit Order has no queue of its own, in Redis or anywhere else: LLM calls are interactive and streaming, so the gateway forwards each request at once and holds the connection open. The only queue is vLLM's scheduler, on the GPU.

Waiting requests are in-flight requests beyond max_concurrency × replicas; without max_concurrency, the controller's last count of vLLM's waiting requests is used. When that count is more than 5 minutes old (the controller stopped, say), every request the gateways have in flight there counts as waiting, so the bound still holds; it may then turn requests away before vLLM's queue is really full. Meanwhile the controller sees the demand and adds replicas (after scale_up_after_minutes, up to max_replicas).

What happens when…

When What happens
A GPU is saturated New requests go to an API route for the same model, or (for auto) another model; sessions on it move too and rebuild their cache. If nothing else can take a request, it waits in vLLM's queue (x-meritorder-queued: 1)
A GPU is saturated, it's the only route, and its queue is full 503 overloaded_error saying so; the client retries. The controller adds replicas if the demand lasts
A burst hits a GPU With max_concurrency set, gateways see it within 2 s and spill the excess; without it, up to a minute of requests queue in vLLM first
Demand drops After 10 min below break-even (and 30 min warm), the deployment drains for 15 min, then stops
A batch arrives while a GPU has room Its requests for models the GPU serves (or, for auto, levels it meets) go there, near free; the worker runs them in the headroom at low priority. Batch work never counts as demand, so it never starts or keeps a GPU
A GPU hasn't run a batch's requests 12 hours in, or it stops or drains What's left goes to each request's provider batch route (handed on, at about half price), as does a request the GPU failed twice; a request with no such route waits for the GPU until the batch's 24-hour deadline, then expires
Demand rises After 10 min above break-even, GPUs start; traffic stays on APIs until they're ready (10–20+ min for big models)
An admin stops a GPU (drain) No new sessions there at once; warm sessions finish for up to 15 min; then it's shut down
An admin stops a GPU (now) Gateways stop sending to it within seconds; the next request in each session goes elsewhere and rebuilds its cache there; shutdown starts within seconds (the cloud takes a few minutes)
An admin pins N replicas Started at once (no 10-min wait, no cooldown), kept regardless of demand, until unpinned or the pin expires; safeguards still apply. A start that fails while pinned cools down for 30 min; pinning again retries at once
Stop all GPUs Every deployment stops, none start, until someone resumes
An auto session's model has nowhere to run It's routed again from scratch to another model meeting the floor
The learned router is in shadow mode Each new task's features and the learned level are recorded with what that level would have picked and cost; routing is exactly what the rules give. Reports → Learned router compares them
The learned router has no model, or it's stale, unsure, or fails The rules decide, and the routing reason says why. A model is stale once it's older than max_age_days (30), the level rules change, or the feature key does
A new learned-router model is trained It's used only if it predicts the newest fifth of the requests better than the rules alone by more than chance; gateways load it within seconds. meritorder router use goes back to another version
A team routes by cost per success New tasks may go to a cheaper model a little below their level, when its chance there is at least the minimum and it costs less per solved task; with no chances to go on, or nothing in reach that can run, the threshold decides
A named model has nowhere to run 503 explaining each route ("stopped by dana: cost review", "OPENROUTER_API_KEY is not set") unless the team turned on substitute_unavailable; then a model at least as good, with x-meritorder-substituted-for
The GPU budget runs out All GPUs drain and none start until next month or the budget is raised; traffic goes to APIs
The fleet hits max $/hour or max replicas Lower-value deployments are held to fewer replicas or stopped
The org budget runs out Every request gets a 429 until next month or it's raised
A team or person hits their budget Their requests get a 429; everyone else is unaffected
An agent loops The session stops at max_session_usd; a spend-spike alert fires when someone's hour is 5× their norm (and at least $5)
A provider's account can't cover the reply (HTTP 402) If it says how much it can (OpenRouter: "can only afford N tokens") and the client didn't set max_tokens, the same route is asked again for N (x-meritorder-max-tokens-source: provider credit), up to three times, since requests in flight reserve credit too and N can shrink between tries; otherwise the next backend
A request could cost more than max_request_usd With max_tokens set: cheaper candidates are used; if none fit, a 400 says what it could have cost. Without: the reply is allowed only as many tokens as fit under the limit
Provisioning fails or takes > 45 min Shut down, 30-min cooldown, alert; traffic stays on APIs. On Kubernetes, waiting for a GPU node isn't a failure (a cluster autoscaler may be adding one) until the 45 min pass
A spot replica is preempted The controller launches its SkyPilot cluster again (or the Kubernetes Deployment replaces the pod); if no replica is ready, the deployment shows "starting" and traffic goes to APIs meanwhile
A SkyPilot launch fails (no capacity in any allowed cloud or region) Whatever it made is torn down; that replica is tried again after 10 min. When every wanted replica failed, it's a failed start: 30-min cooldown
A stop fails at the cloud The deployment stays marked running and the controller keeps retrying; the console shows it in red
The Kubernetes API stops answering A warm deployment whose replicas still answer stays warm; one that is starting keeps waiting (the 45-minute limit still applies)
The controller isn't running (or can't reach its replicas: its machine sleeps, the network dropped, ~/.sky was lost) Nothing scales them. Each SkyPilot replica stops vLLM when its lease runs out (lease_minutes, 15) and SkyPilot deletes the machine autostop_minutes (5) later; Kubernetes replicas stay as they are. Gateways keep using the last published state; the console flags it if GPUs are up
A SkyPilot cluster no deployment wants (a renamed or removed backend, a teardown that failed, a crash halfway through a scale) Torn down by the next controller cycle's sweep (and the first one after a start), and logged in the activity log
A provider is over capacity (429/529, or overloaded inside a stream) The next candidate: the same model on another backend (e.g. Anthropic → Bedrock), or, for auto, another model. Mid-task the session keeps its model while any of its routes can answer; once every route for it is over capacity, the session moves to another qualifying model, and the busy routes are tried only if nothing else can take it. That model is skipped there for Retry-After (or 10 s doubling); its other models keep working; alert
A provider is down (timeouts, connection errors, 5xx) Same: next backend; skipped after 3 failures in a row; alert, and another when it recovers
A provider accepts a stream but never answers Abandoned after first_byte_timeout_seconds (120 s; off for self-hosted GPUs) and sent to the next backend
A provider rejects the key (401/403) Next backend; the backend is skipped for a minute (doubling). Fix the key; meritorder check shows what's usable
A model refuses (stop_reason: refusal, content_filter) auto: retried on the next model, refusal billed and logged. Named model: the refusal is returned
The harness compacts history Every cache for that session is dead, so it's a free moment to re-route
A conversation outgrows its model (prompt plus the client's max_tokens > 95% of the window) auto: the next turn moves to the cheapest model with room at the same floor, even mid-task, and rebuilds its cache there. The floor never rises with length. A named model is sent anyway; the provider decides
A conversation is too long for every model at its floor auto: sent to the largest window anyway (the count is an estimate); if the provider refuses, the client gets "prompt is too long: …" and Claude Code compacts
A provider says the prompt is too long auto: a qualifying model with a bigger window, if there is one. Otherwise, and for a named model: the error, worded "prompt is too long: …" so Claude Code compacts
Claude Code runs a subagent or a side request Routed in its own thread of the session, so the main conversation's model and cache are untouched; side requests at level ≤ 1, compaction summaries ≤ 3
A session's cache expires (idle > 5 min) Moving is now free, so it may move to a cheaper backend
A stream breaks midway The client gets an error event; partial usage is recorded
Redis is down Requests fail (sessions, budgets, and rate limits live there). Use a managed Redis with failover
A burst exceeds the Redis connection pool Requests wait for a free connection (up to 10 s) rather than failing
Postgres is down Static keys keep working, and cached keys for up to a minute; new sign-ins and key lookups fail; ledger rows that can't be written are logged and lost
Someone saves a bad config It's rejected on save; gateways, the worker, and the controller keep the last good version

Every threshold in one table

What Default Setting
How auto chooses among models expected_cost (the lowest expected total cost to finish the task; threshold before decision 62) routing.model_choice; team model_choice
Lowest chance at the level that cost per success and expected total cost accept 0.6 routing.min_success_chance; team min_success_chance
What a failed attempt costs a person (expected total cost) $1 (a minute at $60 an hour) for a level-5 agent task; a request puts a share at stake: a third for each level below 5, less under 8,000 tokens, all of it after a correction routing.human_cost_usd; team human_cost_usd
The success predictor's fitted layer off (shadow: trained and recorded; route: used once it beat the benchmark prior on the newest fifth by more than twice the standard error); needs 200 task starts with an outcome routing.success.mode
Escalations per task (expected total cost) 0, off (up to 2); when on, mid-task only after 3 failures in a row, else at a human message that carries on the task; never once a budget is 90% spent routing.cascade.max_escalations, failures_now
The learned router off (shadow: compare, change nothing; route: use it when sure) routing.learned.mode
How sure the learned router must be for its level to be used 0.8 routing.learned.min_confidence
A learned-router model is stale after 30 days (0: never), or once the level rules or the feature key change routing.learned.max_age_days
Training the learned router when asked (meritorder router train, Reports → Learned router → Train now); on the last 30 days, at most the newest 20,000 requests routing.learned.retrain_hours, train_days, train_requests
Training needs; a model is used if 200 requests with an outcome, at least one of them with a signal; it beats the rules on the newest fifth by more than twice the standard error fixed (meritorder router train --min-examples)
What the learned router reads the first and last 2,000 characters of the text the rules read, hashed into 65,536 buckets; named facts about the request fixed
Recorded request features are kept 90 days routing.learned.keep_days
Judged labels for the learned router off; on: 1% of a team's eligible task starts, replayed on auto at level 5 and graded by the evals' judges, under a monthly cap with no default, starting within 60 seconds or dropped team judged_labels
What a quality score of 5 stands for absolute: a fixed chance on the reference, 0.6994 for coding and 0.7685 for general quality.scale, quality.anchor
Exploration off; on: 4% of a team's eligible task starts, half a level down and half up; a canary takes 20% of its level's team exploration
Request screening off; shadow: findings recorded as ledger tags and metrics, nothing blocked team screening.mode
Budget step-down off; on: new auto and tier tasks capped at level 1 once a budget that applies is 80% spent; no grace past 100% team budget_step_down
Exploring up stops when a budget is 90% spent fixed
A canary is done after 30 recorded task starts at its level, or 14 days routing.benchmark.canary_outcomes, canary_days
A level recommendation needs 200 task starts on each side, and a clear difference at 90%: the level below at least 95% as good, or the level above clearly better routing.benchmark.min_outcomes, as_well
Recommendations applied by an admin (or automatically when the learned router agrees) routing.benchmark.auto_apply; routing.level_map
Share of later turns expected after a 5–60 minute pause measured per team; with little data the organization's, then 0.10, each counting as 100 turns; counts halve every 7 days fixed (pauses.py)
What a measured 5 solves, for chances with quality.source: config not set (no chances: the threshold) quality.measured_best_rate, written when eval scores are applied
Stickiness margin to move a session 10% + $0.01 routing.switch_margin_pct, switch_margin_usd
Expected turns for cost estimates 3–30 routing.min_expected_turns, max_expected_turns
Tokens per turn for cost estimates ~2,000 new (a known session: the prompt's growth, at least 200); 600 output routing.est_new_tokens_per_turn, est_output_tokens
How much more a faster route may cost cost 2%, balanced 20%, speed 100% routing.priority, priority_premium_pct; team priority; X-MeritOrder-Priority
Checking an unmeasured or stale route's speed every 10th new session; stale after 10 min routing.speed_check_every
GPU shadow price below the knee 2% of API price routing.shadow_floor
GPU utilization where the shadow price starts rising 60% routing.shadow_knee
How full batch work may fill a GPU up to the knee: 60% of max_concurrency × replicas, less live requests and other workers' batch requests; none once live load reaches the knee, and none on a deployment without max_concurrency routing.shadow_knee; batches.gpu.enabled
vLLM priority of batch work on GPUs 20 (free upgrades 10, live traffic 0; lower runs first) batches.gpu.priority
When batch work waiting for a GPU goes to a provider's batch API 12 hours after the batch was made, at once if the deployment stops or drains, or after the GPU fails a request twice batches.gpu.handoff_hours
How long the previous batch key is read after a rotation the retention period plus 2 days (9) batches.key_grace_days
Tries per request (failovers, bigger-window moves, refusal retries) 3 routing.max_attempts
Room a model needs for auto prompt + the client's max_tokens ≤ 95% of its context window, the prompt in that model's tokens (estimated by content, corrected by its replies; counting tokens); over 85% is noted in the routing reason models.*.context_window (from the price catalog); 95% fixed
Correcting token estimates per model from every reply's reported prompt size: a 20,000-token prompt is a full sample, none under 500; samples outside 0.4–2.5× ignored, capped at ±25% after 3 full samples; saved every minute fixed
Level rules coding 3 (any tools), simple wording 2, hard wording +1 a sign (up to 2), the hardest wording 5, a correction +1 (tool count only with agent_by_tools); general 2, short question 1 (< 400 tokens), analysis 3 routing.levels
Levels for Claude Code side requests and compaction summaries at most 1 and 3 routing.request_class_levels
Reasoning effort for auto by floor 1–2: low, 3: medium, 4–5: high routing.effort_by_floor
Output allowed when a request doesn't set max_tokens The model's maximum (max_output_tokens), less what won't fit in the context window or under max_request_usd models.*.max_output_tokens (from the price catalog); default_max_tokens (16,000) only where the maximum isn't known
Streaming from the provider for a non-streaming request When its output limit is over 21,333 tokens (or unset), so a long reply can't hit an idle-connection timeout fixed
How long a backend keeps a session's cache warm What the request's last cache marker asked for (300 s, or 3600 s for the gateway's markers on the shipped Claude backends from a session's second turn); else the backend's cache_ttl_seconds (300 s by default); on a GPU, until its KV events or KV-cache metrics say it's evicted (the TTL only without either) backends.*.cache_ttl_seconds
Sending a session back to the GPU replica that holds its cache on, where replicas can be addressed serve.replica_affinity, serve.static_urls
Following vLLM's KV events off (port 5557) serve.kv_events, serve.kv_events_port
A session counts as warm on a replica at least half its prefix still cached there fixed
Skipping a GPU replica the gateway can't connect to 60 s fixed
Skipping a failing backend or model See When a backend fails fixed; Retry-After from the provider
Waiting for a stream to start 120 s for APIs; none for self-hosted unless set backends.*.first_byte_timeout_seconds
Demand before starting GPUs, and below break-even before draining 10 min serve.scale_up_after_minutes
Minimum time warm before draining 30 min serve.hold_minutes
Draining time 15 min serve.drain_minutes
Provisioning timeout 45 min (then 30 min cooldown) serve.provision_timeout_minutes
Break-even margin 20% serve.margin
Cold start a new replica must pay back over hold_minutes (paid, not serving) the average of the deployment's last 10 starts; 12 min before one is measured; 0 for static serve.cold_start_minutes
Target load per replica 70% serve.target_utilization
Replicas 0–4 serve.min_replicas, max_replicas
Requests one replica runs at once (live saturation) not set (64 on the shipped GPU backends) backends.*.max_concurrency
Requests allowed to wait per replica when a saturated GPU is the only route 32 backends.*.max_waiting
Gateways share in-flight counts every 2 s fixed
Controller cycle 60 s (wakes early on admin changes) meritorder controller --interval
Gateways pick up GPU state and config ≤ 5 s fixed
Budget alerts 80%, 100% safeguards.alert_at (org, GPU); fixed for teams and people
Spend spike alert an hour at 5× the person's hourly average over the past week, and at least $5 fixed
Where the console's "Source" link and GET /about point (the AGPL's offer of the source to people using the gateway) https://github.com/therick/meritorder console.source_url (MERITORDER_SOURCE_URL in the shipped config)
11

Evals: measuring model quality

auto routing sends each request to the cheapest model good enough for it. "Good enough" comes from each model's quality scores: 1–5 per task type (coding, general). The classifier gives every request a floor from its work (coding:3 for ordinary coding, 2 for tests, renames and docstrings, +1 for hard wording, 5 for the hardest such as system design; tools make it coding but never set the level; never from its length), and only models scoring at least that are considered. Scores that are too high send hard work to models that can't do it; scores that are too low waste money.

Scores come from one of three sources, set by quality.source. A model's quality_override wins over all of them. Your own eval runs feed the config source or the override, never the published scores.

What's tested. The runner, the grading of each task kind, the sandbox, retries, the cost estimate and cap, scoring, and applying scores are tested in CI against mock gateways and canned replies (tests/test_evals*.py, tests/test_eval_harness.py, tests/test_codebase_suite.py, tests/evals/). Measured scores on real models are not yet a verified result: docs/README.md lists them under what still needs live accounts. The run figures quoted below (pass counts, costs) come from runs made by hand during development.

Quality scores from published benchmarks

By default the scores come from benchmarks run the same way for every model, not from this gateway's own runs: a handful of tasks can't separate the strongest models, and published suites can. The worker refreshes them every quality.refresh_hours (24) and the Models page shows, for each score, where it came from and how it was worked out.

quality:
  source: epoch          # epoch | artificial_analysis | config
  scale: absolute        # absolute | best | range
  anchor: {coding: 0.6994, general: 0.7685}   # absolute: the chance on the reference that scores 5
  reference: {coding: FrontierSWE, general: FrontierSWE}
  evidence: {coding: [FrontierSWE, FrontierCode]}
  fallback: {coding: [Terminal Bench, GSO-Bench, MirrorCode]}
  • epoch (default, no key): Epoch AI's benchmarking data, CC BY 4.0. Epoch places every model on one ability scale (its Capabilities Index, fitted across about 40 benchmarks) and every benchmark on the same scale by difficulty, so a model's chance of solving a benchmark's tasks follows from the two. A model's score for a task type is its chance of solving a task as hard as the reference benchmark (FrontierSWE: for coding, Claude Fable 5.2 solves about 70%, Haiku 5.5 about 44%). For coding, a model's own results on the evidence benchmarks (FrontierSWE, FrontierCode) set its ability where they exist, so coding strength counts, not just general ability; results at the effort auto uses for hard work are preferred. A score estimated from general ability alone is marked with a * on the Models page. A model with neither those results nor an index (some open models) gets its ability from the fallback benchmarks, older coding suites (Terminal Bench, GSO, MirrorCode). They come last because, checked against the 16 models that have both kinds of results, they predict FrontierSWE and FrontierCode results less well than the index does (they miss by about 2.6 points on the ability scale, the index by 2.2), and averaging the two gains about 0.1. WeirdML v3 isn't usable from its file: the index is fitted on a rescaled score the file doesn't carry.
  • artificial_analysis: the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index (a free key in ARTIFICIAL_ANALYSIS_API_KEY), for every task type: it no longer publishes a coding index.
  • config: the scores written on each model, for example applied from your own eval runs.

The scale turns chances into 1–5 with one decimal. absolute (default): a 5 is a fixed chance, the anchor (quality.anchor: 0.6994 for coding and 0.7685 for general, what Claude Fable 5.2 solved on 12 November 2026), and every other model scores in proportion, at most 5; a new model, however strong, changes nobody else's score (decision 58). best: the best model scores 5 and every other in proportion to how much it solves, so one that solves 60% as much scores 3, and a stronger new model lowers everyone else's. range: the weakest model with data scores 1 and the best 5. Scores never go below 1, so any model can take level-1 work.

A harder reference spreads models further apart, which sends more work to the top models: against Remote Labor Index, which Fable solves about 37% of the time, Opus 5.5 would score 2.8 for general work, and ordinary level-3 work would go only to Fable. FrontierSWE keeps level 3 within reach of models like Sonnet while still reserving level-5 work for the best.

A model the source doesn't cover isn't picked by auto for that task type (its score shows as "–" on the Models page): a score nobody measured would otherwise compete with measured ones, and since the cheapest eligible model wins, an optimistic guess would win. Requests that name the model still work, and quality_override: {coding: 4.5} puts it back in, winning over everything else too, for when your own evals show a model does better or worse on your work than published benchmarks suggest.

Models are matched to names in the data in this order: benchmark_name if set, then their route ids (without provider prefixes such as anthropic/), their Hugging Face repository name (hf_id: Epoch names some open models that way, such as Qwen3-Coder-480B-A35B-Instruct), and aliases that aren't patterns. The first that matches is used. For a model whose name in the data matches none of the others, set benchmark_name: "Claude Opus 5.5". Until a source has been fetched at all, the scores written on each model stand.

Offline vs live

Evals measure models. Routing is measured separately, in two places, and neither spends anything:

Offline: the routing simulator Live: the outcome report
What it answers Which strategy costs least per finished task, and fails how often, on a known population Whether each level is right for your work
Where the work comes from Simulated tasks with a known difficulty, calibrated to Epoch's FrontierSWE and SWE-bench Verified results (03) Your own task starts, a few explored a level down or up
What a model's success is Drawn from its published ability against the task's difficulty Outcome signals: tests failing, corrections, resends, raised floors
What runs for real The router, classifier, learned-router path, outcomes.py and the pricing code Everything
Cost None: no model is called Only the explored task starts' differences
When Before a change merges (CI), or by hand All the time, once a team explores
Command uv run python scripts/routing_sim.py run Reports → Levels, GET /v1/reports/levels/outcomes

An eval run is how a model's score changes; the simulator then says what that score does to routing, and the outcome report whether real work agrees. The simulator's replay mode joins the two: it reads explored task starts exported from the gateway and scores other level policies on them, weighted by each arm's chance, without running them (routing_sim.py replay, 03).

The regression check. CI runs scripts/routing_sim.py check: the default strategy (auto as the shipped configuration routes it) and the threshold on the same 1,000 standard tasks (seed 7), with the prices and scores frozen in tests/fixtures/routing_eval_prices.json. It fails when the total per finished task, counting failed attempts (model spend plus failed attempts times a $15 price per failed attempt; a failed attempt costs someone time: noticing it, asking again, waiting, cleaning up, and that price is an assumption you can change), is more than 5% above the stored baseline (tests/fixtures/routing_eval_baseline.json), when the success rate is more than 2 points below it, or when any task class with at least 20 tasks in the check spends more than 10% above the threshold per finished task (model spend only; decision 67), so the default can't drift back to buying strong models for easy work. The baseline file keeps both strategies' numbers per class. The same comparison runs in tests/test_routing_eval.py. Frozen prices keep a price refresh from failing someone else's change; only code and the shipped configuration move the result.

To accept a change on purpose (a new default that costs more but fails less, a new strategy), run uv run python scripts/routing_sim.py check --update, commit the new baseline with the change, and say in the pull request why the numbers moved. To move the prices and scores the check uses, copy config/prices.json over the fixture and update the baseline in the same commit.

Running one

Only admins start, cancel and apply runs. A run goes through these steps, whether the console or the CLI starts it:

A run's status moves like this. Cancelling a queued run ends it at once; cancelling a running one lets the tasks under way finish.

From the console: Models → Evals → Run an eval…. Pick models and suites (starter,frontier unless you change it), read the estimated cost and its warning, set the spending cap (1.5 times the estimate unless you change it), confirm you understand the cost, and start it (see Cost). The worker runs queued runs one at a time, in the background, against the gateway like any client. Progress, cost, and every task's result show on the page. When a run finishes, Apply scores… shows what would change and writes the measured scores into the configuration as a new version, which you can roll back from Config → History. Applying needs Postgres, where configuration versions live. Choose how they're written:

  • Write as quality (the default): each model's quality, which routing uses only with quality.source: config (or before a benchmark source has ever been fetched). Under a benchmark source, routing keeps using the published scores, and the dialog says so. It also writes quality.measured_best_rate, the best measured model's pass rate on hard tasks for each task type: what a measured 5 means. That's what lets routing by cost per success turn measured scores into chances of success (10, How it decides); without it, the threshold decides.
  • Write as override: each model's quality_override, which wins over every source, so routing uses it within seconds. Use it when your own results show a model does better or worse on your work than the benchmarks suggest; remove it in Config → Models to go back.

Run again… starts a new run with the same models, suites, repeat count and task filter. The estimate and the cap are worked out again.

From the command line (on a machine with Docker, so code tasks run too). It needs an admin key (--key, MERITORDER_API_KEY, or the key meritorder login saved) and the gateway's address (--gateway, MERITORDER_URL, the saved one, else http://localhost:8080):

uv run meritorder eval --models claude-sonnet,claude-opus,claude-fable          # shows the estimate and cap, asks first
uv run meritorder eval --models ... --only 'c5-*,a5-*' --repeat 3               # just the level-5 code and agent tasks, 3 times each
uv run meritorder eval --models ... --apply                                      # also write the scores into the config
